Review Text: This is an impressive sparkling, under the BdB banner, but it feels like it delivers much more weight if one had in mind some BdB styles out there to compare that command more of a light/chalky/citrus frame. This wine has a ripe bouquet, verging on some light tropical notes. There’s lemon curd, yellow apple, mango swirl, peanut brittle. But also a refreshing lift of brine and preserved lemon. Then, a hit of sweetness in the middle with a pithy, chewy finish of a lime sorbet. It has fine mousse, silky texture and no shortage of flavour. It’s quite intense, both on the nose and on the palate and thus admirable in that sense. I was a bit overwhelmed at first, but rewarding the bold style and intensity here. If you know J&S Fielke still Chardonnays, you will recognise the style under the bubbles. Definitely one to try.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: KT + Peglidis: Celebrating 20 Years – The Peglidis Vineyard Watervale Riesling Collection 2007-2026
Review Text:
This tasting was a deep dive into a great story of a vineyard farmed by passionate humans, Bunny and Ivonne Peglidis, since 1970. They are now 93 and 85 years old and not even thinking of putting down the secateurs. Since 2006, Kerri Thompson has been creating compelling wines from these now 56-year-old Riesling vines. Gary and I tasted the wines and their evolution over 20 years.

More preamble, ie a couple of remarks. No matter how you look at it, the wines across the board showed great quality. I have given plenty of 93-95s. Felt a bit boring, but this mirrored, for me, the overall great consistency in quality coming from this vineyard and the winery. Yes, there are better and worse vintages, but no crazy dramatic dips or misses; rather, a diversity, a vintage variation reflected in the wine’s profile. All are individual wines telling different stories, but with a common thread of complexity and texture.

Preamble 2: It’s great to taste a line-up like this. Normal thing to taste at pace at an event; first quick impressions are good, but I can imagine looking at these wines with time in the glass and over a few days, again and again, and those scores would potentially shift by 1-2 up or down, but that’s really the spread.

[Vintage notes from KT]
[All wines marked as 12%, only 2007 marked as 12,5%]

2007 12,5%
Mid-January rainfall provided relief from a warm, dry season, producing concentrated fruit & generous flavour.

KS: Deep golden colour. Lemon slice and a milk lolly quality. Development in full swing, but the acidity, albeit soft, feels very fresh. Beeswax, honey cake, even a note of cold brew coffee, herbs and more wax, preserved lemon in brine. Moving into smoky, peaty-almost notes. The apogee of what you’d like to taste in an aged Riesling; maybe it’s an indulgence just for a glass but a sensory treat. 94 points, drink now
GW: Rich, honey, Bickfords lime, toast, mint, even some spice. It’s a richer style showing plenty of development but it still has a fresh line of juicy acidity through it and finishes well.  A bit of lime marmalade too. Lovely wine. Still has some cellaring potential but likely at peak now. 94 points

2008
Defined by early, compressed ripening and a dramatic late-season heatwave.

KS: Some development here, but lots of freshness too. Wet slate, a vegetal, earthy edge, very savoury profile, led by citrus, maybe a hint of green papaya skin and orange pith. Super zingy, slate-y acidity to close. A curious disparity between this and 2007, only a year difference, but more lush development in 2007. Both tasty. 93 points
GW: Quite a tangy expression, a bit jangly, some hay-like character through lemon drops and lime. Sort of nutty with a citrus zest finish of good length. A little bit chalky in texture. Not quite the length but interesting and no hurry. 91 points

2009
Cooler conditions delivered elegance, tension and natural acidity.

KS: Flint and sweet citrus, oregano, dusty hay, wild peach. Lemon blossom, chalky palate that grips upfront. Crunchy green apple and jasmine, delicate and pure but impactful. Impressive and so fresh still. 95+ points
GW: Juicy but has tight acidity, lemon lime, a bit richer sort of a halfway house between 2007 and 2008. It’s a little spicy and dusty. A sherbet tang and a bit of grip on a finish of excellent length. Impressive. Has a bit of a burst to it. 95 points

2010
Generally even ripening conditions created wines of balance, freshness and longevity.

KS: Waxy citrus skins, crushed slate, mango skin, almond blossom, then smoked almond perhaps and candle wax. Acidity is cool and calm, but a bit broader than 2009, with a pink grapefruit finish. Just feels a little hollow in the middle, but it’s a good wine. 93 points
GW: Sits a little flatter and rounder in the palate, a light chalky feel, old orange flavours, some lime, with a nutty finish of solid length. Good drink. Very ready. 91-92 points

2011
One of the coolest and wettest vintages on record, with only one in three bunches ultimately picked.

KS: Sweet tones, with a ripe durian edge, and a vegetal sweetness, grapefruit and cucumber. It opens up with air into lemon lolly, frangipani perfume, and feels a touch musky. It has a deep flavour midway, just a bit less tension in that line than in some previous wines. 94 points
GW: A more apricot and cumquat character here, kind of exotic but I like the Germanic feel and some hessian complexity, and it drinks really well, but the point of difference is a really good thing. Like it. Tasty. 93ish points

2012
Benchmark Clare Valley mild conditions produced wines of purity and expression.

KS: Milk lolly creamy quality, lemon curd, creamed honey. Palate is broad in a way but spread evenly, with plenty of flavour, mostly light and flinty-salty on the palate. A bit warmer in the aftertaste, but it has something interesting going on, lightness but impact too. 94 points
GW: Ansieed riding very high, caraway, ripe lime with an exotic touch. Its very juicy and flavoursome, covers the mouth with flavour but in a gentle way, finishes limey and long. A superb wine,. Pleasure zone now nut no hurry. 95 -96 points

2013
Warm conditions delivered flavour intensity and early appeal.

KS: Green orange, smoked lemon, sage, fleshy citrus, pithy, a bit nervy flow, energetic. Some more papaya at play, with a salty finish. Brisk wine. 93 points
GW: Cut fennel, fresh mango, lime, a floral note. It has quite a bit of chalky powdery grip, a core of cool acidity, and impeccable length. This is so delicious with texture a bit of a highlight. A zesty tang on exit. Great. Love this. 95 points

2014
Warm, dry conditions followed by relieving mid-February rains and cool nights made for excellent fruit concentration.

KS: Rather quiet, restrained start, mostly citrus-led, developing into blossoms, gentle flow, lemon flower, almonds, savoury flinty nuance, lime sorbet vibes, with a very smooth, silky palate. Pretty wine. 94 points
GW: A slight petrol note, not a thing but the first time noted in the wine. A bit of hessian, fresh pineapple and lime, a light grip, with a rounder more waxy finish. 91-92 points

2015
Dry conditions produced wines of depth and structure.

KS: A bit musky perfume, sugar almond, parsley root, cool flow of flavour. Green fennel, pickle brine, salty and sweet-sour in a good way, à la green mango. No huge tension here, relaxed in style. 94 points
GW: Fennel, a little tropical, ripe lime, floral. It’s fresh, has some grip, a fleshy feel, almost a glycerol touch, with a spicy finish of good length. Very nice. 94 points

2016
Balanced growing conditions delivered exceptional varietal expression and purity.

KS: Apples, peaches and hot rocks, flint, lift and tension on the nose, very linear, bolt of lightning acidity, very pure citrus, slice of lemon on tongue, bitter lime finish. Very much wet slate texture. Pure and racy. 95 points
GW: Caraway, spice, lime, some floral things. It’s dry, a bit tangy, with a quite tight acidity, lime pith on a finish of good length. More to come. 93-94+ points

2017
Cool conditions favoured finesse, tension and longevity.

KS: Fresh start, green mango, lemon curd, golden kiwi, crushed slate. Raw nuts and herbs, smoky element. Very vivid and crunchy, slippery and youthful for its age. Pure and lifted. Has a lot of potential energy. 95+ points
GW: A bit of perfume here, lemon barley, lemon zest, leaf and mint, a little spice, a smoky touch. Lighter style, almost peppery, citrus, a kiss of sweetness rounds out a charming and different vintage for this wine. 94 points

2018
Warm, dry, low-yielding season delivered width, generosity and early appeal.

KS: It feels heavier than 2018, richer; mango, orange, hint of apricot stone, herbed honey, acidity is ripe but has a salty finish for a good balance, just a bit shallow here and there but it’s still a good wine. 92 points
GW: A more tangy lime zest and lemon affair, peanut butter, white flower. Acidity is a bit bitey but it does have intensity, and a lemon biscuit finish of good length. 92 points

2019
Dry conditions and smaller crops produced intense fruit concentration.

KS: Very concentrated from sniff to sip. Honey cake, lemon tart, apple tart, add a baked lemon. Seems very ripe/baked, but it’s of a style, and the palate has a huge concentration of acidity and comes with a big swoosh. There’s so much mid-palate weight here. Stony texture with wet chalk finish. This reminds me of a Germanic late harvest European style. Even though it’s delicious, it may feel at its capacity of development, so perhaps drink now/soon. 96 points
GW: This has the fruit volume turned up. Green mango, lime, spice, lime leaf. It’s intense and tight in the mouth, a chalky grip, almost a lime pickle intensity on a finish of excellent length. Very good. Could do with a bit more time as some rugged character to it, but good makings. Very good. 95 points

2020
Difficult season marked by drought conditions and exceptionally small crops.

KS: Quite concentrated at first, mirabelle plum, golden mango, softer and sweeter than 2019, also broader, and a bit loose and with a bitter lime in the back end. A tad clunky (tough gig when measured against its vintage peers). 92 points
GW: A fleshy wine, sits a bit flat, ripe lime, a light grip to texture, a rounder style with less energy than some but it’s still a nice drink. 89-90 points

2021
Near-perfect growing conditions produced wines of elegance, detail and remarkable balance.

KS: Smoked fruit, water on hot rocks, slate and salt, jasmine and lemongrass. Beautiful fabric of acidity, tight but so smooth, flowing with ease. Firm peach, peach blossom, green apple, and that note petrichor tone – the wet slate thing following through. Eyewatering acidity will allow it to age. 95+ points
GW: Perfumed, lemon/lime, a bit stony. It’s tight, very chalky, lots of lemon like, a good bite to it, with very good length. Good energy. Excellent. 95 points

2022
Cool, dry weather through summer and into autumn provided favourable ripening conditions, producing fruit with good natural acid levels and varietal flavour.

KS: Green mango skin, lemon lolly, lime cake and a flinty tension. Great acidity, very high, tickled my nose, watered my mouth. Nervy tension with salt. Good one. 94+ points
GW: Quite perfumed, vanilla bean and white flowers, white peach and lime, Japanese ginger. A more juicy experience, a lightness to it, and spice, with a light chalky grip and a grin and tonic finish of good length. Nice. 94 points

2023
Cool conditions encouraged purity and aromatic lift.

KS: Something nutty, musky up first, dusty/compact powder note, a bit of ripe tropical skin like durian; then more sweet citrus, mandarin, pomelo, sweet and briny-pickly flavours. The texture is pithy and phenolic, with bitter-sweet citrus peaking up in the finish. Peculiar but good. 95 points
GW: Green banana, lemon barley, lime, dried herb and lime leaf. It’s grainy, has a grapefruit tang to acidity, a good burst of flavour with a limey finish of very good length, again some quinine bite. Like it. 94 points

2024
Balanced season produced wines of brightness and energy.

KS: Love the perfume, fennel in brine, quite herbal wine, with raw almond and pear; it’s a bit closed at first, but gives a really beautiful pure fruity flow. The finish is pleasantly bitter and with salt over lemon. It has an X factor; can’t name it, that’s what the X factor is… 95+ points
GW: A softer and finer style, lemon and lime, a powdery feel to texture, some lime juiciness, with a zesty finish of good length. Very nice. In evolution, of course. 94+ points

2025
Dry conditions delivered smaller crops with flavour concentration and drive.

KS: Bright yellow in the glass. It smells like lemons, lemon sorbet, yellow apples, peach. It’s a very pretty wine, plenty of concentration. Stony texture, salty, and a bit chewy. 95+ points
GW: Lime, lemon, stony, a bit of of a mint and leaf perfume. It’s tangy, some tonic water, a chalky thing, quite some energy, a zesty and slightly rugged finish, but a wine of excellent character and intensity. 94+ points

2026
A complex season with significantly diverse weather patterns. A cool Spring then warm, dry Summer, followed by late season harvest rain.

KS: Very fresh and estery and yeasty, a bit lychee and kiwi and grape juice, with ginger spice. Super fresh aromatics, mint and blossoms. It’s a bit hard to see now, steaming cake straight from the oven; let it cool, give it time. Has the bones. 94+ points
GW: Highly perfumed, green ginger, fresh lime and lemon. It’s fresh, on the cusp of ripeness, but has a certain sort of energy, with a light herbal tang, a salted lime finish of good length. I like it. 94+ points.

This is a new one for J&S Fielke, and it’s only fair to make a quick note on how it stacks up against the Lenswood Chardonnay 2025. Things come in abundance in this wine but with certain grace and purity. Red apples, almonds, firm nectarines and oats. It has intensity and concentration but with a tight line of acidity, and a notion of coolness in the fruit profile. Beyond this, there’s a note of shortbread, a whiff of white chocolate and flint, with plenty of balancing bitter citrus. The texture is smooth, peach yoghurt-like, with a tingling ginger spice in the long finish. Elegant, lifted and fine. Another steal.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Almost every day, before or after I taste wines, or just before or after I post the reviews, I run a conversation in my head about the objectivity of things and the silliness of the work that I do, but in fact love doing. It’s a dialogue, perhaps; I take into account all the arguments about tasting wines blind, to remove any bias, but then actually how to tell the story if it’s all blind, because isn’t the context the most important thing about wine? The people, the place, the motive? Anyway, I think I just wanted it to be known that I go through this every single time: the duality of things, the existential crisis of a tortured wine taster trapped in a material world trying to communicate the spiritual (don’t pity me, it’s a cool job). So, about this wine, I pondered on it, in the ‘biased context’ over two days. I actually do that with many of the wines that I taste: give them time, give them air, second chance, trying to understand the background and what the artist wanted to communicate… Rant over.

Day 1: First up, a whack of black olive tapenade; there’s definitely a vibration of green olive here too, leafy-stemmy notes (fully destemmed wine) and a woody bitterness. It has some compelling perfume that changes and improves with air exposure and time, but it’s quite a sour-savoury expression, perhaps a bit lean and feels ‘bunchy’, although it’s not. I’m baffled. 89 points

Day 2: Given a second day chance, as it was bothering me. Still peculiar. Lots of savoury, slightly vegetal tones, wet forest, moss on stones, fresh woody spice, pine needle resin, dark amaro bitterness; this can be a difficult wine, edgy, moody, quinine-driven. But now, it’s intriguing, compelling. Has a character and made me stop; this must count for something in the AI era. Maybe needed time. Who doesn’t. 92 points

Review Text:
Just noticed, Mount Henry’s climbing up the premium price tag ladder. In this rhythm, next year it will be double its 2021/23 price. Shiraz in Pinot disguise. Seemingly light and delicate, but it has depth and concentration. Beautiful, vibrant colour and perfume. Sweet forest berries, raspberries, some blue, some black too. Aromas are bright, with light shining through, but flavours are dark, deep and spicy. It’s a sunny day in a damp forest. There’s wet bark, rose potpourri here, cherry wood, mint tea, black liquorice, and a medicinal edge to it all, with a bit of iron-like aftertaste. I feel the detail is coming in with time, with air. Let it be in the glass, give it time and say what you will, these two can go together very well, the Shiraz and the Pinot Noir.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Yangarra High Sands Grenache: Celebrating 15 Vintages (2010-2024) [Nov25]
Review Text:
I have no words except the ones I wrote a few days ago. Peter’s voice is still saved in my phone’s recordings file. I transcribed some of it. I wasn’t sure whether to post this or not, but perhaps my reflections from this very special tasting can serve as a tribute. It was a true privilege to taste with Peter this very last time. Here’s what I wrote and was about to post this morning.

My dad used to collect rocks and had (still has) a pretty amazing knowledge of minerals and precious stones. We often ventured to the Sudeten Mountains in the Lower Silesian district of Poland to dig in the white mud, the kaolin clay. Such fun! We’d find different types of quartz, agate, chrysoprase, tourmaline, pyrite… As a teenager, I remember browsing through the miniature rock collection at home and memorising the astral-sounding names. Little did I know that one day I’d be collecting rocks in a liquid form, or at least, what I’d like to think is a liquid interpretation of the terroir. Such fun!

What I tasted at the Celebration of 15 Vintages of Yangarra’s High Sands Grenache was a true collection of gems. Some shining bright, some a bit more rough and perhaps fading, but all equally precious. It was very interesting to see the vintage variation in the glass, but also clear to note that the soil sets the foundation, literally and metaphorically, for the high quality—seen across the board. It’s important to know that High Sands vineyard is not simply white sand dunes. As Peter Fraser explained, “The [High Sands] vineyard sits in the Maslin sands geology, which is not to be confused with sand [per se]. That references the red ironstone, which lies beneath those vineyards. You’re going to go on the hill and see that red ironstone, and you’ll see it in various pockets where it’s at the surface. Highly ferrous, got that real red colour, and often you’ll see those little sand grain kind of characters. Above that sits the clay layer, which is orangey red because of the ferrous nature of the bedrock that influences that clay. So the water passing across it basically releases all of that mineral. And then in these various pockets, there aren’t that many of the Grenache vineyards that are actually really white sands.”

Among the 15 vintages, Peter identified four distinct seasons and weather patterns, indicating a variety of corresponding styles. The vintage groupings were presented as follows.

Cold and wet vintages
2011 cold and wet
2017 just cold
2020 odd one because it was a lower crop from a hot spring but then it was cold
2022 another odd one, cold vintage with a heat spike (looks warm but has tightness, hence held back)
2023 was very cold, maybe the coldest ever, with a low crop

Mild, classical vintages
2010, 2012, 2013, 2016, 2021 was cooler of the mild ones

Warm with low crop vintages
2015, 2019, 2025 perhaps

Hot vintages with a generous crop
As Peter described, “[…] they tend to have that lush, much juicier kind of palate, but also can be still really fragrant and look a bit lighter because of that slightly elevated crop.”
2014, 2018, 2024

2010
The colour is intact, very vibrant, deep ruby with just a light brick hue at the very rim. Tertiary development in full force in the form of soft, aromatic leather, roasted coffee bean, rose potpourri, and roasted sage leaf. It shows concentration and density on the palate, remnants of cherry-scented oak. Tannins are rocky, dark, dusty, fine pumice stone, more of an iodine/sage extract in the finish and a ripe, mature pomegranate juice acidity line. This is to drink now, but in great shape. 95 points

2011
Feels a bit muted/subdued on the nose. This has a lighter, more ethereal and translucent profile than the 2010. The wine has a very clear acidic tension, which is the first thing that hits the palate. It’s tight and lean, skeletal a bit in a way, and hence, oddly, doesn’t really show its age. It does come across a bit anemic and fading. There’s a cherry menthol lolly here, some red fruit. Nothing wrong with it, good for a glass or a couple of sips. It crossed my mind that it may be a sleeper, but it didn’t show lots of energy per se. This is probably the weakest link in the whole lineup. 89 points

2012
Again, a darker appearance than the previous vintage, deep ruby core. And as expected, it smells of dark fruit, mulberry and black cherry, black raspberry, elegant oak, cedar and dark chocolate, with cherry smoke. Plenty of flavour, juicy, meaty, chewy tannins. This is a big boi. Smoked plum and plenty of spice in the finish, it’s all dark and fibrous, charry in a good way. Start drinking now. 95 points

2013
This also shows great concentration and density on the eye and the nose, roasted coffee bean, a hint of Bonox, very ripe, drying fruit, and cherry pip. Big flavour, juicy, sweet-sour, cherry cinnamon and cola root, black liquorice, it’s almost black current themed. With a heap of fine puckering tannins borrowed from the Nebbiolo department. It feels like this still has room to develop. 96 points

2014
Ripe perfume, but with lifted strawberry and red cherry. Very fine stony tannins, dark slate to feel, and a pomegranate finish. Juicy and translucent on the palate, seemingly light, but in fact, it has a great presence and packs a punch. Plenty of liquorice, red and black, with exotic spice, musk. Very admirable. And long. Solid. 96 points

2015
Aromatic summer berries, mulberry, and boysenberry. There’s ripeness here and great concentration, really running deep. The acid line is ripe but long and built around wet chalky, fine clay texture. Peppery spice builds up in the aftertaste. This impresses and satisfies. 95 points

2016
This has a blueish/bruised hue. And what comes on the nose is bloody, cool, fresh, meaty, with the perfume of violets and salty black liquorice. The palate is velvety too, with blue damson plum, mulberry, cool acidity, something like a tobacco leaf too and bitter cold brew in the finish, chewy alpine herbs. Delightful. 96 points

2017
A bit lighter in appearance than its predecessors. Very pretty, floral, with almond and orange blossom lift, tarragon and roses, very fine detail in the perfume, wild strawberry, blueberry. Fine, lacy web of tannins. Super lovely wine, but it seems a little less concentrated than 2016. It’s just a bit more fruity and easier on the palate with a leaner tannin muscle. Drinking very well now (for Pinot drinkers). 94 points

2018
Pure deep ruby colour, violet rim. Cool perfume, raspberry, mulberry, roses. Some exotic spice in the mix, too, cinnamon, star anise. The flavour is very energetic, great balance of acid and tannin. Drinking with ease, very approachable. It delivers the concentrations upfront, but then the flavour splashes out and disappears a bit early. Delivers a great first impression, even if slightly more watery in the back end. Juicy, fruity, chewy. Drink now. 94 points

2019
Very red fruited to start with. Juicy, well-balanced, not overly tense or tannic, a bit loose to the finish, but delivers a very pleasing combo of sweet fruit, spice, chewiness, red liquorice. Tannins linger, but the flavour dissipates a bit on the way. 93 points

2020
The perfume is serious; none of that tutti-frutti. It’s all savoury, potpourri, meat, dried blood, bitter herbs, spice. Very concentrated and long, spicy, dense, velvety texture, it has a ripe sweet-salty core, very much black liquorice, amaretti biscuits, glossy cherry, but it’s savoury-bitter on the outside with wet clay tannins, and chewy spice. Powerful, delicious. Great wine. 97 points

2021
Deep ruby, purple reflections. Tense, lifted, cool nose, full of blue fruit perfume and a ripe red fruit base, a note of alpine amaro, violet, orange peel, blood orange bitter-sweet acidity. This is a beautiful drink, all classy, fine, pretty, high tones, great acid, long finish. 97 points

2022
Wow, what a vibrant, ruby colour, with a purple hue and hot pink edge. Almost the same is the perfume, vibrant, electric. Acidity is through the roof, carrying fine, squeaky tannin; the palate is like chewing on the bitter-sweet-sour skins of red plums and blackberries. Powerful with acidity as a highlight for sure will allow it to live long. 96+ points

2023
Jasmine green tea perfume. Lovely. Roses and violets, red fruit, red apple skin. It feels more Pinot-esque in a way. Approachable tannin profile, juicy, fruity, very pretty. For Pinot drinkers. Acidity is very perky, frisky, white chalk-like, lots of finesse here, fine detail, prettiness. 95 points

I scored it 96-97 on previous (early) tastings; this time around landed on 95, but probably somewhere between that and 96.

2024
This wine has 10% whole bunch. Beautiful translucent violet colour. Freshly picked strawberries with the tops on. Perfumed, orange blossom, almond blossom, wet tobacco leaf, or wet green tea leaf, jasmine. A bit of bresaola, green peppercorn. The palate is like hibiscus tea, or stewed rhubarb, that light red fruit brew, peppery spice, crushed bitter herbs, chalky palate. This is a good wine with an aromatic green edge, so if you’re not fond of it in wine, you may not love it. It has fine detail but is a bit loose in the back end. Very Pinot-esque, super pretty. However, it’s still early days. Release in May 2026. 93+ points (for now)

 

Vale Peter

Review Text:
KS: Where are you from originally?

MH: From Healesville, in the Yarra Valley. I have a French mother, a Dutch father. He immigrated as a young man to Australia. He settled in Melbourne and got pushed off into farming. He travelled back to Europe a lot. Met my mother in the Swiss Alps, and the relationship very quickly blossomed. They got married and came back to Australia. I was born in Toolangi, and then we moved to Healesville. At 18, I needed to run away, and I ran away to hospitality and then skiing all over the world. 

KS: Do you remember when the wine bug bit you?

MH: Wine always was part of the family dinner. But I remember this particular job where I was in charge of the bar, and we had to go and get the bottles from the cellar. This was when I worked for a guy called Walter Bourke in Melbourne. He was an institution in Melbourne, and he had a wine bar called Walter’s Wine Bar. And it was then—on a Saturday night—I would have ten glasses lined up with Burgundy—and I just went:

Shit.
 Wow.
  Boom.

My mind exploded. Heightened emotions, it was just insane. So that really was that moment when I realised that I was looking at something transformational. Something impossible to grasp. Something that transcends just an alcoholic beverage. It’s more than that.

It talks of place.
 It talks of emotion.
  It talks about our culture.
   It talks about how we eat.
    It’s everything that we are.

And that was a huge moment. And then one day I just announced: I’m going to make wine.

KS: Just like that! Please tell me how it started and how you ended up at Yarra Yering.

MH: I wrote to everybody who was anybody. There was a book, the directory of Australian winemakers. I got it out, and I wrote to every single one of them. And I’ve got all their replies somewhere. I even wrote to some dead people, which was hilarious, when their children wrote back to me and said, “Thank you so much for your letter, your very interesting letter—oh, my mother’s dead—but thank you so much for your application, right at the moment we don’t have a position for you.”

(laughs)

And then I had a reply from a guy called Bailey Carrodus at Yarra Yering. He got the letter and he said, “Oh, it was interesting.” That was typical Bailey Carrodus. He was a very inquisitive man, and he questioned everything. He wanted to know everything. So he said, “Yeah, sure, you can get a job. You start at the bottom. You are just going to work in vineyards.” And that was in 1999, I’d landed at Yarra Yering. And then very quickly the relationship was built, and we formed a friendship. It turned into a ten-year apprenticeship—in the true sense of the term—the apprentice and his master, where you become an understudy. It was the grounding I needed to have, a place where I could focus my mind.

And Bailey was very strict.
 Mad on focus.
  And his wines were about focus.

KS: You worked there for 10 years. How did it evolve and end?

MH: By 2001, I had started to become much more involved in the winemaking. Fast forward to 2009, that was the changeover year—Paul Bridgeman joined—I was already leaving. Bailey had died in 2008. So that was the catalyst for me to think about where I was going to go. Yarra Yering was changing. And for personal reasons, I needed to go back to Europe. That was quite an emotional time leaving something as important as Yarra Yering.

KS: How did you find yourself in Burgundy?

MH: I had a friend in Burgundy whom I approached, and I said, “Look—I’d really like to start making some wine.” And he said, “Okay. That’s fine. In exchange, you help me through harvest.” And that was an amazing opportunity to be given a chance to have a space, make my wines, help him make his wines, and get exposed to Burgundy without being totally out of control, because I had that backing there. And that developed quickly. We started making the first 2009 Saint-Romain.

I wanted to make my wine.
Create my identity.

So 2009 was the first year I made wine. There are labellings of 2007 and 2008, which were pure négoce wine from finished ferments—I bought the barrels, blended, and created those first wines under my label. Then 2009, I started with Bourgogne Pinot Noir, Gevrey-Chambertin, Bonnes-Mares Grand Cru, and Clos de Bèze Grand Cru.

KS: That’s… not exactly starting small.

MH: (laughs) No—for someone just turning up in Burgundy and starting with five wines like that—that’s quite extraordinary. And it describes perfectly how different Burgundy was 15 years ago. The evolution of the micro-négoce hadn’t reached where it is now. Today, there’s a new one every day. Everyone’s trying to find a way in. So that was the beginning. And I developed a reputation very quickly, selling my wines in London to begin with. I had these contacts from Yarra Yering.

KS: Were you ever ostracised as an outsider in Burgundy?

MH: In the beginning, not so much, because I was unimportant, and hidden behind the person I worked with. But then Jancis Robinson found the wines. And went—

“Wow.”
 She gave me Wine of the Week for the 2010 vintage.
  And it blew up.
   Boom.

I was selling wines comfortably. We were expanding. So I started to look around to build my own winery. In 2016, I bought my first piece of land, not a vineyard, just land.

KS: How does one just buy land in Burgundy? How much money do you have to have? Or who do you need to know?

MH: What we need to separate in Burgundy are vineyards and practical facilities. The value is in the vineyard. So I found a piece of land for sale where I was allowed to build a shed and make wine in it—a winery. That was 2016. 2017 was the first vintage in my own place.

Around the same time, I also came across the first piece of vineyard land in the Mâcon. It was bare land, no vines, but classified as vineyard land, and no one wanted it, because it was a bit ugly and difficult to work on. So I bought two hectares and then, of course, I had to prepare the land, plant vines, install trellising. I bought the land in 2017 and planted it in 2018.

KS: And when was the first harvest?

MH: Well, it should have been 2021. But in 2021, we had a major frost. We lost a lot. A real kick in the backside. Very upsetting. However, I wasn’t entirely devastated because, also in 2020, I bought a small domaine in Gevrey-Chambertin, about two hectares.

KS: (laughs) As one does.

MH: (laughs) Yes. I was very lucky. I knew the people who owned the domaine. I had been buying fruit from them since 2009. So we had a long relationship, and we became very good friends. One day, they said, “We are finishing”. That was a shock. And then they said, “Would you like to buy the domaine?” And that was the beginning of a massive turn in my life. So from 2016 to 2020, I went from nothing to:

a winery,
 four hectares of vineyards,
  a domaine in Gevrey-Chambertin.
   It was huge for an Australian outsider.

KS: And yet—you weren’t ostracised.

MH: Clearly not, because the people I bought it from offered it to me. I worked at maintaining those relationships. Paying growers properly. Respecting their work. Showing up. Not being a dick. That stuff matters. You do create your own luck.

KS: Now, let’s chat about your vineyards and wines. First, tell me about your vineyard in Mâcon.

MH: In Mâcon, the vineyard is very steep, east-facing. It’s in the north of the Mâcon, so much closer to Burgundy proper—meaning cooler. I make a fresher style of Chardonnay—not the heavy, round style like some make in the lower parts of the Mâcon. My parameters are:

finesse,
 character,
  expression of place.

The wine is delicious—I’m not afraid of that word—delicious, juicy, friendly, something you want to drink.

KS: What’s your approach to Chardonnay then? How do you achieve the deliciousness?

MH: Chardonnay is a powerful grape. I want freshness and the natural opulence of it. I’m not interested in the reductive, super-salty, “matchstick” Chardonnay style. Those wines have no love in them. They’re difficult wines to discern place. I don’t want to hide from the power of Chardonnay. I want that power that’s balanced and precise. So I use minimal wood, often large, maybe 10–20% new. No heavy lees stirring. I don’t want winemaking tricks. I want the place.

KS: So tell me about Saint-Romain—what’s special about it?

MH: Saint-Romain is one of the first vineyards I started working with. I have such a good relationship with this grower—Nicolas Ruelle—that I put his name on the label. It’s unheard of amongst the négoce. These are very old vines. Saint-Romain is outside the big three—Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet, Chassagne-Montrachet—so it often gets overlooked. Which is insane, because the vineyards are stunning. You smell the wine—it has opulence—but then the palate snaps into freshness. That’s the contrast.

KS: You also make the Chassagne-Montrachet. What’s the approach there?

MH: For Chassagne, I don’t buy fruit—I take juice and swap it for my Gevrey-Chambertin grapes. It’s a small cuvée—five barrels—one new. Chassagne is not for today. This is a tomorrow wine. It opens slowly. It reveals itself over hours and over years. You see more tension, more line, more depth.

KS: And what about the Pernand-Vergelesses site?

MH: I’m really trying to champion Pernand because I think it’s an area of Burgundy that hasn’t had enough recognition, not enough love. Les Pins is the lieu-dit, and that comes from the very top of Pernand-Vergelesses. High—we’re at 350 meters, facing west with a pine forest behind. The vineyard is set on very deep white clay that overlays the limestone below. So all of these attributes create a very cold site—I call it a glacial Pinot Noir. Every vintage we need to wait. I’ll always pick that as the highest alcohol, generally 13–13.5%, but it doesn’t show heat. It’s an expression that I love—it’s so different to Gevrey. It has the green spectrum that I like with a little bit of spice, just to emphasise that savoury feel.

I want the sensuality, big time, involved.
 And I’m a bit of an acid junkie.

I love wines that have really clear acidity. I don’t want bubble gum—I want real precision. Pinot Noir for me has to have energy, needs to have that brilliant focus. Similarly to the whites, in the reds, I don’t want to focus on wood. It’s not a thing for me. I’m very conscious not to over-extract. I’m thinking about that more lifted, aromatic feel of Pinot Noir.

KS: Finally, tell me about Morey-Saint-Denis.

MH: This is a set of three vineyards that you find above the Grands Crus on the edge of Gevrey-Chambertin and Morey-Saint-Denis. So, Latricières-Chambertin, Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis. The three Premiers Crus up on the top are Monts Luisants, Les Genavrières, and at the end Les Chaffots. They’re a really spectacular set of vineyards, all grown on roche mère—mother rock. It’s basically the bedrock that was laid down under the sea hundreds of millions of years ago and pushed up with tectonic plate movements. It’s a very thin soil. It’s a very steep vineyard, exposed to the east. We have a lot of morning sun driving the vineyards to growth.

KS: You’ve spoken a lot about freshness and balance. How does climate change fit into that picture for you? Is it getting too warm for Pinot Noir in Burgundy?

MH: Burgundy is in a revolution at the moment. Right now, there are a lot of us who are really thinking about where the next step Burgundy takes in the next 50 years. We are at a critical point right now, for Pinot Noir especially. We must understand where we’re going. This is a big conversation. There are people in Burgundy who are absolutely committed to understanding how we’re going to keep making Pinot with greatness, great elegance, beauty—all these things that we love to talk about.

Now, we’re looking at raising our canopies, clone material, rootstocks, ground cover, pruning techniques, and foliage management. There is so much thinking on how we can manage our vineyards in the right way. Changing row orientations would mean uprooting vineyards, but we discuss it. A lot is being thought about.

It’s not the end of Pinot.
How about this—we’re in a golden era for Burgundy.

Look at what we’ve been doing in the last 10 years—the consistency of the wines. We just need to be vigilant with picking times and not rest on our laurels.

KS: If Pinot is doing fine, why did you plant Syrah then?

MH: I’m a shit-stirrer, and I want to challenge. I want to ask in my hypothesis, in my experiment: can we consistently ripen Shiraz every year? That’s my question.

KS: And can you?

MH: For the moment, yes. But what’s right? Is it 13%, 14%, or is it phenolic ripeness? I’m not interested in alcohol. The grapes all come in at around 11.5–12%, and they’re phenolically ripe. You wait and wait and wait, but the grapes just won’t get more sugar, but they turn out absolutely extraordinary. So vibrantly fresh, spicy, energetic, not massively tannic. These are still very young vines—they were planted in 2019, one year after the Chardonnay.

KS: So, will Syrah replace Pinot Noir in Burgundy one day?

MH: I’m not suggesting for a minute that this is to replace anything. All I’m suggesting—that maybe it will happen in certain areas that become uncomfortable for the Pinot. Cahier des charges is so strict. It tells me what underwear I’m allowed to wear on Tuesday (laughs) So, I want to give our industry an opportunity to come and study, to come and learn, to come and see what a proper vineyard—not just a couple of rows—but 0.3 ha can produce as a small commercial batch of wine and ask that question. That’s it.

I remember once, with Bailey, after a big day, we were maybe a bit tired, and we drowned our emotions in a couple of good bottles. We decided by the end of the day, we weren’t very good at making Pinot Noir. And we left it at that. Then, I came to Burgundy, and I learnt very quickly that actually I’m irrelevant when in front of great vineyards.

The winemaker and his ego are the worst enemies to great vineyards.

So I asked myself: How do I remove myself from the equation as much as possible and allow that space, that land to express itself? I’m constantly trying to work it out. And that takes me back to those questions with Bailey, that we weren’t very good Pinot makers. We might not just have had the best Pinot site. And that is as simple as that.

Mark Haisma’s wines are imported to Australia by Ethereal Wines.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
The Latin phrase at the top of the label—lux et umbra vicissim sed semper amor—usually appears on the sundials, and it means: light and shadow by turns, but always love. On this occasion, in keeping with the lofty tone, I’d like to add another two Latin phrases that accompany me through life: dum spiro, spero (while I breathe, I hope) and vanitas vanitatum et omnia vanitas, which in a loose translation means…it’s all meaningless—each one for the opposing ends of life. But there’s always amor and soleil, so let’s stick with what’s on the label and in the glass!

On the wine. For the second year, the wines of Aeon come to life and to my tasting bench. Made by Alisdair and Kenisha Tulloch. The Semillon comes from the Latara vineyard (right in front of their house). It’s been 100% barrel fermented and aged in 2nd and 3rd use oak, then matured on lees for 8 months. Only 50 dozen made. Even though it’s 100% oak raised, the wine keeps the light touch but gains a nutty edge and textural nuance. I’d say more Semillon in oak please!

The wine is very good, indeed. Dubbed a fumé Semillon, and it is. Super flinty nose, with sour white apple, crunchy pear, firm nectarine, and watermelon rind in the fruit department. There’s also lemongrass in perfume, and palate delivers oyster shells saline juiciness, with some raw cashews, savoury pastry, smoked lemons and light lemon yoghurt. Pretty tight and mouthwatering, with blinding rays of acidity, clean line, and driving minerally with a fine dusty chalk texture. Such luminous things in New South Wales. Orta recens quam pura nites!

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Jeff Byrne’s ‘regular’ Chardonnay 2024 scored a no-blinking 95 points from me on the blind bench during judging at the Orange Wine Show this year (it’s $35, a note will follow soon). Its previous vintage also got 95 points from me a year ago, when I visited the region. This says a lot, mainly that the wine is delicious and bloody great value. The wine in review, however, is Jeff’s first single barrel release. It’s the best fruit selection, fermented and raised in a 2,500L French foudre. This wine is delicious already, but it will be even better in a few years. Out of curiosity, I checked the last time an Orange Chardonnay scored 96 points on TWF, and I found only one, and it was Rowlee Single Vineyard Chardonnay 2016, tasted in 2017 by Campbell. Interesting. If you ask me, there are some exciting Chardonnays coming from Orange these days.

The execution is perfect. Seduction comes here in many forms. At first, shimmers of struck match, quickly moving into flint and peach blossom, grapefruit skin and just a hint of brine. This wine is very expressive even when cold but deserves a large bowl to handle its perfume and allow it to change with time. Perfectly ripe fruit forms the core of this wine, with apple, peach, melon and pomelo. All wrapped in delicious oak spice; there’s nougat, milk powder, and custard tart, with notes of cinnamon—none of which is overwhelming the fruit—all flows in balance. Long, satin-textured ribbons of cool acidity hold these layers in tension. It’s a full package, this wine. Full of flavour, full of grace and big on hedonistic satisfaction.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Artus might be more attractive sometimes, but I love Purus. Artus and Purus—sounds like the names of two brothers from a mythological story. Two different wines, two individuals. Anyway, they are cool names. I like personifying wine, so this works very well for me. Lower scoring, Purus is my preference over Artus.

Purus is composed mainly of French clones. It sees 40% new French oak, no lees stirring until the very end of the maturation (in stainless steel) and no malo. Last but not least, the name comes from the purity of the fermenting juice, as opposed to Artus, which contains more solids responsible for some more reductive aromas (the family of struck match).

It has that savoury-nutty, almond start, the base is full of crunchy green apples with cinnamon dusting. Very fine, milky texture, and the flavours develop into white peach and pear, pomelo, lavender, fennel seeds, fresh mint leaf, green melon… The acidity and texture combined feel like the slippery juiciness of watermelon rind. It’s a very minerally wine, fine boned and long. You may notice that the stylistic signpost is pointing towards Chablis. Yes, it is far away, but that’s the spiritus of Purus.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Mount Pleasant Love on Mount Pleasant Semillon 2025
Review Text:
Mount Pleasant released a limited edition art series featuring Semillon and Shiraz Pinot, with labels showcasing paintings by Garry Shead from his “Love on Mount Pleasant” series. Garry Shead is a 1993 Archibald Prize winner and a multiple finalist throughout the years. He also happens to be Maurice O’Shea’s nephew. I went to a Mount Pleasant event at the Art Gallery of NSW and met Garry. He reminisced about his childhood, remembering uncle Maurice. Very special. What a wonderful combination: wine and art. Wine IS art. Happy to say that there’s a pretty wine behind a pretty label, too.

The grapes for this wine come from a sliver of the Lovedale vineyard (planted in 1946). A sliver that ripens ever so slightly earlier than the rest and makes this bottling a little different than the flagship Lovedale. The one descriptor in my dictionary that gets overused when it comes to young Semillon is lemon blossom, and there’s plenty of that at the start of this wine. Honeysuckle and jasmine come right after with a little time in glass. It has that light touch, that very light texture, but it’s packed with flavour, with all things lemon, a hint of lemongrass, pear, hay, Papirovka apples (those crumbly sour ones), but also a hint of baked apple and rolled oats. This flavour palette is underpinned by a crisp and refreshing flow of spa water-like minerality. Acidity is on point, persistent yet soft. The flavours build up slowly in the back, making for quite a long finish. This is still very fresh, and you could enjoy it now, but it will age well, no doubt.

This wine satisfies the eye and the tongue. And it’s only natural to compare it to Mount Henry, THE Shiraz Pinot blend of MP. The wine is ripe and textural, but it doesn’t have the same fine, ethereal detail of Mount Henry. Nevertheless, it’s a very enjoyable drink, with layers of interest. It sits at medium weight, the fruit is dark and spicy with mint and dark chocolate shavings in the finish and a flicker of purple flowers. Tannins are medium and sandy in texture. It feels that Shiraz really takes over, where in MH the smaller portion of Pinot usually shines through. Anyway, this is lovely as is.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Gaius Octavius was 35 years old when he adopted the name of Augustus, meaning ‘venerable’ and ‘majestic’ (it might be time for me to change names). Ten years later, the month of Sextilis, originally sixth in order of the Roman calendar, was renamed in his honour (this month was moved from number six to number eight earlier with the introduction of January and February that pushed it forward). This was meant to praise Augustus’ battle victories, just as July was meant to glorify Julius Cesar. At the same time, Octavian (as Gaius was also called) established a holiday in his name symbolising the end of civil wars—Pax Augusta, and a time of well-deserved respite for the people after harvest. With that, a day of rest—Feriae Augusti—was born, and is celebrated to this day across Italy in conjunction with a catholic feast of the Assumption of Mary. This free-of-work day is now called Ferragosto and happens on the 15th of August.

But why do I go on about Romans, you ask? Well, it’s 1 in 365 chance, but that day happened to be a day I spent at Etna’s north and east piedmonts, hoping to casually visit a few wineries (OK, I didn’t check ahead). Despite almost all wineries being closed that day, I managed to lock in two visits thanks to Michael Zaccaria of Quel Vino (big thank you). In a way, it was nice to celebrate a day of Augustus’ Rest with a glass of Italian wine and the company of people who welcomed me kindly at their wineries and houses. How silly and lucky me!

PART 1

First up, Gustinella. I drove from Catania in the south of Etna towards Randazzo in the north via the western slopes of the volcano, to reach Maletto, a small village wedged between two famous appellations—Etna DOC and Pistacchio Verde di Bronte. Maletto isn’t famous, nor an appellation, but for Sonia Gambino, this is not a problem. In fact, she was the one to take the old vineyards of Maletto quite seriously and began to call them vino di confine—wine of the border. The story is as romantic as it can be during the early days of the pandemic, when unexpected opportunities presented themselves in dire times. Sonia left Mediolanum (aka Milan but keeping the Roman tone) to spend some time in her family’s house in Sicily and soon after met Don Vincenzo, an out-of-work, elderly Etna train driver, who, as it turned out later, owned a bunch of old vines. She decided to buy some grapes from him (in exchange for 365 bottles of wine as requested, one per each day of they year) and start a fun project of making wine. After some time spent in Maletto, tending the vines and getting serious about making wine, Sonia was recognised by the locals as the granddaughter of Peppe Gustinello, who, a long time ago, owned a local palmento—a traditional communal winery. Gustinella was a natural name choice for Sonia’s unexpected wine project in her grandpa’s village. Now, she’s very proud of her collection of 12 small plots with old vines (60-120 years) grown at 1100m above sea level. The old vineyards are a mix of varieties, the local ones and the remnants of the experimental time during British control (many French grapes were brought back then).

Sonia’s first vintage was 2020; the wines were released in 2022. She makes the true, traditional field blends and uses neutral materials: concrete, glass and stainless steel, looking for purity and a ‘mountain feel’ for her wines. I tasted four of them and they all were compelling and heartfelt.

Gustinella Jungìmmune Vino Bianco 2022, 12%
Jungìmmune means ‘to come together’ in Sicilian. This wine is a field blend based on Grecanico Dorato (Garganega), other grapes are Minnella, Albanella, Moscatella, Trebbiano and more. It tastes like sun-dried lemons and dusty air, pink fruit skins, dried herbs, aromatic salted almonds, very minerally, gently textural, very thirst-quenching. 92 points

Gustinella Jungìmmune Vino Rosato 2023, 12%
Approx. 12 different varieties from the highest vineyards at 1200m of elevation. It has a beautiful coral colour. Pink berries, dusty rocky tannins, the most ‘natural’ Aperol vibe, blood orange and zing of acidity, crunch of green apple, olive, almond, and sweet fennel. Delightful. 93 points

Gustinella Vino di Confine 2023, 12%
‘The vines are born together and they finish together’, says Sonia. Another true field blend and a flagship ‘wine of the border’; a red in colour wine based on Grenache with a portion of white grapes, mostly Grecanico Dorato, but also Alicante Bouschet (brought to Sicily back in the day by the British). It smells like bush berries, there’s freshness here but also wilderness, crushed caraway, dried sage and thyme. It has a dusty clay grip, but a light frame; it’s lifted and zingy with crunchy acidity. It can be one to chill, but not necessarily. Very versatile and very tasty. Wish I had spent more time with it. 93 points

Gustinella Jungìmmune Vino Rosso 2023, 13.5%
Mainly Grenache here (in Sicilian dialect Granazzu—I like the sound of it). Dusty raspberry, sour cranberry and rhubarb. It’s an alpine expression of Grenache, for sure, that kind of ethereal, perfumed wine with stony structure, with sage and dark sugar crust aftertaste. Characterful and ‘of the place’. 93 points

PART 2

I paid a second visit to Giuseppe Lazzaro. Giuseppe worked for 20 years with Frank Cornelissen, remembering the ‘not so great’ days of these wines, right before they skyrocketed to fame. Truly connected to his home, Giuseppe eventually left to create own expressions of the volcanic wines. Before you ask, let it be known, Giuseppe’s wines that I sampled were not only sane but more importantly, super delicious and honest. One of his vineyards is located on the eastern slopes of Etna, near Milo in the Contrada Praino, right along the mareneve line—a place between the sea and the snow. Due to the eastern exposure and Mediterranean winds, it’s believed that Etna whites, Catarratto and Carricante, are doing best here. However, Giuseppe cultivates, on these stony terraced slopes, predominantly idiosyncratic expressions of Nerello Mascalese. Interestingly, sometimes he uses propolis harvested from his own bee hives (also makes his own honey) as a natural preservative for the wines. Pied de cuve yeast starters provide the mother for his fermentations.

We start with on-the-spot disgorged sparkling version of the Nerello, named Zoé. In front of us, over the precipice, in the distance of 7km—the Ionian Sea; behind us, in the halo-looking sunset glow—her majesty, Etna (fuming gently). What a moment, what a place. The fizzy, ancestral Nerello is fun, full of maraschino cherries and marzipan, tarragon and lively blood orange twist with playfully pinching bubbles (11.5%, 90 points). Next, we taste five wines in Giuseppe’s little vineyard hut, right on the edge of the vine-covered terraces overlooking the ‘void’. 

B4.2 Bianco 2024
The grapes are Carricante, Catarratto, Minnella Bianca, Inzolia, Grecanico and Moscato. 4 varieties undergo maceration for five days and 2 are directly pressed, hence 4.2. Dusty, herbaceous and floral, very smooth but textural, dense, based on ripe yellow fruit, like quince and mirabelles. The flavour builds up with minerals in the aftertaste. Moreish. 92 points

Spariggiu Rosato 2023, 12.5%
This is 100% Nerello Mascalese made 3 ways: direct press, short maceration and long skin contact. The proportions change each year. This rosato, along with some other examples often made from Nebbiolo, carrying similar savoury notes, is simply super. The perfume of hibiscus and pomegranate skin is complemented by red brick texture and fine tannin. There’s oregano, pink peppercorn, and salumi to be found in its medium body, full of dusty rocks and mouthwatering acidity. You just want to drink it by the bottle. 94 points

Acqua Tinta Rosso 2023, 12.5%
This wine is partly made with re-pressed pomace and fresh juice. Acqua Tinta refers to ‘bad water’, a term used in the past for adding water into pomace for additional extraction, just as it is done in the piquette-making process (this is not a piquette). Nerello Mascalese and friends, Sangiovese and some white varieties. Pomegranate and liquorice and red earth, chewing sage leaves, crunchy, fresh wine with blood orange, spice, pepper and dried elements, and you get that extra grip of tannin, but the wine is pleasantly medium bodied. 92 points

Russucori Rosso 2022, 13.5%
100% Nerello Mascalese; 80% of fruit comes from the north and 20% from the east side. Eastern vineyards boost the acidity, fruitiness and freshness and northern exposure adds structure and deep ripeness of flavours. This is exactly how this wine presents itself, with a strong note of black cherry and melograno, clear structure of firm tannins, depth and length; purity of fruit with a light veil of aromatic smoke. 94 points

V 1981 2021, 14%
This wine takes its name from Etna’s extensive and dramatic eruption that took place in March 1981 when the lava flow ran only 5 metres from the vineyard located on the northern slopes. It’s a single cru in Contrada Pirao Randazzo at 1000m, just outside the prescribed by DOC Etna altitude of 800m, so Terre Siciliane it is. The vines are 60-90 years old and the yield is very low, only approx. 400 bottles are made. The wine stays with skins after fermentation for 30 days, and then spends 18 months in terracotta amphora, and then another 18 months in bottle. This is Giuseppe’s ultimate expression of Nerello Mascalese Etneo. The wine is dark-fruited, dense, structured, yet it has a graceful touch. The proverbial iron fist in a velvet glove suits here very well. Purity, Sicilian pomegranates, iron, blood plum, dust, balsamic glaze, hazelnut skins, crushed fennel, raspberries and red flowers. It’s a statement. 95 points

For the prices and availability of wines please turn to Michael from Quel Vino. Many thanks! (or I will update them once I know them)

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Marco De Bartoli Vecchio Samperi NV
Review Text:
Disproportionately long intro to the review of the wine in question, but here we are, passion on digital paper.

Subtitled ‘Perpetuo’, this Vecchio Samperi is a very special wine. In translation, it simply means the ‘old Samperi’, which is a contrada (district) in Marsala, Sicily. When Marco de Bartoli started his Marsala winery in the 1980s, he didn’t immediately confine himself to the customary Marsala production, ie fortification. He wanted to revive the forgotten pre-British style, highlighting the terroir; hence, he made a wine without any spirit addition and named it in honour of the old tradition and the place. He knew that Grillo grapes grown on limestone in a hot, arid climate of western Sicily (albeit with some humid winds from the Mediterranean) can naturally ripen to a level that gives the alcohol of 16% and more. Not very fashionable these days, but you can’t feel the ethanol heat, so strong are the aromas and flavours that develop during maturation in the vineyard and in the winery. Marco also decided to use only Grillo grapes (permitted for Marsala are also Inzolia, Catarratto, and Damaschino), for its high acidity, and quality of the aromas and flavour concentration. From ‘back then’ until now, the grapes are handpicked, soft pressed, wild yeast fermented in oak and chestnut vats at room temperature. This wine is made in a perpetual system, the fractional blending a la solera, where each year barrels are topped up with fresh wine. It is aged for an average of 15 years, so it is a NV wine. TWF’s good practice tells me to make an identifiable reference to the wine tasted if one can’t reference a vintage, but I was so taken by this wine that I didn’t snap a picture of the label or note any particular batch number, mea culpa! HOWEVER, I can’t imagine this wine having a bad or heavily varied ‘draw’ from the barrel at any given time, so no reference is necessary in this case in my view.

One last thing, a little poetic touch that I liked, found on the Vecchio Samperi’s label that read: “Wisdom of man, vocation of the territory, strength of the vine, respect for tradition, character of the grapes, quality of the wood and time…”. (from Google translate so might be a bit off).

De Bartoli’s true, old Marsala has an old gold colour with green patina reflections. This feels apt to what’s about to follow. The nose is tantalising; painted with strokes of green fruit and herbs on golden-ripe but savoury canvas of flavours. Where to start? Fresh fennel, green walnut, green mango, green almond, pistachios, capers, roasted spices. This is absolutely delicious. Definition of elegance, power, depth—all in harmony despite the alcoholic strength. Everything comes together naturally. Idiosyncratic wine beautifully reflecting its terroir and history.

Today, the estate is run by Marco’s children: Renato and Giuseppina. (His other son, Sebastiano, sadly, died earlier this year). If you’d like to try the wine, you can buy it in Australia thanks to Piero Fonseca of The Standard Wine Co and I strongly recommend that you do but even more so that you make your way to Marsala.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Williams Selyem Williams Selyem Estate Vineyard Pinot Noir 2022
Review Text:
These wines emerged as a ‘garage project’, started by Burt Williams and Ed Selyem in 1979. Interestingly, Williams Selyem winery started its life under the name of Hacienda del Rio with a hand-crafted, cool-looking label (look it up), but soon after received a cease and desist letter from another Hacienda winery (Hacienda Wine Cellars?). A few years later, the name changed, and so did the label, which now looks pretty iconic. This wine, or more accurately, its predecessor from 2007, previously under the Litton Estate Vineyard name, earned 100 points from Wine Enthusiast Magazine in 2009. Litton Estate Vineyard was later renamed as Williams Selyem Estate Vineyard, hence the elongated, repetitive name. Importer: Saint Wine

It’s painted with eye-dazzling purple. You can’t look away! And why would you? But you could close your eyes and smell it from afar too. It’s so intensely perfumed, inviting, posh, in one word—seductive. Loaded with aromatic herbs and spices, pink peppercorn, sage, violets, rooibos tea and nutmeg. It has great tension in its structure, it’s blood-rich, minerally, with precisely managed oak that sucks you in with mahogany wood scents. Tannins are fine and sink right into this immense red and black-fruited flavour. Another beautiful Pinot Noir from Williams Selyem.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Tyrrell’s Vat 9 Shiraz vertical tasting (+ 2007 of Old Patch, 4 Acres, Vat 8) @ Hunter Wine Tasting Club [July 2025]
Review Text:
Hunter Wine Tasting Club invited me for a vertical tasting of Tyrrell’s Vat 9 Shiraz with Mark Richardson, the chief red winemaker.

I jotted down some notes… Nothing revolutionary, as GW has been reporting on Tyrrell’s wines more than meticulously and intimately for years and last time on Vat 9 vertical in 2022 here. Nevertheless—my addition below.

I also would like to thank David Holmes, the club’s cellar master, for the invitation.

PS The Club is looking for new members if anyone is interested…

Vat 9 vertical

2024
‘Don’t eat the cake straight from the oven’ applies here too. No surprise, this wine is so fresh, so young. It’s pumping a nose-tickling perfume, with tension, red and black fruit, liquorice and mint, cherry wood, campfire and rose potpourri. It’s ripe, but nothing is sweet or jammy. Smooth palate, invigorating acidity and juiciness. All as separate parts still, but this is undoubtedly at least a 95-points wine, just give it time.

2023
This comes across as a complete wine right now. Still very youthful but all in place. Plums and leather, sarsaparilla, spice, salt and muscovado sugar. It has a potpourri nose, a density of floral notes, rose, violet, wet leaves, and a smidge of camphor. It’s ripe but has a wild/meaty edge, depth of flavour, and it’s a touch warm, but it wears it well. I like it. 95 points

2022
Restrained at first. Then comes blue fruit, very savoury tones, sour blackberry, iodine line with a bit of boot paste top note, cedarwood. The acidity is fresh, the tannins are silky. It has a bloody note and dark chocolate with salt. Savoury all the way. A beauty. Probably my pick from the youngest 95-point trio. 95 points

2021
This wine sits mainly in the back of the palate, and seems slightly hollow upfront. It’s a bit of a tomato leaf-y with green coffee bean, soft, braised meat, smoked prune, sweet paprika… all this amongst a solid frame of fruit when you look at the big picture. Just not quite hitting the spot like some others, but it’s still a nice drink. 93 points

2019
Sweet berries, light Earl Grey tea tannins, there’s spice and burnt sugar, and some wet forest undergrowth with zing in the back palate and a pomegranate tang. Medium bodied, ethereal. It’s a pretty wine, but seems to be ever so slowly losing ground. 94 points

2018
Immediately very impressive. First sniff and wow. Blackberry coulis, mulberry, smoked meat, herbs, tension, freshness, zip in the back. It has the ripe fruit, but it holds it tight. Power. So good. Potent but very good. With a bit of age, but still so lively. This was the first wine in the second bracket, and it was a tough act to follow. 96 points

2017
Pink peppercorns, brick dust, aromatic tea leaves, steady, a little autumnal in vibration, tertiary aromas creep in, some coffee and dried button mushrooms. All in all, it’s a very good wine, maybe starts to be falling off the bone, seems it might be time to drink? 93 points

2016
Red fruit, hibiscus, rooibos tea, wild rose, with pomegranate tension. Salty finish. It has something like a Pinot Noir charm, but it doesn’t stand strong amongst the others, probably not a big problem in isolation. 91 points

2014
Lots of hype around this vintage, but I reached a quiet consensus with Mark during dinner that the—perhaps overshadowed—2013 was better. Ripeness, mulberry, plum, blackberry and coffee, Ribena and boot paste. Density in texture and perfume, sticky date pudding, smoked bbq, spice, chocolate, but the acidity holds all of the usual suspects in line and place. This is obvious pleasure. A bit broad to finish (a little worrying), but giving. 95-96 points

2013
Colour is still purple bright, the wine is minty with notes of dried eucalypt leaves (good), pepper, juniper berries, lots of spice detail, dark chocolate, chewy tannins, rubbed red fruit skins, sage extract. This is a more of a ‘difficult pleasure’. To be fair, I scored it similarly as 2014, but 2013 is my pick. 96 points

2011
Strawberries first, it’s light in a way, tart rhubarb tart and caramel almond. Compelling old wine, silky, energetic stream of poached strawberry and cinnamon concoction, dried fruit tea, dusty brick tannins. A bit dried out on the outside but with a bright spark inside. Would probably only drink a glass or two but somehow landed on 92 points

Horizontal of Vat 8, Old Patch, 4 Acres and Vat 9

Vat 8 2007
2007 of Vat 8 was a straight Shiraz. It shows sweet tones of stewed cherry, plum, mulberry, blackcurrant, violet, raspberry, and peppery spice with smoked salt. The fruit fades, but you’ll still find some solid enjoyment here. 91

Old Patch 2007
Amazing colour, amazing perfume, brightness amongst darkness, a beam of acidity in the dark fruit spectrum, soft, silky palate, tongue stained with flavour. Laced with exotic spice, sweet but spicy, opulent, and the texture has a density of fine velvet fabric. Blueberry and raspberry, dark polished wood, granite, aniseed and pepper. More detail just keeps coming but I’ll stop typing, you get the gist. It’s generous and very cuddly. 95-96 points

4 Acres 2007
Tobacco leaf and cherry wood, there’s a crimson silky ribbon-fold of fruit here, the note of raspberry and dark chocolate pralines. Flavour sinks deep. The fruit is very pure and bright, clear definition with no false notes. Singing. 96-97 points

Vat 9 2007
Zippy acidity, slate tannins, currants and cherry syrup with mint, some iodine tension, a bit of cherry cola and pomegranate tang with woody spice. It’s mostly drying and firm in the finish but holding up ok. (I’ll be honest with you, I missed scoring this wine, given it was the finale and a good night; however, tone reads: older wine that was enjoyed, but probably don’t wait too much longer).

Thank you very much.

FIN

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Why is the Monopole so special? The Monopole bottling is special because it can be traced back to that single barrel that made it, and hence, a particular part of the vineyard. Mark and Andrie Whisson believe that a bit of extra TLC with the pruning etc, does the magic. Also, Mark tells me that these four rows are the longest in the old block, and as they slope, they stretch from the coldest area with a very poor soil at the top of the hill to a warmer area at the bottom, giving a variety of expressions, thus making for a complete composition in the wine. The proof is in the pudding, indeed.

Serious wine, made with a clear connection and inspiration to Burgundy, and the execution is meticulous and characterful. Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: The new Old Bastard – Kaesler Wines Icons Release Barossa Valley [May 2025]
Review Text:
I had the pleasure of spending a day with the Kaesler team earlier in May.

It was dry in the Barossa, dams were crying out for water. The landscape was painted in sepia and ochre. The vines were holding on to the leaves on their unpruned canes sticking above the trellis in what looked like a crazy, rustic wire tangle. Turning-the-colour leaves still help the vines store for winter in this dry climate, as I learn later from the guardian of the vines.

Nigel van der Zande, the viticulturist and general manager at Kaesler, tells the stories of the land as we drive around the region. We talk about regenerative farming, challenges and learnings. We talk about Eutypa and how it’s managed. We talk about in-house compost making and row, and undervine management. Planting trees and encouraging native species to live in symbiosis with the vines. Nigel is a very passionate viticulturist; he’s put in a lot of work at Yarra Yering the year it was acquired (2009) by Ed Peter and Reid Bosward. Owned by the same people, Kaesler is very much a separate business where Nigel puts his heart and soul into. I could listen to his tales of the land for hours.

After a short stop by the 12 rows of 132-year-young Old Bastard vines, we visit the winery. I chat with Tim Dolan, who took over as the chief winemaker in September 2022, and Stephen Dew, who has been making wine at Kaesler since 2002; he’s an integral, spiritual part of this place. We talk about the use of oak, the style, and the expressions of old vines, of course.

I taste the wines at the cellar door with the Old Bastard wall-print looking over the room. The new Icon release is here and looking very smart.

Old Vine Shiraz 2022
“Old Vines” planted in the 1960s, so not as old as the “Alte Reben”. Perhaps it sounds older in German.

Richness and lifted aromas define this wine. It’s built with red fruit on the outside and a concentrated line of black fruit on the inside. The perfume holds the tension of cherry blossom, hazelnut oak and rose petal potpourri. The flavour is luscious but carries the same lift of red fruit as the aroma. The tannins are tense and spiked with iodine, that kind of earthy, salty nuance, balancing between dried fruit and dried blood. There’s something very pretty but a bit rusty about this wine, giving ethereal and umami at the same time and this combination is hard to resist. 96 points

Alte Reben Shiraz 2021
Old vines, planted in 1899.

The oak spice and the peppery pinch of Shiraz come together gracefully in this wine. The notes of vanilla and toast go hand in hand with ripe black fruit. This wine has a mahogany, rich, luxurious perfume. Roasted coffee and warm woody undertones, exotic spice, smoked meat and light char to tannin, steaming cherry pie with some dusting of cinnamon, leather and just a hint of boot polish. It’s dense like freshly brewed coffee and textural like very high quality, silky cocoa powder. You could sink into its cosy perfume and plush fabric of flavour for hours. 95 points

WOMS Shiraz Cabernet 2022
Weapon of Mass Seduction. Indeed. It does feel like this blend is built for wide appeal and instant gratification. Nothing wrong with that. Tickling the senses, blackberry tart with vanilla custard and a dusting of sweet spice, ripe and vibrant core of fruit, a mix of blackberry and black currant. Notes of dates and caramel whiffs mingle with a strawberry type of finish, loads of black chocolate tannins, and ground coffee mouth perfume. Needs a bit of time, perhaps, but it’ll seduce you as is right now too. 94 points

Age of Light Cabernet Sauvignon 2022
Planted in 2017, “Kids Cabernet” block, right behind the winery, not far from the Old Bastard. 120 dozen.

Elegance in liquid form. It’s the Cabernet’s DNA and quality oak marriage perfection. The minty-creamy filling in dark chocolate, notes of new leather, cassis perfume, cherry wood smoke, raspberry and boysenberry in the mix, along with hints of vanilla in the back palate. Complete composition, all very well measured and elegant, fine-boned, smooth, with long ropes of fine ebony tannins. Flavour is kept in line with the acidity and coolness of fruit, and it feels smooth and soft yet firm and strongly built underneath. Finishing effortlessly already, but will age very well too. 96 points

Old Bastard Shiraz 2021
Planted in 1893, 12 rows.

Very old vines and a wine that is still very young. However, with time in the glass, it starts to shed its perfume gradually and gives detail one by one, layer by layer, showing the complexity that it carries. It’s not all quite merged yet, but time should do its job. First come the blue fruit, vanilla bean and braised meat. It has minty spice, liquorice, star anise, and tarragon family of aromas. The texture is this thick fabric of fruit that rolls out in a velvety manner in the mid-palate and tenses up on the sides. It keeps a long line of flavour, and sends iodine-bloody electric shock waves through your taste buds. Spice and perfumed cherry wood smoke flesh out in the back palate. Tannins are shaped in long slabs of graphite—shiny, smooth and fine to feel. It’s very much a moving and living wine that has a long life ahead. Funnily, the old bastard on the label doesn’t seem to age like the fine wine it has in the bottle. 97 points

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
The variety is Devín, a cross of Gewürztraminer × Roter Veltliner obtained in 1958 at the VSSVVM research centre for oenology and viticulture in Modra in Slovakia. This wine, Intacto, is a two-vintage combo, 2022 and 2023, there’s skin contact involved, untopped barrels, flor development and solera blending… Copying here Marek Uhnák’s (the owner winemaker of Pivnica Čajkov) back story of this wine… Importer: Cardwell Cellars

“Devín is the child of communist times – somebody in Slovakia once had the idea that we need our own type of Traminer, one that can survive our crazy winters. Thus, this grape was born: son of Traminer, daughter of Rotweisser Veltliner, aromatic yet resilient. Tbh, I never liked the wines it produced, but fate brought me a vineyard with some of it. I thought I’d pull it out as soon as possible, yet time went by and the vines still stood there, intact and proud. So, I dropped the attitude and took up the challenge. Using lower yields, a slightly oxidative elevage and multi-vintage blending, I turned my once-Nemesis into a new friend.”

Such a complex wine. Rubbed herbs and spices, cloves, caraway with citrus zest essential oils, mix of lemon, lime and pink grapefruit. Fresh yeasty dough top note and green walnut, walnut husks, chamomile tea with stony minerality and smooth yet engaging texture. So much to dig out, continually evolving in the glass. Thinking wine.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Pivnica Čajkov’s website has immense detail of the history, region, varieties, winemaking, and all beautifully told too. Wines come from the Nitra region of south-west Slovakia, the grapes are grown organically (not certified) on the foothills of the volcanic mountain Sitno. Rustical is an amber wine made with Pesecká Leánka grape (Fetească Regală). The grapes are destemmed and macerated on skins for a few days in open top vats. At around 5% alcohol, the wine is moved to barrels (off the skins) where it finishes the fermentation. Gentle tannin management is the take here. Unfined, unfiltered and minimal sulphur at bottling. Importer: Cardwell Cellars

Rustical is all about going back to the old ways of doing things. Marek Uhnák follows the winemaking of his grandparents. The result is a wine with honeyed bouquet, apricots and peaches tossed through, persimmon and papaya skin leading the senses, with a strong drive of bitter herbs like sage and thyme. So pure on the palate, fine texturally, with that wet slate soft-but-firm touch, and herbaceous tones sprinkled throughout. A wine with a soul and for the soul. And the label is spiritual too.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Andrew Wyse of Cardwell Cellars based in Melbourne continues to bring Central/Eastern European wines to Australia to my delight. We’re getting closer and closer to my motherland—Poland—in the wine sense. We’re not quite there yet (no Polish wines are imported to Australia), but I like what I see coming from the ‘peripheries’. The wine in question is from Slovakia. And here, a quick personal rant time: recently, I heard someone again referring to the country of ‘Czechoslovakia’ in the present tense, and frankly, it’s been 32 years since Czechia and Slovakia became two independent countries, so it’s time to get on with the program. Rant over.

Čajkov is a place, a municipality, situated in the Štiavnické hills in the Nitra region of south-west Slovakia. The owner of the winery is Marek Uhnák. Pivnica Čajkov’s history goes back to the year 1666 when it received the rights to trade wine from the Archbishop of Estergom. The historical seal, and the symbol of that moment in time, appears on the winery’s labels. The vineyards spread over the foothills of the volcanic mountain, Sitno.

Princess is a wine made from Pesecká Leánka. This variety originates from Romania, and it’s known there as Fetească Regală, which translates into ‘royal young girl’. With some time on skins pre fermentation, technically it’s not an orange wine but has some textural elements of one. Low intervention winemaking. This is a breakfast wine, yes, your alternative for OJ, and they suggest that on the winery’s website, too. I can see this. It has texture, it’s a cloudy, pulpy juice, chock full of vitamin C coming from the citrus notes of orange peel and pith with a mix of herbs, side of jasmine green tea, quince and honey, ginger and peach stone. Morning sunshine and a great start to a fun day.
