Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Hello friends,

How are you doing?

It’s November and I’m in Orange. Summer’s at the doorstep. I love Orange, it has such distinct ‘European’ seasons. And great wines. I wanted to send your way some wine notes.

I spent here three days and I sampled just a bit over 100 wines. I visited nine wineries (but tasted additional drops from other wineries). I took 15 pages of notes. These are my highlights—one wine from each winery.

Note: This is still very much only a snapshot of the region and not a full list of highlights, missing some of my favourites like Canobolas Wines or Swinging Bridge…

To sum up in one sentence: Orange has a seriously strong Chardonnay game, plus Riesling and other aromatic whites, along with great sparks of Pinot Noir and a few alpine-expressions of non-mainstream varieties—all to watch (and taste).

Special thanks to David Cumming from Define Wine Marketing & Communications who facilitated this visit.

Slow Wine Co Tribus 2023 $27
Starting with Slow Wine Co. This is a white blend and I feel like many white blends don’t get enough attention. Prêt-à-Blanc from Schmölzer & Brown, Sang de Pigeon Blanc from Michael Hall and Sol from Riley Harrison to name a few that I tasted recently delivered the goods. And, similarly, this one from Slow Wine Co.

This is an Alsatian-styled blend of Pinot Gris, Riesling and Gewurztraminer. Crisp fresh white full of aromatics with some meat and fat on the bone giving body and texture, almond biscuit and pink grapefruit with a hint of warming spice all in place and balance. It’s a very moreish and refreshing sipping. 92pts

Strawhouse The Naked Pig 2022 $25
This is a blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon with some barrel action and lees ageing. It effortlessly brings together the joy of fruitiness and lightly creamy-nutty texture. Citrus curd, green apple, and greengage with quince and green grapefruit, a note of roasted cashew and green almond, and a lick of phenolics with a line of fennel and nettle in the aftertaste. Yet another crisp white wine at a very good value. 92pts

ChaLou Riesling 2024 $35
She’s done it again. Nadja Wallington’s off-dry Riesling shines year in and year out. It’s pure lime juice, lime sorbet with mint leaves folded through, with jasmine, crushed lilies, the acidity is piercing, cutting right through that tiny bit of sweetness, which ultimately feels like melting icing sugar spiked with citrus juice. This sensation finishes with the softness of talcum powder at the same time feeling like a good crunch of green mango and firm white peach. This is a beautiful wine in its purity and crispness. 95pts

Macquariedale Organic Wines Riesling 2024 $35
Macquariedale Organic Wines’ cellar door may just have the best panoramic view in Orange, although to be honest, there’s a great view anywhere you go in Orange. Ross McDonald, the owner and the winemaker, planted Pinot Noir at, arguably, THE highest altitude in Orange, higher than the one of de Salis. To be watched.

Orange does Riesling so well. This is delightful. Crab apple, chamomile and wild honey, the bouquet is full of meadow flowers. Then comes a very satisfying ripe but fresh tone of melon skin and pink grapefruit. It’s a wine that has a touch more richness and width but it works very well with a cool slate-like acidity that sits right under the tongue tickling well the salivation glands. Mouthwatering and moreish this is. 93pts

Hoosegg Jade Moon Cabernet Franc 2018 $140
I feel like Orange does well the crisp white wines and light-bodied reds, like Pinot Noir, and the Cabernet family doesn’t always shine, but boy, does Philip Shaw know how. I liked his 2018 Double Lucky Cabernet maybe a bit more than this 2018 Jade Moon but wanted to share some love for Cabernet Franc. Here it comes with a beautiful alpine freshness. Raspberry and nettle, red apple skin and rhubarb, some rose hip, tarragon and a hint of violet. It’s silky with iron rock minerality, very smooth and firm, slate-like tannins. It opens up with a rich dark chocolate aroma, but it’s lifted on the palate, intense but ethereal at the same time. Just lovely. 95pts

For starters, it has a pink grapefruit note and packs a punch of flavour with juicy acidity balancing zesty mid-palate bitterness. There’s salt and crushed slate, raw oats and milk powder, more grapefruit and a very tantalising note of watermelon rind. It’s a refreshing, vibrant wine with nutty creaminess, talcum powder detail of texture and underlying minerality. And it’s only 35 lire. 95pts

Colmar Estate Block 1 Chardonnay 2022 $40
Another great Chardonnay from Orange delivering the well-framed flavour. The oak spice, the acid, the fruit, the overall drinkability all wrapped in one delicious package. It starts with low key fruit, gentle citrus tones, orange pith then evolves into hints of nougat, bitter peach, toasted nuts, peaches and cream. It feels generous but still elegantly presented. Lots to love here. 92pts

Rikard Riesling 2023 $35
I’ve sampled Will Rikard-Bell’s Riesling before and it’s always a show-off in his portfolio. Silky-soft and cool satin-heavy texture with lime curd, crushed flint, orchard fruit aplenty, sweet, bitter and salty all at once striking a great balance, refreshment and a line of flavour vibrating long. Lots happening, all seamlessly. 95pts

Mayfield Vineyard William Pinot Noir 2022 $65
Here on Pinot Noir but of note are also Chardonnays from Mayfield Vineyard. This wine comes in a suit of tart forest berries, with notes of bark and spice and caramel whiffs. It’s a Pinot of savoury freshness, fruity core and elegantly crafted finishing touch of oak. Powerful elements yet graceful and alpine-fresh. 93pts

Cooks Lot Allotment 9 Pinot Noir 2023
I haven’t tasted a LOT of this producer’s wines but this one gets a mention. It comes across as a bit dark and rough. It has earthy, mossy, smoky and flinty characters evolving into milder tones of peppermint, wet autumnal leaves and then juicy black fruit flowing underneath. Feels like it needs a moment in the glass or a few more years in the bottle to relax, but I enjoy its slightly rugged character right now too. 92+pts

Stockman’s Ridge Signature Range Gruner Veltliner 2022 $45
Here’s a barrel-fermented Gruner Veltliner from Orange. Yes! It’s spicy with wild honey, textural with crushed shell minerality, ripe with citrus pith and a hint of vegetal notes. Lemongrass, a touch of aniseed with a crunch and spice of radish and ginger building up with time. It’s a well built wine with substance and interest. 92pts

See Saw Fulcra Pinot Noir 2021 $80
Monica Gray makes a lot of wine at See Saw. I tasted 21 wines there alone! This Pinot Noir from Fulcra range is a serious offering, composed of dark fruit, spiced plum, plump black cherry with a dusting of spice bringing out the flavours on a velvety layer of tannins. Core is sweet-fruited with a cherry pie note. All delicious as a whole. One to hold. 92+pts

Angullong Sagrantino 2022 $30
Angullong has an extensive range of wines that include tasty Sangiovese, Montepulciano and Barbera amongst others. I liked their Chardonnay a lot but decided to highlight something different for a change—the Sagrantino. A red that has bright forest fruit and amaro notes, a solid grip of texture lending amazing power to the wine with a light and effortless flavour of raspberry, rhubarb, rose hip and the avalanche of stony tannin. What a combo. Very ‘Italian-alpine’, very delicious. 92pts

Looking forward to golden Orange autumn. See you soon!

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
I haven’t tasted many Chinese wines but the ones that I have gave me a feel as if they were a mix of Old World earthy and rustic and New World ripe and glossy fruit (I know, I know—the Old World and New World is not the best description anymore but that’s how I felt about them…). I also love seeing new descriptors for these wines, the spice, herbs and fruit connotations like ‘shiso leaf’ which I wasn’t too familiar with and needed to look up. It’s otherwise known as Chinese basil and spread across Asia. I suppose it’s like gooseberries or mirabelle plums for non-Europeans and I always felt a bit bad using these in my notes as some people can’t refer to them. But I’m happy to see connections to more local flavours being used.

Marselan is a Vitis vinifera, a cross between Cabernet Sauvignon and Grenache. It’s been quite popular in China and you might know that Penfolds makes one with Cabernet Sauvignon under CWT 521 label, but I haven’t tried it. The one in the review comes from producer’s ‘Natural Wine’ range and it hasn’t been filtered. It was aged in 100% new French oak barrels.

There’s definitely ripeness in this wine and an assortment of mostly black fruit, some fresh, some cooked and lightly jammy, and a special mention goes to raspberry. It’s quite meaty and peppery, a bit smoky with dark chocolate, cocoa nibs, with a mushy texture tightened by a rustic/earthy note. Lots of spice and toast, meat and pepper, firm but smooth tannins. It all works and it handles the oak well. I liked it the most (along with the sparkling), as it had a bit of a Southern Rhone vibe and good balance.

Review Text:

What a nice start! Neon coral colour. It’s a rose fizz with sweet orange, blood orange, pink grapefruit, hints of rose water and musk sticks, strawberries and cream. Fun, gastronomic drink and definitely interesting to try a Chinese sparkling wine combining well the sweet and the savoury.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Last year, on the 2nd of January, I posted a review of Champagne Salon. Well, this is a different start to 2025, hope it’s not gonna project on my whole year… In my ‘defence’ I was buying Arras Brute Elite when I saw Dolly Sparkling, and prompted by a recent request to review it, I couldn’t resist. I spent $20 (!) and I tasted a glass of it, here’s to the new year’s sacrifice. Actually, it’s quite important to know these styles and the marketing around them etc, so I don’t mind the lengthy note either. Not that it’s a wine to ponder on for its flavour, but these styles of wines are often dismissed as we’re only oohing and aahing on the top of the game, where and while this is the one that makes the most money on the whole. Just saying.

The wine. You only learn from the website that this is a blend of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, not from the label. From the label, you learn Dolly loves butterflies. The region is Australia. Produced by Accolade. This is it. The tasting note on the website is way too ‘fine’ for it. Why can’t it be: ‘It’s simple but you’ll love it if you love Dolly’?

I tasted it icy cold. So it was sort of shy in aromas at first—perhaps a good thing and mostly likely an inherent thing anyway. The notes were rather sweet and ripe of syrupy peaches and cream, icing sugar and generic confected fruit-basket-type of aromas. Flavour—simple, short and sweetish (not overtly) a la creaming soda. Singular dimension is where your tastebuds find themselves, adding some excitement ‘thanks’ to a coarse bubble. Nothing here is offensive though (unless you find the above offensive), and in a marketing exercise, with your name as the centrepoint of the wine and no single mention of the grapes, ‘Australia’ in fine print pushed to the side, this wine gets 10/10. This will sell and it’s not cheap for the shelf it sits on. And confirmed—it is better icy cold. Hard to score, as technically nothing is wrong with it, just simple and one might argue flabby, but in that commercial sense, it’s made correctly and market-appropriately. Whether this is where we want to head, of course—

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Mornington Peninsula: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir regional tasting [Dec24]
Review Text:
Earlier in December, I visited Mornington Peninsula and I tasted a bunch of wines. I have to say, the region showed off its high and even quality spread across a beautiful selection of Chardonnays and Pinot Noirs (and Pinot Gris!). Not that it’s any news or surprise but it’s nice to be reminded and share the love and be proud. Many of these have been reviewed, but hey, let’s call it a recap and drink up. Happy New Year to all!

Chardonnay

Montalto The Eleven Chardonnay 2016
This wine feels complete, the perfume has a lot of detail, all merged together in harmony, there’s lemon tart, peach, toasted almond and apple, and nougat. Supple palate, citrus-driven, with a gentle, creamy core on a firm ‘mineral’ bed. Beautiful to drink now but still quite fresh so it can be kept a bit longer. 95pts

Pt Leo Estate Chardonnay 2017
This is rich and punchy. Strong perfume of sweet spice, toast, vanilla curd, ripe orchard fruit. Intense citrus and pineapple skin line of acidity, with notes of toasted almonds and some struck match. It’s a richer style, with a sour-sweet theme and notes of cream throughout the palate. It will bring flavour satisfaction. 93pts

Polperro Mill Hill Chardonnay 2022
Notes of ripe apples, ginger, toast and citrus tart, lots of tightly packed flavour, it sits in the back with gingerbread and lemon peel and it builds up with each sip. There’s underlying sweetness here and the flow is easy. It seems that it may need more time to come together. 92+pts

Paringa Estate The Paringa Chardonnay 2022
This is just-so-yum! Pistachio nougat, apples, pears, citrus, in a pure crisp form. Very precise palate, yet smooth and seamless, with a clean, decisive line of acidity carried by the flavour and supported by the fluffy mid-palate weight. It has all the components clearly defined and perfectly matched. Very elegant and in an effortless way. Cuddles for the tongue. 95pts

Kooyong Single Block Farrago Chardonnay 2022
Wow, the acidity here! It’s the definition. Lime and green apple crunch. Very lively and energetic wine. Love the acidity but maybe it needs a hot second to settle it in its form. There’s a cool mountain water minerality in this wine, which is quite lovely. Might just be the one for the long haul. 94+pts

Crittenden Cri de Coeur Chardonnay 2022
Very inviting, quite ripe in flavour, round and giving, spicy, mostly in the mid-palate. Curd and tropical notes, ginger and something medicinal like crushed fennel or almost liquorice, masala mix. It’s quite rich and toasty, with a minty note and with a warming lift to finish. 94pts

Moorooduc Estate McIntyre Chardonnay 2022
This one has everything in place, it’s of a gentle nature and well-balanced. Starts with vanilla cream, lemon curd with pineapple skin and notes of flint and grapefruit. All understated, nothing is overt. There’s a bit of texture here, chewiness. All in all, it’s a well-integrated and appealing wine. 93pts

Ten Minutes by Tractor Estate Chardonnay 2023
Such a smooth and seamless wine. Pretty and detailed. Gentle yet assertive. Great energy captured within a well-balanced melange of fruit and oak. All in line, even and going hand in hand. Ripe lemon, white peach, green melon, pink grapefruit. Notes of toast, light nougat and cream sink into the fruit in harmony. Peak of flavour in the back. Just lovely. 95pts

Garagiste Terre Maritime Chardonnay 2023
Savoury tones to start and a ball of flavour sinking in the mid-palate. Lots of apples and a nutty nuance. It’s mouthwateringly textural and crunchy, with a gingery tingle on the tongue. With a little warming moment in the glass, it shows cinnamon apple toast. Yums. Lots of satisfaction in this wine and high drinkability. Happy days. 95pts

Stonier Reserve Chardonnay 2023
There are lots of appetising nutty notes here, toasted and baked into a tart, with hints of caramel and flint, fennel and aniseed. The fruit is ripe and sits comfortably in the background, acidity takes care of the flavour drive and the long finish. Wait, there’s more. It’s ever so lightly creamy in texture with an underlying saltiness and a very delicious cinnamon-dusted apple tart theme throughout. Elegant, layered and serious wine. 95pts

Nazaaray Chardonnay 2023
A wine of character that shows a certain understated richness. It’s ripe and round in texture and the acidity is carving a valley through the peaks of flavour. Red apples and sweet citrus with a gentle herbaceous note, mint, fennel and a sweet dusting of toasted almonds. Very tasty. 93pts

Yabby Lake Single Vineyard Chardonnay 2023
Ripe fruit and lemon curd notes to the front. Citrus skin perfume, lots of concentration mid-way, toasted nuts and just an abundance of spice and generosity of flavour. All that still very much vibrating and not quite aligned with acidity as yet. But they should come good in a few years. 93+pts

Ocean Eight Verve Chardonnay 2023
Restrained to start, a bit tight, not a bad thing, shy at the beginning but evolves slowly and gracefully in the glass. The combination of savoury and sweet is the first impression, chicken skin, hazelnut sponge cake, apples, vanilla bean, citrus and salty notes. All of it makes for a tasty combination finished on a toasted/flinty aftertaste. Yes, this is very good. 94pts

 

Pinot Noir

Main Ridge Estate Half Acre Pinot Noir 2023
It’s a wine of command. Pure flavour of strawberries and cherries tossed with gentle wood spice and fresh herbs, warm toasted almond whiffs—all just enough to support the fruit. Rhubarb and bloody meat. The palate is silky, the tannin smooth but very much present, there’s a note of roses and green coffee bean composing a mouth perfume. Cool and melting acidity. Firm structure. It’s a full picture, flesh and bones. 95+pts

Eldridge Pinot Noir 2023
A mix of herbs and fruit, potpourri and cloves, then notes of dark cherries and a tiny note of caramel toffee apple. It’s a really nice combo. Fleshy palate with fruit power and a sense of completeness. Very good. 94pts

Paringa Estate Estate Pinot Noir 2023
Dark profile of the fruit, cherries and plums, rubbed fresh herbs and sour raspberries to taste, some sweetness of cinnamon and a smooth slate-like bed of tannin with a deep note of iodine. Very lifted perfume and red apple skin palate making it an ethereal wine. 95pts

Montalto Tuerong Pinot Noir 2023
Fresh coffee bean to start, then it evolves with ginger/almond oak, with dark cherry core and a note of red plum. It’s quite chewy midway with very appetising plummy/fig sweetness. All falls well into place on the palate. 94pts

Kooyong Single Vineyard Estate Pinot Noir 2023
Blueberries, mulberries, and figs wrapped in milk chocolate paper. Very succulent with a note of white pepper and flinty tones to tannin, a bit salty and with a strong DNA of blue fruit and lavender. It’s cool and perfumed, very pretty and very tasty. 95pts

Yabby Lake Single Vineyard Pinot Noir 2023
A strong plummy character with a note of caramel. Then quite a bit of peppery spice and a deep, cool, stony wall of tannin developing into an Earl Grey grip. It’s tidy and strong with powerful drive and assertive flavour. Good stuff. 94pts

Handpicked Capella Vineyard Pinot Noir 2022
It’s a polished wine with bergamot black tea lift, quite plush and soft in texture, with orange peel note of acidity, cloves and allspice. Elegant and steady, well-measured. Chewy finish. It all starts very clean cut and buttoned up and loosens up in the finish. 92pts

Stonier Reserve Pinot Noir 2022
This one is a bit quiet to start, tightly packed and spicy, with textural tannins, a bit sandy but not coarse, rather textural with a steady flow. It has a meaty character with restrained perfume. Perhaps a bit more time needed or some air with decanting. 93+pts

Quealy Seventeen Rows Pinot Noir 2022
A mix of herbs, lavender, potpourri, red and black fruit, deep bloody flow with an appetising bitterness, a la amaro notes of bitter herbs. This is characterful and just simply very delicious. 94pts

Crittenden Cri de Coeur Pinot Noir 2022
Lifted perfume, rubbed herbs, meaty notes, bright crunchy cherry, a note of Campari which adds lift and depth, lovely vibrant line of acidity. Cherry wood smoke. All with a strong definition, drive and length. What a banger. 95pts

Moorooduc Estate Mcintyre Pinot Noir 2022
Fruity whiffs from a basket full of forest berries. The structure is relaxed, a bit loose, lighter on the palate than what the nose might suggest, led by strawberries and cranberries. Good energy and lingering white pepper note. A bit of an Earl Grey grip of tannin. Nice. 93pts

Pt Leo Estate Pinot Noir 2021
Lots of ripe red fruit amongst tart black fruit. This juicy mix is quite pleasant with a loosely knit fabric of soft tannins, fresh cherry pie aroma, it all travels with a sweet-sour theme. Nice but maybe a touch on a riper/stewed side. 91pts

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Made by Ramiro Ibáñez based in Sanlúcar de Barrameda; Palomino grapes fermented and aged in old Sherry casks under flor for approx. 3 months. Importer: Global Wine Merchants.

This is Vino de Pasto, a white wine of Jerez, that focuses on expressions of the white albariza soil, is unfortified and briefly matured under a layer of yeast. This isn’t a new thing in Jerez, but as of late, it has resurfaced, perhaps due to the fortified wines’ decline. And indeed, a light take on the alcohol front makes it quite special. If you’re into Fino and Manzanilla or some of the Jura wines sous voile, you’ll enjoy this wine with el velo de flor very much. Thanks to flor ageing, albeit short, you get a tantalising combination of aromas: bread dough, green apple, raw almond, chamomile tea and a whiff of fresh truffles. It all comes with utter lightness and refreshment on the palate: lemons, crunchy apple and pear, earthy quality and salt. This is such a delicious mix. It might just be a great alternative to the Jura craze, which can never be replaced but seems to be getting out of hand.

There’s always one benchmark that I refer to, Mount Henry of Mount Pleasant, being the most serious expression of the blend (in my view and known to me), taken seriously, the one to pull apart, to enjoy the nuances of Syrah and Pinot at the same time (greedy), to drink over three days and to see it switch back and forth between Syrah and Pinot, and to put away. Black olive tossed with raspberry and red apple skin. Under the House of Adlib label, it’s a collaboration between two winemakers, James Hopkins (Adlib) and Guy Palmer-Brown (Mighty Isle). Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
A debut! Quealy’s Ribolla Gialla was planted in 2018 in Balnarring. 2021 is the first release. The new additions to the Turbul range (and produced in the past Friulano), now include also Malvasia Istriana and Moscato Giallo. From the website: ‘Turbul is Friuli dialect for cloudy, a name suggested by Nikolas [Juretic] a then young Friuli winemaker working with Tom McCarthy at Quealy for the first vintage in 2011.’ Despite the extended time on skins, these wines are not rough or austere. So much character and beautiful detail here. Tom says ‘it’s more about seasons than time’. This Ribolla was picked in April, destemmed and fermented in open steel tanks on skins for approx. 4,5 months. Then pressed to seasoned barrels at the start of spring, when all awakens. Matured on light lees for 30 months before bottling in early 2024.

Rich on the nose. Complex bouquet, lots to unpack. It’s toasted hazelnuts with grapefruit peel. Frangelico liqueur with mouthwatering bitter citrus skin flowing deeply into the back palate. Powerful wine, slightly warming but it carries it with style. Packed with flavour, it has an aniseed/cumin lift amongst bitter herbs. Green melon flesh of slippery texture, quince and green apple peel with salt. Amazing. So good. It’s a serious orange wine. To be honest, I hesitated on 94pts but it’s impressive and I ended up drinking it so there you have it, only fair at 95.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
PSA. Hear me out. I fell into a very deep rabbit hole. While writing this review, I wanted to check some background information on the vines and two hours later I found myself analysing Chardonnay clones in NSW brought by Busby, Webber, et al. I surfed the internet and my home library and most notably while standing at my kitchen counter, I skimmed through the passages of Andrew Caillard’s Australian Ark, volumina I, II and III, naturally. What a magnum opus it is. It got me completely absorbed. Two hours later (maybe?), back to Winamark’s vines. Or so I thought. …vines planted in 1972 from Tyrrell’s cuttings of Short Flat Vineyard which in turn, were planted in 1968 (and make Vat 47), which in turn were ‘pinched’ from, Penfold’s owned at the time, HVD Vineyard planted in 1908. This material could have come from the Kirkton Vineyard which could have been brought from Sydney Botanic Gardens but there are some speculations… Back to the wine, AGAIN. Planted in 1972, hence the name of the wine in question. The juice of the 50 years old vines is in the bottle. There is a deliberate and confusing (or annoying) white space between the ‘7’ and the ‘2’ to make you read it as single digits and not as ‘seventy-two’. 50% new and 50% 1-2 year old oak.

Believe it or not, my reading wasn’t exhaustive nor satisfying for that matter by extension. The question remains: if Winmark’s predecessor, Pooles Rock, was established in 1988, then who planted the Chardonnay in 1972 and did they make wine? This isn’t of any great importance for the review, but now I simply need to know. If anybody… Thanks!

I tasted this wine twice, a month apart, and came to two different conclusions which only means it’s a style that is either polarising or needs time to resolve. No doubt, there’s great intensity on the nose, the perfume is opulent, albeit with a strong reductive, smoky, toasty drive. The drinker must have a struck-match fetish to enjoy this fully. That’s the disclaimer. It’s creamy mid-way, with stone fruit and grilled pineapple and orange oil. It’s a fine line, but despite the reductive/oaky saturation, it still belongs to the fairly elegant side of things. It needs time, I think.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
More or less recently, I visited Launceston and a few wineries in the area with a group of like-minded people via Wine Tasmania. We did a bunch of comparative tastings with a focus on sparkling wine, still Chardonnay and Pinot Noir flights (and many more in between).

Lots of these wines were already tasted on TWF but for good exercise I ran them through my taste buds and for good sport I wrote what follows.

Tasmanian sparkling wine flight was a highlight tasting for me (the only one featured here, otherwise you’d be scrolling for hours)
Wines were tasted amongst their Tasmanian peers, which is all well and good, but I missed international benchmarks thrown in and blind
Tasmanian wasabi as a garnish for oysters is a thing, and a beautiful thing matched with Tassie sparkling!

 

Bracket 1
Bellebonne Vintage Cuvée 2020, $82.5, 12%
This is 60% Chardonnay, 40% Pinot Noir. 5-6g residual sugar and full malo. The colour is golden. A wine that balances just-ripe tropical fruit with mouthwatering salty, briny quality. It has scents of pastry, flint, crushed oyster shells and creamed honey. Powerful acidity and ripeness, preserved lemons, sour apples. I do like the savoury-sour character of it, a bit of warming pickled ginger and gingerbread to the end of things. Characterful. 94 points

Josef Chromy Brut Finesse 2019, $50, 12.5%
70% Pinot Noir, 30% Chardonnay. Red apple skin and peach, pear, white blossoms and an assortment of citrus. All of the orchard fruit blended with sweet pastry and sugar almonds. It’s quite light and quite peachy. Pleasing. 92 points

Pirie Vintage 2019, $55, 12%
Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier. It’s ripe, rich and racy, firm bubble and heavy on the baked goods. Toasted almond, hazelnut sponge cake, baked apple but the rush of the mousse and limey acidity cleanses the lot. Immediate appeal and instant gratification. Feels bold and somewhat commercial but well—very enjoyable. 94 points

Ghost Rock Catherine Sparkling 2019, $60, 12.5%
Golden hue. Ginger biscuits, hazelnut sponge cake. Baked apples. Feels a bit broad on the palate but it has a pleasant mineral water tone, sea mist. Papaya with umami/mushroomy and ruby grapefruit finish. Enjoyable aromas and flavours but seems a touch forward. 92 points

 

Bracket 2
Bellebonne Bis Rose NV, $45, 12%
15% Chardonnay, the rest is Pinot Noir. Lots of tasty pink-hued stuff here. Strawberry, cherry kernel, brine, ruby grapefruit, pink rock salt, rose hip. Just a hint of sweetness rounding the texture and a large dose of savouriness, fresh yeast dough and pink ginger finish. 93 points

House of Arras Brut Elite Rose no 1801 NV, $68, 13%
64% Pinot Noir, 27% Chardonnay, 8% Meunier. 4 years in tirage, 2.5g dosage. Pale salmon colour, quite smoky to start, flint, dark rocks, mushrooms, fine bubble and almost a meaty density, fruit is here but all is heavily umami dipped. Plus a strong oyster shell aftertaste. Gotta love the savoury. I do. 94 points

Jansz Vintage Rose 2019, $57, 12.5%
100% Pinot Noir. Lots of juicy fruitiness, balancing between red fruit, stone fruit and citrus. Bitter peachy skin to finish and hints of peppermint. Musk sticks and a bit of cherry pie perfume in the mouth. Easy drinking, appealing, pretty and relatively simple. 91 points

Freycinet Radenti Vintage Rose 2017, $70, 12.5%
Claudio Radenti wasn’t able to call his sparkling Freycinet due to the Spanish Freixenet… Maybe it’s for the better, I just leave it at that. Radenti it is. 60% Chardonnay and 40% Pinot Noir. Pale onion skin, fresh yeast, button mushrooms, ruby bitter grapefruit, dried herbs, fennel or caraway. Cold smoke. Almost green tea character. Bitter peach, peach stone. Develops into a well-toasted croissant. Shows plenty of character and complexity. 94 points

 

Bracket 3
Moorilla Muse Extra Brut 2018, $56, 11.9%
Very citrus-driven, lifted flavours, lemon curd, lime leaf and lemongrass, a whole heap of acidity and strong oyster shell ‘mineral’ line running on the side of the tongue. Ginger, citrus biscuits, lemon tart, fennel, aniseed, grapefruit and lemon oil. In other words pure citrus and a long line of racy acidity. 94 points

Jansz Single Vineyard Chardonnay 2018, $68, 12.5%
Sweet pastry, icing sugar, white blossom perfume, a bit of wax and white stone fruit. It has a general appeal, and it’s a good sparkling, albeit no extra thrills. 91 points

Delamere Cuvée 2017, $55, 12.5%
Chardonnay and Pinot blend. A touch of colour development. Nashi pear, melon skin, foamy mousse and slippery texture. Baked peach and a steely, slightly broad finish. Good ripeness and apricot stone, waxy quality and a hint of aniseed, marzipan on the nose and on the palate and more mandarine peel in the aftertaste lending a bitter hold. 93 points

Freycinet Radenti Grand Vintage 2016, $75, 12.5%
Blend of 60% Chardonnay and 40% Pinot Noir 6 years on lees. Ripe citrus, orange blossom, ruby grapefruit. Flinty, smoky overtones and a bit of mushroom umami-sweetness, almond nougat, fine bead… Delicious wine. 95 points

 

Bracket 4
Arras Grand Vintage 2015, $125, 13%
66% Chardonnay, 33% Pinot Noir from a mix of regions, 6 years on lees, low dosage at 2.6g of sugar. So much umami, a bag of mushrooms. Lemon curd, salty shortbread, yellow grapefruit, palate has a grilled pineapple and rock salt, roasted almonds, almost tamari. With a lick of sweetness and crème anglaise. Super fine bubbles make it a very smooth wine. Silk on your lips. 96 points

Henskens Rankin Vintage Brut 2015, $105, 12.5%
70/30 Chardonnay/Pinot Noir with 3g sugar dosage. Very rich, hazelnut-driven, ripe fruit, stone fruit and pulpy citrus. Full-bodied, flavourful, lingering, rich and opulent yet elegant, which is what Frieda Henskens says she likes making. Continued… pastis top note, almonds and candied citrus peel. Very satisfying in its richness. 94 points

Henskens Rankin Vintage Brut 2014, $95, 12.1%
2.5g of sugar. Amazingly aromatic, lifted and fresh herbaceous perfume. Seaside shrub. Pink peppercorn, juniper berries, hibiscus, fine bead, focused acidity and tight palate. Pink peach. It’s so much fresher and tighter than the 2015. Both delicious, no less, but this better. 95 points

Delamere Late Disgorged Blanc de Blanc 2012, $150, 12%
Developed colour. Honeyed, wild herbs, a mix of exotic spices, caramel nuts, vanilla curd. Bitterish finish, dark rock, it’s quite rich, flavourful, almost salty black liquorice. Very nice maturing sparkling. 94 points

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Vite Talin is Sandrone’s top wine. Thanks to Luciano Sandrone’s meticulously selected cutting tended to since 1987, Vite Talin has been eventually recognised as a new Nebbiolo clone and registered, not that long ago, as an allowed cultivar for Barolo DOCG. The story is a romantic one, of a grape that was gnarly and somewhat diseased but different from others and gave quality fruit. While I appreciate a good story and the sentiment, this seems to me simply a form of Sélection Massale, a practice done by many vine growers around the world. In a way, ordinary thing to do, but serendipitous to find good planting material, no doubt. So why is it so special? Being a bit geeky, I tried to research more about it, including scrolling through the Italian clonal vine registry for much longer than one should… There’s no mention or reference of this particular grape and no link I could make between the name, Vite Talin or Sandrone and the more technical clonal number that the registry is filled with. The point of all this is not to disprove its registration or uniqueness but simply to understand how it varies from other clones. I’d be left wondering for now. I also asked Chat GPT for help. It LIED to me, immediately providing an exact clonal name/number and upon my asking for the source of this information, it couldn’t answer and… apologised. Ekhm. I tasted the first release, the 2013 in 2019 but I didn’t take any notes, so I can’t compare it with the 2017, so never mind… I did, however, meet Barbara Sandrone back then and it was very nice to see her again when she was in Sydney last month. Importer: Bibendum

This wine is of top quality and detail. Dense ripe perfume. Dried apples, red apple skin, dark chocolate dipped cherry, Maraschino liqueur, like Luxardo. Jaffa biscuits and milk chocolate wrapper. Very textural with a mix of spice and dark pumice tannins. Meaty and chewy. But also with a delicate potpourri and rock salt touch. The whole spectrum from top to bottom is nuanced, perfume and palate carrying a great deal of energy locked in concentrated flavour and long finish.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Recently, I had a chance to try a mini vertical of The Vicar, going back to 1990 when it wasn’t called The Vicar yet and was made by Pam Dunsford. I also had the pleasure of meeting and chatting with the current chief winemaker Michael Fragos, viticulturist Rachel Steer, as well as prof. Tom Nelson, the man who bought the chapel in 1971 and planted the vineyard in 1972. With the 1975 harvest, the 2024 marks the 50th vintage for Chapel Hill, and a call for celebration with a ‘new-old’ addition to the lot, The Devil [click here].

On this note, if you haven’t in the past, this is your chance to (re)watch a short motion picture about Pam Dunsford made by Campbell, [click here]. He tells her story so beautifully and artistically, as ever, in only 5 mins.

The Reserve Shiraz 1990 (The Vicar’s prototype)
In 1993 the Reserve Shiraz was renamed The Vicar for the first time. Pam Dunsford created this bottling and in the past it often contained some Cabernet Sauvignon to complement Shiraz.

I call it ‘old wine’s charm’. It’s old, almost as old as me. I’m not tired yet and hopefully still have some charm. This wine is a little tired however, it’s well-matured, with dusty exotic spice, dried fig, prune, the panforte of cooked, caramelised fruits. It has an interesting red fruit sweetness and a bit of a strawberry lift, salt and earthy density on the palate with soft to the touch but a bit flat tannins, slate-like. Finishing on a cool, minty note. A glass it is. 88points

The Vicar Shiraz 2008
Made by Michael Fragos since 2004 and later along with Bryn Richards, the senior winemaker. French and some American oak.

Full of glossy ripe black cherries and blackberries, shiny and pretty, tart fruit speak of still present freshness and ripeness tangled with umami, liquorice, creamy salted fudge, a bit of coconut slab and iodine, soy sauce palate with lots of energy. Great drinking now. 93-4points

Wine / Article: Chapel Hill The Devil House Block Shiraz 2020
Review Text:
A new name in the repertoire of Chapel Hill wines released to celebrate their 50th vintage (2024). The first vintage for Chapel Hill was 1975, but not for this particular wine. These Shiraz vines were planted in 1977 on the 0.8 ha block on the Chapel Hill Estate. Following the regeneration project, the chief winemaker Michael Fragos and the team felt that the vines were in great shape and ready to sand alone as a new flagship wine, The Devil. Before, the grapes from 1977 vines were used in the House Block bottling (formerly The Chosen) and this part of the name transfers into the new one. The bottle is heavy with an elegant, minimalistic ‘label’ or print that shapes the chapel’s window and quite nicely reads like a book’s spine while resting on its side, presumably for years, in the cellar. The impression is polished, potent wine. Staining, bloody, ferrous and peppery, salted black liquorice, black olive tapenade, violet pastille. Thick, dense and velvety flavour blankets the tongue. Sooty and chocolatey tannins, vanilla oak linger for a while. The power of concentration is here, locked tightly in the glass and only time will tame it. So give it some. I’m pretty certain this is a 95 point-er.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Surprise! Before you get to the 2022 release, a mini vertical of Abercrombie, 10 years apart.

2002 13.5%
Museum Release. Michael Kerrigan era, an era of 100% new oak. This is a blend of fruit from Mt Barker (60%) and Margaret River (40%).

Ah, the old wine charm. There are still some vivid reflections in this wine amidst its predominantly garnet colour. Strong tertiary pull, old polished leather, dried red capsicum, dried herbs, nuts and a glimmer of red fruit, spark of orange peel and some meatiness, like biltong for the lack of better comparison. Interestingly, it’s quite light, almost translucent and with soft, brittle graphite tannins. Surprisingly, at 22 years of age and 100% new oak, this wine doesn’t strike as either of these things on the face of it. A glass will do, however. 88pts

2012 14%
For this vintage Janice McDonald was in charge. It’s 60% new oak. Still then led by Great Southern fruit in the blend.

This wine makes a statement. Dark, brooding, boot paste, fresh leather and ripe black fruit, dense and fine velvety tannins, creamy core but ferrous on the edges with the grip building up, mint and sage refresh the lot. It’s full-on, soy sauce and a fair bit of toast, cocoa dusting, stewed meat, dark chocolate and all the density. All dark and sweet-toned. I have to say, this drinks very well now. I saw some age brackets ‘out there’ till 2047 and sure, it will survive, but honestly, I wouldn’t want to drink it at its very end. Drink it in the next 10 years perhaps. 94-95pts

2022 14.5%
This one is Nic Bowen’s wine. Oak pulled back to 25% new and 30% second year use and the rest is three years old barrels. All Margaret River.

Black tea leaves, tobacco, mint, lavender. Bright red fruit, currants, hints of raspberries and even blue fruit. Vanilla and hazelnut oak, sandy texture, lots of freshness, blue-fruited on the palate, lovely lightness but impactful flavour, with graphite tannins, still very fresh, stony and pure fruit finish. 94+pts

Bonus: I dug out my note of 2022 when I tasted it a year ago [May23]
A good mix of red and black fruit, black cherries and raspberries, and a hint of blue fruit too. It’s a blood-rich mouthfeel, electric almost, lightly salty, with plenty of velvety tannins, elegant oak, all well-measured. Powdery finish. It’s a cool, calm, collected wine with purity of fruit, quality tannins and a great potential to age. Very fresh now! 95+pts

2021 – wasn’t made.
2020 – I tasted briefly some time ago but from memory it didn’t show as well, however, will leave this open-ended.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Australia & New Zealand wine tasting [APR 2024] – Terre à Terre, Blank Canvas, Kumeu River, Flametree, Holm Oak, Greystone, Polperro, Prophet’s Rock, Elephant Hill, Eisenstone, Obsidian, Taltarni.
Review Text:
Just as Australia and New Zealand have a friendly rivalry going on, and no less on the wine front, I’d like to think there should always be a friendly push and pull of forces within the wine community. The healthy competition if you will in the spirit of ‘sharing is caring’. This and a few other thoughts popped up in my head while tasting and comparing all the excellent wines from AU and NZ. This happened at a sommelier tasting led by Huon Hooke and Stephen Wong MW under the banner of The Real Review. Reporting back from competition, you’d think! On a personal note, I worked briefly with TRR and enjoyed it thoroughly just as I enjoy writing and tasting for The Wine Front. And as Huon said about the pairs of Australian and New Zealand wines we sampled and inevitably compared, ‘It’s not a competition, it’s a celebration’ and I see this fit largely in life. Hear, hear! Funnily enough, after a quick preference vote at the end of the tasting (can we help ourselves?), it was clear and as noted by Stephen, New Zealand… won. Fine by me! I think I spread the love equally. Notes as follows.

Terre à Terre Crayères Vineyard Sauvignon Blanc 2022, 13.5%
Lemon sorbet! What a fantastic pure fresh lime flavour with flint, smoky undertones, lime leaf, crushed lemongrass and that beautiful elusive balance of softness and tension creating a smooth experience hard to capture in wine. Fine wine. It finished on a zing and preserved ginger note releasing warmth while carrying a green sweet apple and ‘minerality’ long into the aftertaste. 95 points

Blank Canvas Abstract Three Rows Sauvignon Blanc 2019, 13.5%
Comes across as a richer, fully flavoured style with grilled, white stone fruits and sweet citrus. It has a just-ripe character which is quite satisfying with a hint of vanilla bean note in the after-sniff. Then more toasted cashews and papaya flesh plushness in texture. Flavours and aromas are somewhat weighty, sitting low, filled with sweet almond perfume and ruby grapefruit. Satisfying all up indeed. 93 points

Kumeu River Hunting Hill Chardonnay 2022, 13.5%
It speaks understated power straight away. That kind of quiet confidence. Needs time to open up. There’s a strong sensation of yoghurty creamy notes with lemon zest. Cool river stones, flinty stream of freshness with Nashi pear, white flowers, yellow grapefruit and green melon. Very elegant detail spectrum. Minerally and savoury. It warms up and gives oaky notes more prominently in the likes of barky spice, hints of cinnamon and cloves, dusty wood. This is such a lovely wine when given time. 95 points

Flametree SRS Chardonnay 2022, 13%
Big boi here. Caramel and burnt orange peel, mint, with a hint of popped corn, tropical fruit curd, punchy stone fruit mid-palate, ricotta peach pastry. It’s a mouthful! It’s a bit chewy and fleshy with more descriptors pushing on the tongue like pineapple flesh and grapefruit pith. Being picky, lacks a note of finesse or that effortless elegance, having a bit of sweet-sour steely finish. Good wine, nonetheless, of a style and rewarding opulence. 93 points

Holm Oak The Wizard Pinot Noir 2021, 13.5%
A prominent bouquet of assorted ripe red fruit. Juniper berries, cloves, pine needles type of highly pitched fresh aromatic green note. It’s plush and soft and spicy, a bit stewed and peppery with a juby tone of red liquorice. Bitter and perfumed, almost grapefruity finish, a bit broad to end with some lingering bitterness of dusty peanut husk and dried peppermint. All that held together by gentle, silty, soft sitting tannins that build up with each sip. Nicely put together. 93 points

Greystone Pinot Noir 2019, 14%
Ripe on ripe, red and black fruit, black liquorice, cherry liqueur and exotic spice. The whole structure feels broad-shouldered with hints of beef stock, dried mushrooms, and it’s a bit splintery to end with whiffs of coffee and dark cocoa tannins. Lacks a spark and some brightness but there’s a hidden charm in this darkness. Perhaps a bit more time is needed here. 92 points

Polperro Talland Hill Pinot Noir 2022, 13.5%
Let me say, there’s a lot of Pinot in this Pinot. Rose water, red liquorice and raspberry with a firm crunchy red cherry and tart cranberries. Super silky flow, very slippery with dark rock ‘minerality’ and moist forest floor underlying, hints of toast, mushrooms, bringing on a fair bit umami in this wine, add spice, bitter-acidic tension that peaks to finish, cloves, sage and you have a great complexity and great balance in a glass. 95 points

Prophet’s Rock Home Vineyard Pinot Noir 2022, 13.5%
I swear this drinks like Syrah. Tight with reduction, toasty and dark in profile, black cherry and plummy juice, roasted coffee, dried lavender and quite elegant sweet spice with aromatic pine resin but dark and bitter in flow, almost amaro type of feel. Slate-like tannins, cool and smooth but with a fine-grained texture and peppery to finish. Delicious medium-bodied, rich Pinot. 94 points

Elephant Hill Stone Syrah 2020, 13%
Dense perfume, sweet berries, liquorice, panforte, violet pastille. Quite meaty and bloody and for that matter all in all savoury on the palate. Smooth and silky. Plummy and staining. Minerally finish, iodine, salt and sage but still much fruit infusion with bright acidity. Tannins are leathery. Love the poise and grace here. 95 points

Eisenstone Ebenezer Shiraz 2021, 14.5%
Exotic spice, richness and forward fruit. Very juicy, very oaky, slippery, glossy too and creamy mid to finish. Figs and prunes, dates, plums, and cherry pie. In its richness, it manages to pull off a certain elegance and coolness to fruit. Finishes with dark rock dust grip and some iron tension. Lush style. 93 points

Obsidian Reserve The Mayor 2020, 14%
Red fruit led, cherries, currants. Pencil shavings, hints of violets and hazelnut oak. Delicate, gentle flow, medium weight and tannins are stony but soft and agreeable. Very approachable now. Quite pretty, floral and lifted. 94 points

Taltarni Old Vine Cabernet Sauvignon 2020, 14%
Grip and grit, spice and punch of flavour, black currant juice, with some rust and cola, then sweet, sour and bitter flavour contributing in thirds. It’s a vibrant, energetic and punchy wine. Perhaps more time needed to soften the edges. 92+ points

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Terre de l’Elu Magellan Cabernet Franc 2020
Review Text:
Charlotte and Thomas Carsin purchased Clos de l’Élu in 2008 and in 2010 converted it into certified organic farming. In 2018 they decided to leave the AOC and reclassify as Vin de France changing the name to Terre de l’Elu (the word ‘Clos’ is not allowed for Vins de France). Fine by me. The Magellan is a single parcel of 70+ years old vines. The soil is composed of volcanic ashes (ash tuff) and specific to them square stones, known as cinerite. Importer: Brix Fine Wines.

Very savoury and serious, dark fruit profile, restrained perfume shifts the focus onto texture. Dark rock, dark earth, bitter skins, bitter herbs. The perfume that slowly emerges is of roses and freshly ground coffee. Texture is thick and staining the palate with almost molasses feel and sprinkle of salt. But in general, it’s not too heavy or cloying or sweet at all. Beautiful and fine composition. This Cabernet Franc has all the grace.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Pedro Parra, the flying terroirist hired at Alikna works closely with the head winemaker Amelia Nolan. There’s a great focus on terroir and how individual patches of dirt may influence the wine at Alkina. Pedro compares Barossan vineyards to the Burgundian philosophy and he aims to produce as revered Grenaches as the ones of Comando G. The ambition is great. The wine is great too but it could always be greater. Polygon No. 3 is born of limestone and schist. 70% whole bunches.

Red berries, red cherries, red plum stain, lots of substance mid-way. White pepper and cinnamon pinch, hibiscus and sage, cherry kernel and almond nougat. All the fine notes. All so pretty, firm and assertive. It has a depth and vibration of flavour, it’s shapely and lithe. A steady stream of fine sandy tannins rolls smoothly on the tongue along with the detailed flavour. It’s textural but soft. It’s a lovely wine of greatly thought structure.

Seems Mitolo folk like to use oak. And that’s fine. I took a long, hard look at oak in wine and its quality and amount, given there’s a good fruit base. Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
I travelled to Europe in December (2023) and I promised myself it would be the last time I do this in winter. I have a huge aversion to snow and darkness. Good thing they make wine there. The trip started with Champagne and during my two-day escapade to the region, I managed to visit three houses of different production sizes and philosophies. The flashy, Disneyland-like, filled with abstract art installations in every corner of the historical chalky cellars (crayères), Vranken-Pommery, made an impression of being… well, a Disneyland for adults. Charles Heidsieck, much more elegant, somehow looked modestly (against the V-P) and had a modern-designer tasting room with neat, plain crayères underneath. To get to the last place, I had to take a train from Reims to Epernay and then a cab to Vertus.

From my brief taxi ride observations, I thought Champagne was a pretty flat region, Vertus was a small village and everything looked quite miserable on a rainy winter arvo just as if it was taken from Baudelaire’s Fleurs du Mal Spleen II.

‘When low skies weightier than a coffin-lid
cast on the moaning soul their weary blight,
and from the whole horizon’s murky grid
its grey light drips more dismal than the night;’

Then, a ray of sun peeked out of the darkness—a sparkling wine from people who take care of their land and get muddy shoes. It’s not common to get muddy shoes in Champagne despite all the rain. In many places, the soil is overworked with chemicals, making it compacted and hard to mix with water. So some people work in the vineyards wearing sneakers. And they laugh at those who wear gumboots, like Sophie Larmandier. She was telling me this story, while her son, George, showed me around their property. Larmandier-Bernier winery is a modern, squeaky clean space filled with warm wood and bright light. The majority of base wine matures in barrels. There are a few ceramic and concrete eggs nursing wine experiments. We walked through the barrel room and then downstairs to a relatively small cellar. There were no wooden pupitres showcasing manual handling aka riddling. But there were efficient gyro-palettes and no pretending how things are done here. There were no expensive art installations. But the plain and rugged, pure chalk walls surrounding stacks of wine. So um, yes, there was art there—closed in the glass.

All of the NV L-B bottles have a very fine code imprint at the base denominating vintage and disgorgement time if you’re want to be super exact. E.g. 200223 – 2020 harvest, disgorged Feb 2023. My tasting notes are below.

Rosé de Saignée 12.5%
For this rose approximately 10% of Pinot Gris was blended in. At L-B vineyards in Vertus, Gris is planted amongst and in place of some of the old Pinot Noir vines consequently adding complexity and interest to this wine. It’s a true field blend too, Noir and Gris are harvested and macerated together for around three days. Bled-off and pressed juice are used. I tasted the 2020 harvest base wine disgorged in February 2023. What else could you ask of pink bubbles? Bright raspberries, cranberries and freshly cut roses. There are plenty of sour-umami notes, cooked rhubarb, red apples, blood orange, rosemary, gingerbread and a light note of wet forest and mushrooms. All firm, tense and long. Pure and so darn delicious. 94pts

Latitude Blanc de Blancs Extra Brut 12.5%
Latitude comes from the same area as Rosé de Saignée, south of Vertus. 100% Chardonnay, 40% perpetual reserve wine, 2020 harvest, disgorged in February 2023. Citrus, candied orange skin and ginger biscuit, almonds and aniseed top note. The texture is like silk with nuances of Beurre Bosc pears, lightly baked apple, dried mushrooms and rock salt. There’s that haunting umami theme here. It’s a fine combination of flavours. 93pts

Longitude Blanc de Blancs Extra Brut 12.5%
Longitude comes from the vineyards of Vertus, Oger, Avize and Cramant, which form a line close to the 4th meridian. 100% Chardonnay, 40% perpetual reserve wine, 2020 harvest, disgorged in April 2023. In this edition, Longitude feels richer than Latitude. The creamy element is more evident here but it’s still a linear and elegant wine. Hints of sweet ricotta-filled pastry, lemon zest, vanilla curd, marzipan and a gunflint note to close. It’s solid, ripe fruit underneath with density and length. 93+pts

Terre de Vertus Brut Nature 2016 12%
This wine is an expression of a single terroir. It’s a parcel called Les Barillers, situated mid-slope in Vertus. A more careful oak regime is applied in the form of a big, old foudre. One word. Minerality. You can understand the meaning of it in this wine. Crushed rock dust, scents of wet rocks and fresh air after rain, then hazelnut husk, built on pure citrus, lemon, a hint of orange and grapefruit skin. All so smooth. So minerally. 95pts

Teaser: I got to taste the 2017 release, it will be ready for European spring 2024. It feels more powerful than 2016, vibrant with hazelnut pastry and paste, dark slate and meaty bits, a bit denser and richer, with a strong dairy/cheesy character and chewy mid and back palate. We shall revisit. At this stage 95+pts

Les Chemins d’Avize Extra Brut 2015 12.5%
2015 was a hot vintage. Grand Cru. From the website: ‘Originating from our two vieilles vignes vineyards in the heart of Avize and the latest of special Champagnes, this distinguished cuvée should be tasted on “alone together” occasions…’ Awww, cute. It’s a powerful wine. Full in flavour, generous, broad and it feels like thick velvet blanketing comfortably the taste buds with a limey acid and grapefruity chewiness. There’s a raisin toast lifted aroma, ripe citrus and rose water top note, with caraway seeds to match. Excellent. 96pts

Another teaser, the taste of coming in spring 2024 release Les Chemins d’Avize 2016. 2016 was a cooler vintage than 2015. The wine at this stage is very lactic, packed tightly with gunflint and grapefruit pith and peel, much much tighter than the 2015. There’s rock salt and crushed sea shells with sandy-feeling bubbles. For now it’s 95+pts, great potential is there, for sure.

Vieille Vigne du Levant Extra Brut 2014 12%
From Cramant Grand Cru Chardonnay vines of min. 56 and more than 80 years old. It used to be called Vieille Vigne de Cramant but because it was confused with ‘crémant’ sparkling, it took on the name of its place, Bourron du Levant. This has moved into the tertiary development and merged ripe fruit with sweet spices. Hints of caramel and nougat, yellow peach and a hint of dried pineapple. The concentration is amazing, sinking deep and with a satin, cool mouthfeel. Stunning. 95pts

Special Club Extra Brut 1995 12%
Well, this was… special. The other name for the Special Club is Club de Trésors, founded in 1971 to highlight the unique terroir in wine of each participating grower-producer. Larmandier-Bernier has been a member, produced some Special Club bottlings and has left since. Others come and go too. This is 100% Chardonnay from Vertus disgorged in November 2018. It has strongly moved into the tertiary zone with spice, caraway, dusty oak, rum raisin, hints of dried pineapple and some cooked mushrooms, super soft but still lively bubble. Dried apricot, dried chamomile and that spiky bright acidity making the final spark and a statement. Aged beauty. 92pts

Review Text:
I visited Oliver Rapson during my stay in Victoria for the Victorian Wine Show earlier this year. Here’s a new thing from Mount Pleasant, a Light Dry White. It’s a blend of three grapes, Fiano, a high acid cognac variety—Montils from original O’Shea’s planting and old vine Semillon. Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Rippon Retrospective + New Release Tasting – October 2023
Review Text:
How often do you look at wines from a cosmic perspective?

Nick Mills didn’t start the tasting with descriptions of his wines, winemaking techniques or not even the history of his winery. No, he zoomed out on the big picture and told us how we got THERE. The story of the journey. I haven’t been to Rippon yet, nor have I met Nick before but the unparalleled connection to land, understanding of natural forces and unconditional dedication to the living thing were, to say the least, palpable within the first minute.

He talked about the creation of the rocks and phrases such as ‘lunar formation’, ‘skin of the rock’, and ‘film of life coating’ filled the room. And they resonated. It was a bit like listening to a mad scientist. It reminded me of my uni days during physics lectures that didn’t talk about the equations but the magic of the forces that rule this universe. I fell in love with physics that day.

Nick spoke so beautifully. About fruit precision and articulation of tannins, articulation of detail. ‘It all speaks through the winemaker himself’, he said. About terroir, ‘It’s shape, form and feel coming from the living tissue of its own accord. You can’t smell a seed—it’s about the shape and the tannin.’

He refused to define the wines in aroma and flavour descriptors, but he turned our attention to the body, the energy and the flow of the wines instead. I couldn’t help but write some blatant descriptors myself, though definitely felt the vibrating life encapsulated in these bottles. And you’d be mad not to.

MB was on the wines a year ago and he has a much better feel of the place and the history than I do. Nevertheless, we share a bunch of the same scores, so I think it’s a pretty good outcome and good to see the wines on the roll. Thanks for the stories, Nick.

Sauvignon Blanc 2021, 13%
Razor-sharp aroma reaching deep into the nostrils. The purest form of the freshest ginger. Then warm flint rocks and lemongrass. It’s firm white peaches, limey zing and a hint of honey. It’s a wine of ultra purity, clarity and clean-cut definition of fruit. The execution of aromas and flavours is flawless. Amazingly, it’s plush to the touch, talcum powder softness and fine texture, yet it travels far with precision and firmness. So beautifully aware. Next level experience. 95

Rippon Rippon Pinot Noir

2020, 13.68%
Very seductive start, with a savoury toast of oak as a top note. There’s an amazing tension in this wine, with blood orange zing and a tart cherry lingering in the back of the hazelnut skin. It’s a piercing tension of flint and iodine. Tannins vibrating chaotically but they will fall into place. 94+points, drink: 2026 – 2036+

2019, 13.6%
This is the current release, as of the end of 2023. Gee, the END of 2023. A wine that immediately presents itself a as complete picture, even if only at four years of age. The fruit shines, acidity drives, tannin assures. In other words, it’s crushed rock, dusty old wood, clay, and fresh forest floor, it’s juicy and detailed with raspberry and cranberry, wet bark and haunting perfume of bitter herbs and roses. A bit of meatiness for good measure and savoury balance. 94 points

2016, 13.4%
2016 was a perfect year apparently. This wine is still waiting to be released. I reckon it’s in a good spot already. It’s very firm and savoury. Stony and full flavoured but not heavy. Blood orange territory, red brick tension, dried blood, button mushrooms, autumnal leaves, juicy and bitter finish, cherry kernel note follows through. A sea of black tea tannin. Interestingly, I feel the foreshadowing of tertiary development or is it just so much umami? Hard to tell. The distinctive tension and vibrancy hold it all high and tight, however. The quality is undeniable. 95points, drink: 2024-2034

2008, 13%
It’s a sweet sixteen. Warm year. And man, you can feel it in the glass. Brown hue. It feels tertiary to me with truffles and lipstick, figs and sarsaparilla or muscovado sugar and pomegranate reduction lending the lift. Awashed with black tea, the flavours leave behind a trace of sweet briar rose and savoury rye whisky spice, it’s warming, but the tannins are of great quality, still fine and flowing. It’s its time, but the charm remains in its veins. 91-2points

Emma’s Block Pinot Noir

2020, 13.5%
High notes of acidity and perfume reaching high up in the nostrils. Bit of a cherry pie, some toast and hazelnut/almond nuance. Juicy and infused with blood orange, red fruit spectrum, bright crunchy cherry, squeaky and with a hint of ground coffee. Beautiful. It has a bright future, this one. 95points

2019, 13%
Lifted perfume, there’s some oyster shell, seaweed type of high note, also a raw meaty element, chewy and lifted salty palate. Spiced cherry. Silty tannins and ultra savoury, mushroom and pepper finish. Keeping up with the rest in finesse. 95points

2018, 13.7%
This one is gamey, with dead flowers, some dried petals, and dried blood, feels bigger than others, sitting mainly in the mid-palate, chewy and with a high rolling wave of fine tannins. Long-steeped black tea, a darker feel of fruit in it, almost plummy profile. Cedarwood, elegant but strong clove perfume. Broader and fuller. Comfortable. 94points

Tinker’s Field Pinot Noir

2020, 13.72%
Deep into the cherry spectrum, fresh and cooked, some hints of bitter-sweet almond. Some plum and fresh fig too, power and presence yet elegance and a very cool wet river stones flow. Meanwhile, it’s juicy and with a blood orange tang, a hint of coffee and fine-grained silty tannins. Poise. Tension and fine fine detail. Peppery finish. Very graceful. 96+points, drink: 2025-2040

2019, 13.6%
Feels riper than 2020, with sweet cherry and bitter herbs, some toast with almonds, and an even flow of flavour, spread but taut at the same time, all balanced. Bit of tar and cold smoke. And bitter-sweet finish. Fresh rose and fresh forest after rain feel and lots of substance too. 95points

2018, 13.2%
Cherry-themed with a decaying element, meat, dead flowers, rubbed spice and sous-bois, potpourri, iron-mineral undertone and dusty red brick. It’s all power and elegance, grace with confidence. So well structured with black tea tannins, silty, fine-boned, cumin crushed spice and aniseed aftertaste. Just stunning. 97points

2021 Gewurztraminer, 13.5%
Pink guava and sweet cucumber, it’s a hyper-refreshing wine. Just off-dry like watermelon with mint and a hint of rose, candied pink grapefruit, almond friand and a brown lime. The texture is pithy and lightly phenolic but the feel is melting and satin-cool. You just want to guzzle it. Amazing. 94points

2021 Mature Vine Riesling, 12.5%
Lemon curd and lemon balm, candle wax, lemon tea and peach, a hint of pineapple and mandarine. Off-dry with a wild honey vibe balanced by bitter grapefruit tang and umami cheese rind. Texturally alluring and very nourishing feel. It’s good for you. 94points

2015 Mature Vine Riesling, 12.3%
It’s developing, no doubt. It’s so complete too. Maturing. Honey biscuit, almonds, quite nutty and honeyed finish with bitter lemons. It has a cold Hot Toddy feel with green tea tannin. Burnt sage, nuts, toast. It has it all. 95points

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
So, GW handed me the big guns, the Double Zero EGW 21 and VGW 21, and I swear I heard, “All right, everybody be cool, this is a robbery!”

Capital letters on the label for a capital CHARDONNAY. Pineapple tarte Tatin, cinnamon bacon pancakes made with baking soda, very American-themed. There’s that fatty, salty electric type of sensation rounding off the mouthfeel. A truckload of flavour. 18-wheeler. This is a solid block of Chardonnay’s DNA and artifact taken to a mega-sized level. And you chew on it, and you chew on it and it opens up and lifts the back palate penetrating long and deep. YET, it manages to grace with a soft, talcum powder (baking soda?) and slate-like touch. There’s so much to unpack, it’s a very detailed wine. It’s peaches and cream, shaved nutmeg and thick grapefruit skin. There’s sweetness and spice. Utter power. Walks such a fine line between being hungry for more and being full to the brim. Just escapes the flabby, the too oaky, the inelegant loud type. So powerful you can overdose but you keep coming back for more. Just what I did. This is, in essence, the statement of excellent quality and winemaking skills. No doubt you’ll get your satisfaction here.

Caveat: must love strong expressions of Chardonnay, Honey Bunny.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Southern Light Vineyards Ghostgum Vineyard Chardonnay 2021
Review Text:
A new wine from the hands of Anthony Fikkers, the head of winemaking and viticulture at Joval Family Wines. As Anthony puts it, the Joval is negociants turning into vignerons, at least for some of it, with the focus on viticulture and intention of growing own grapes. In Mornington, they bought part of the site and lease the other, at the top of Main Ridge and its red volcanic soils only planted to Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Ghostgum Vineyard wines are first Mornington expression of the varieties for Anthony. 20% new oak, 30 year old vines, hand-picked. 150 dozen made.

A hit of lively aromas, orange peel, tarragon, cumin, melon skin, peach. The perfume turns into the likes of pastis, herbal with a sweet tune, laced with cedar, crushed bark spice, and almond friand for the leesy notes. Excellent mid-palate weight, filled with stone fruit and a hint of pineapple, concentration is there but the wine is not heavy. Chalky aftertaste follows with a high cleansing acidity but it’s milky soft. Elegant and satisfying flavours are spread evenly. Pretty good debut with Mornington fruit but I guess it’s no incident, just good fruit and skilled winemaking. Touch and go 94pts as GW would say.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Louis Roederer Philippe Starck Brut Nature 2015
Review Text:
Bear with me on the ramble below.

A thought-provoking and appetite-inducing Champagne class was organised recently by John Noble of Champagne Bureau Australia, in company with panel chairs present Annette Lacey MW, Kate McIntyre MW and Peter Bourne. The question of dosage in Champagne was raised along other comments on Champagne not ever falling into the low-intervention category given how much is done to it during production (drink pet-nats?). Anyway, back to the sugar addition. An article by Tom Stevenson was brought up and his views on Champagne ageing gracefully only if there’s a certain level of sugar involved. A whole lot of chemistry was mentioned to support this but not any scientific research particularly targeting the issue (maybe it’s been done since). However, the article was a great starting point. Generally, for wine to age, good quality of fruit, depth and length as well as high acidity are needed. Aside organoleptic sensations and preferences for wines with or without sugar, it poses a question if Champagne’s chemistry (disgorgement process too) is different to other still and dry wines and their ability to age gracefully. What’s your experience with aged zero dosage Champagne? Over to you, but first, let me tell you how delicious this brut nature was.

46% Chardonnay, 37% Pinot Noir, 17% Meunier. 0g dosage and no malolactic conversion took place. 2015 was a pretty hot vintage.

Plain raw citrus, crunch and flint dust. Candle wax and waxy green apples. Wow, this is hyper-racy, bone-dry on the palate, pure, crisp and clean-cut. Preserved lemons and briny quality, faint sweetness of just ripe Mirabelles and quince. Salt pushed to the edges of the tongue, squeezing saliva out of the cheeks. It finishes on raw bread dough and green grapefruit. It’s a delicious savoury style, appealing to umami-craving drinkers. The texture and the bubble are of mineral water, tonic spritz and a light Fino sherry. I don’t think it will necessarily get much better with time but sure am curious how it would age and develop. Sprinkle instead of lemon on oysters, said Peter Bourne. I’ll take it.
