Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
I took a Pelican flight to Mudgee and I don’t ride roller coasters of any sort voluntarily. I used to play RollerCoaster Tycoon, that’s how far my need for adrenaline rush goes when it comes to small metal constructions dropping in the air. Nevertheless, the 19-seat twin turboprop airliner Jetstream 32 took me safely to Mudgee’s airport, the tiniest of airports. From there I joined Mudgee Readers’ Festival gatherings, where I listened to the stories and talked about putting wine into words.

Rhys Gard, the Festival’s Creative Director wrote a wine-crime novel set in Mudgee’s vineyard landscape, titled Four Dogs Missing. I haven’t read it yet, but will do so soon as it combines two of my reading interests, fermented grape juice and cold-blooded murders. Overall, it was very refreshing to meet authors of various genres at the Festival and not talk about wine technicalities for a little while (yes!). Just when I thought I was out, wine pulled me back in and I found myself in front of a row of bottles made by Mudgee-based producers (OK, I asked for it). Hence this article and a tasting report.

Disclaimer: Not all wines that I tasted came from Mudgee-grown fruit, as many winemakers source grapes from neighbouring Orange and Hilltops regions. I call it a Mudgee tasting to turn the attention to the local community, the potential of the region and the skills of local winemakers. But, it surely does raise a question of why Orange fruit plays such an important role and why Mudgee winemakers proudly put their Orange-sourced wines to the front. Regardless of the grapes’ origin, it was great to see creative expressions of non-mainstream varieties. Yet, many don’t reach the East Coast, which is mainly due to minute quantities. This may change in the future, or simply put, you need to visit Mudgee. Also, I added a few other drinks to the tasting, a spritz and a beer-wine hybrid. To all the producers I missed in my tasting, I’m looking forward to catching up with you next time.

Mudgee is a buzzing little town with an energetic community, blossoming Manchurian Pear trees, full of boutique shops, artisan cafes and hip beer joints. Its history is rich and dates back to the 1850s. Cabernet, Shiraz and Chardonnay still take the lead in the region’s production. However, there’s great potential in aromatic, textural whites and bright, alpine reds.

Last thing, I just purchased and started reading (while walking), the new Max Allen book, Alternative Reality; the immediate connection between alternative varieties, Dr Thomas Fiaschi and Mudgee region was made. As I learnt from another book that I also purchased recently (in Mudgee), Some of My Best Friends Are Winemakers by Gil Wahlquist, Dr Thomas Fiaschi brought Italian and French varieties to Australia, planted them at his Hawkesbury River Tizzana vineyard and then in Eurunderee, which he called the Mudgee Vineyard. He was a renowned surgeon and once delivered a lecture on The Various Wines used in Sickness and Convalescence. He strove to improve the quality of agricultural shows across Australia. No less, Gil Wahlquist was a great advocate and promoter of organic farming and low-intervention winemaking. In 1971 he started Botobolar in Mudgee, one of Australia’s oldest certified organic wineries. This is probably a good moment to conclude and reflect one more time, that Mudgee has a great history and a bright future.

Yeates Albariño 2023, Mudgee, 13%
I met Sarah Yeates as she was running around the busy cellar door. Busy is good. Nice to see a Spanish white variety doing well here. This is its second vintage from an organic vineyard. It’s a moderately aromatic Albariño, with lemongrass, apples and stone fruit on the slightly underripe crunchy side, lemon balm, salt crystals and a bit of yellow grapefruit juice with a very pleasant bitterness to finish and briny residue. A lovely drink. 91pts

Edan Sauvignon Blanc 2022, Orange, 13%
From a young duo, Carla and Ashton, who source organic fruit and pursue minimal intervention in the winery. This Sauvignon Blanc is a Fumé in style with an attractive flinty overtone, nuttiness, stone fruit, yellow plums, river stones, tonic with mint and cucumber and pithy pomelo vibes. It’s very light, very refreshing and super pleasing with a gentle and fine texture of talcum powder and a little spice to finish. So appealing! 92pts

Jessop Riesling 2022, Orange, 11.5%
Chris Jessop has experience honing his Riesling vinification skills in Germany and the proof is in the Riesling. This one is unfined and unfiltered, fermented in old oak and left on lees for 6 months. It tells a story of texture. Preserved lemons, grilled nuts, and ripe citrus with ripe stonefruit. It’s full of flavour and continues with sweet blossoms, ginger spice and lavender. Pretty smooth but thick in a way like creamed honey. Lemon tea refreshment at the end no less. So very good. 93pts

Logan Ridge of Tears Riesling 2022, Orange, 12%
This wine won Bester Riesling trocken aus der Neuen Welt at 2023 Meininger’s International competition receiving 90 punkte. While getting the accolade is great, how it’s 90 points, I’m not sure. Wild yeast fermentation in old neutral oak with a year on lees. Smells very fresh with high notes of lime leaves and salt, like a mezcal Margarita with a flinty/smoky aftertaste. It’s briny with the perfume of lavender, chamomile and orange skin in the mouth and a hint of candle wax. Pure and sleek feeling flavours, seamless flow and a lingering finish. Very well done. 93punkte

Slowfox Chardonnay 2022, Mudgee, 13%
Slowfox is a family-run project with a couple, Kate and Rob, standing behind it. Wines are made with minimal intervention in mind. What a beautiful wine this is. A pleasant step down from big and buttery and a step up in freshness. There is some spice and concentration on the palate, apples with cinnamon dust and ginger, cashews, and lightly smoked almonds. Lots of good energy, piquant flavours and a satisfying mid-palate chew. With substance and bite. 92pts

Skimstone Chardonnay 2022, Mudgee, 14.4%
At Skimstone, the winemaker and vineyard manager, Jean-François, takes steps to implement sustainable farming. This is a richer style of Chardonnay with caramel swirls and honeyed nuts, a bit of peach and cream, chewy pineapple slices. Good hit of flavours, lingering, a bit of tinned corn aftertaste, but the concentration holds up well with the alcohol content it has. Generous old-school vibes that may need a bit of fine-tuning but will bring satisfaction to some. 89pts

Manners Wine Übergew 2022, Mudgee, 12.5%
James Manners is the man who made this Gewürztraminer. Wild fermentation in the barrel, unfined and unfiltered. This name reminds me of a line from Friends about a laundry detergent, ‘Uberweiss. It’s new, it’s German, it’s extra tough.’ Übergew is back, it’s Mudgee, it’s extra good. Orange blossom, golden kiwi, papaya, honeydew sweetness, less of the rose water perfume. It’s more of a candied citrus profile, almost watermelon kind of freshness, some ruby grapefruit and raw almonds. It feels dry, beautifully refreshing, minty and very well-made for an aromatic style. It finishes salty, a bit like an electrolyte type of drink. It has layers and a character and I like that a lot. 94pts

Manners Rosé of Sangiovese 2023, Mudgee, 12.5%
This is a pretty straightforward rosé with no obstacles on the way to your enjoyment. Cherries and cranberries at the core, a bit of sweetness with cinnamon spice. It has the feel of a peach iced tea. Simple and refreshing but well made and easy to drink fast. 89pts

Edan Pinot Shiraz 2022, Orange, 13.2%
Here is one of my fave blends. Made with partial carbonic maceration. It takes over as a Pinot with green olive crunch, sour cherries, cranberries, a bit of compote style, but also tart red fruit show their zing. It finishes on a pomegranate bitter tang, it has some notes of decaying leaves and bark, wet earth and mossy wood which add a savoury element and a fresh green lift. 90pts

Skimstone Barbera 2021, Mudgee, 14%
It’s a reductive start, smoked wood, roasted beetroot, red fleshy plums. It’s a bit twiggy and drying with cocoa powder tannins and dusty oak. The tannin structure is, however, well-fleshed and complemented by ripe fruit. The finish has a fine dust of black pepper, coffee and sweet-sour tones. Comes out as a medium-weight and drinks as a generous style. 88pts

Edan Sangiovese 2021, Mudgee, 13.5%
Beautiful to look at, bright ruby colour. It’s also bright in the mouth, with tart cranberries, pomegranate, fresh button mushrooms and wet clay feel of tannins. Savoury with a hint of liquorice or crushed cumin, cloves, tarragon and a hint of sweet almond. Succulent and mouthwatering with a sour cherry and gently warming finish. No brainer delicious drinking. Pizza night it is. 92pts

Samantha May Cabernet Franc 2022, Orange, 14%
Sam Sutherland is based in Mudgee and works with Orange fruit at Gilbert Family Wines. She’s done AgriFutures Rural Women’s Acceleration grant in Georgia. Exciting. Super small production, with three wines on the website and all sold out. Now I know why. Super enticing perfume, a mix of violets, cherries, wet earth and leaves. It’s built with a great mid-palate red plummy fruit, chewy, spicy and textural. It’s aromatic a bit like sweet red vermouth, bitter herbs, spice of black pepper, raspberries, hints of fresh leather. Tannins are medium and dusty and this drinks like a charm. Like a charm. 93pts

Slowfox Cabernet Sauvignon Malbec 2022, Mudgee, 14.5%
Immediately gets you with a Cabernet appeal. Full of red and black currants, lifted perfume of wet tobacco leaves and more fresh berries thrown in. There’s a melange of sweet and tart flavours, raspberry and fresh green pepper spice and bright acidity. Medium on the tannin front and perky. It’s quite fresh in style and of moderate weight making it easy to sip on. 92pts

Samantha May Syrah 2022, Orange, 13.5%
Neutral oak, unfined, unfiltered. Amaretti biscuits lift the perfume to start, then olives, raspberries and ripe cherries. It’s quite light in flavour, flowing but not smooth, there are some chewy red plum skins and a slightly gritty texture. It’s all energetic and perky. Some more notes of green peppercorn and freshly ground coffee come along. Lacks just a touch more drive towards the finish, but it’s very easy to drink and enjoy. So please do. 91pts

Logan Ridge of Tears Shiraz 2021, Mudgee, 13.5%
I like my Shiraz meaty. And this one is. Bloody steak dusted with black pepper, juicy, very savoury, with ripe cherries and raspberries carrying the umami notes on top. It’s mostly red fruit but just ripe, nothing overly jammy. It has lifted potpourri fumes and just enough squeaky tannins to be moreish and not overwhelmingly drying, finishing with a clean Earl Grey tea flavour. All in place and charming. It’s a very appetising style. 93pts

Manners Shiraz 2022, Hilltops, 14.5%
From a Moppity vineyard in Hilltops. Perfumed, potpourri, iodine tones too. It’s chewy with lots of flavour and aromatic orange skin spiked with cloves. It has a great mid-palate concentration, hits you with flavour, spice and herbs, and freshness. There’s plenty of fruit and oak that could use some time to merge. 92+pts

Yeates Shiraz 2019, Mudgee, 14.8%
This is such a joyful Shiraz. Mix of fruit, juicy plums, tart blackberries, sweet cherries and some blue fruit too. It’s medium-bodied if not light, just super easy to drink, sloshy and fruity, slightly beetroot-earthy. Let me say, Beaujolais-esque in style. Lively and fresh. Mouthwatering. I’m happy. 89pts

Yeates Jack Roth Shiraz 2018, Mudgee, 14.5%
Wine made by Jacob Stein. It feels serious. Dried fruit, ripe blackberries a mix of Chinese five spice, dusty cocoa powder tannins. The flow is good, albeit tannins are ample. There’s a milk chocolate creamy weight in the middle. The oak feels a bit too much to my liking but it may need more time to settle and some food. 89+pts

Heslop Touriga Nacional 2019, Mudgee, 13%
Heslop family makes small amounts of sustainably handled wines. Touriga in Mudgee! How cool. Full of dark fruit, spice and ripeness, fresh leaves, stewed meat, and blackcurrant concentration, just like Ribena. But hold on, there’s a savoury and meaty edge to it. Sweet-sour a bit fizzy finish, but overall very interesting, with a solid flavour hit and refreshment factored in. 90pts

Heslop’s Mr Rascal Bush Botanical 2022, Mudgee, 18.5%
Liam and Bob Heslop made this wine. It’s a co-fermented White Frotnignac, Chardonnay and Vermentino fortified and aromatised with native Australian herbs. Something of a medium-sweet white Vermouth. Cool! And fair enough, it’s syrupy with Bergamot orange, candied citrus, sweet herbs, tarragon, lemon myrtle, liquorice, sweet blossoms and cucumber tones. It may be a bit too much on its own, so I see it go down well on ice, perhaps with a splash of soda and a slice of lime, which, sadly, I didn’t get a chance to put to the test. 89pts

Three Tails Brewery Two Worlds Collide Rosé/Shiraz Lager, Mudgee, 7.9%
This is the hip beer joint in Mudgee I was referring to at the beginning. Wine and beer combos are not new, but always fun to explore. TTB does collabs with winemakers. For 2023 they teamed up with Robert Stein. Direct pressed Shiraz juice blended with Lewis Street Lager. It speaks change of seasons. Invigorating for spring and comforting in autumn. No doubt, there’s a fruity lift, strawberries and cranberries with light bitterness and a herbal, dark amaro twist. Nicely done, but one is probably enough. 89pts

Edan Spritz, Mudgee, 8%
Well, this is something else. Pomegranate juice with Muscat and Gewürztraminer. The blush colour comes from pomegranate juice, but just. It has more of an aroma than the taste of pomegranate. There are strawberries, sweet red apple, hibiscus and other sweet blossoms and a light bitter grip for good balance. It has some Prosecco vibes with melon skin and pear drop. Super refreshing, lightly sweet bubbles and a fun drink, something different, a great alternative to a sparkling Moscato. I can see this work very well with spicy food. 90pts

Review Text:
Vincent Couche makes excellent idiosyncratic expressions of Champagne but clearly, he has talent with still wines too. The truth is, and the ultimate test when bubbles are gone, that great sparkling wine is first a great base wine, so it all makes sense that he does well without a second fermentation. 100% Chardonnay, Kimmeridgian limestone and marly clay, aged 2 years in amphora (30%) and oak barrel (70%).

Lively and energetic from the get-go. There’s something herbal about it, fennel, almonds, citrus skin. It’s pithy, limey, with a hint of cheese rind, yellow apples, and pears, all laced with salt and cool river pebbles mineral feel. A complete wine with a high pleasure index.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Domaine Vincent Couche Voulez-vous Couche avec moi? NV
Review Text:
With a surname like this, well, hard not to use this sentence. Of course, it’s all about drinking Vincent’s wine. Would you like to Vincent with me? Vincent does to his Burgundian creations what normally is done in Champagne, i.e. non-vintage and blends of red and white grapes, and vice versa, he does to his Champagne bottlings what regularly is done in Burgundy, i.e. single vineyard expressions, the importance of terroir, barrel fermentation etc. Therefore, this is a still multi-vintage blend of 2/3 Pinot Noir and 1/3 Chardonnay from the years 2018-2022, aged in amphora and oak barrels. Vin de France as obviously some very serious breaking of the rules happened to be called Bourgogne Appellation Contrôlée.

Interesting expression of a white wine, with lots of red berry and blossom aromas. Red apples, strawberries, hibiscus, pink peach. It’s salty and acidic with a great tension keeping the red and pink aromas alive and savoury. A bit like drinking flat Blanc de Noir but in a good way!

Review Text:
Cépage is 50% Pinot Noir, 50% Chardonnay. Pinot grows on Kimmeridgian limestone in Buxeuil, and Chardonnay on chalky-flinty soil in Montgeux. Also, there’s no dosage and fermentation happened in tanks as back in the day Vincent used more stainless steel than wood (which he does more of now). Late disgorged: May 2022.

Imagine all the aromatic baked goods, caramelised apricot tart, vanilla slice with flaky buttery French dough. Yes, all here. Then comes the ever refreshing bitter-salty mix, feel of slate ocean rocks with oyster shells minerality. Cool and smooth. What a fantastic balance. This wine, recently disgorged and 20+ years of age, is still so fresh, with pastry, umami, ocean breeze and zesty citrus. Such impressive stuff.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Let me introduce you to an exciting set of wines. From Slovakia. And please don’t say it’s from Czechoslovakia.

Bott Frigyes grows grapes on the volcanic soils of Južnoslovenská’s subregion of Muzsla Hill, where the Danube River sets the border between Slovakia and Hungary for nearly 150km. Vines are cultivated organically and biodynamically (uncertified) and are low-cropping. Ambient fermentation takes place in wooden barrels and amphorae. Most of the wines are bottled unfiltered with a minimal addition of sulphur.

These wines are brought to you by Andrew Wyse from Cardwell Cellars in Melbourne. He’s been to the region, met vignerons, drank wines, touched the soil and saw things. He’s done the tough part of importing them to Australia, and I’m happy to take on the tougher part of tasting them and spreading the news further…

Furmint. This dry Furmint is something else. Firstly, it’s not hugely aromatic. It gently invites with flint, curd, bread dough and nuts. Understated. Mouthwatering acidity, detailed, silky-smooth feel. Almost feathery touch. Mineral. It continues with chamomile tea, yellow grapefruit tang and a long-long dusty crushed slate finish. Reminds of a tonic water sensation, the lively, lifted mouthfeel. There’s a bit of everything here, a touch of sweetness, umami, flint, fine dusty texture and chewy acidity. Perfect drink.

Review Text:
I met with Vincent during his recent Australian tour showing his biodynamic Champagnes. Vincent doesn’t speak much English, so I decided to use my 10-year-forgotten and broken French. It went like this (for all the wines), I took a sip, my eyes widened, eyebrows lifted, I started to nod in affirmation in an awkward full-mouth smile and didn’t spit. Once swallowed, I exhaled and said ‘oh là là’. My best French and my best review. Or did Vincent understand Polish? Well, wine knows no boundaries.

‘Élégance’ is a blend of 84% Pinot Noir, 16% Chardonnay, 4g dosage and partially barrel fermented as many other Vincent’s wines. Base vintages are 2011-2019 and it was disgorged in July 2022. The release that follows this one (I haven’t tasted) has a new label, slightly different proportion of grapes and is Brut Nature. And I’m sure it’s as tasty.

At an entry level, this wine brings together a delicious combination of saline and nutty flavours. Appetising complexity of sweet perfume and brine. Ripe lemons, apricot Danish, red apple skins, oyster shell, apple pie, peanut brittle. Baked and fresh aromas with salt flakes and a bit of ginger spice to finish on a crisp note. What a start!

Review Text:
I went to a Champagne lunch the other day. The day that was probably the warmest on record in July in Sydney. Champagne lunch felt like the right choice on that glorious 24+C winter afternoon. Such a complete wine. It pushes flavour to the corners of the mouth. Complex and detailed. It’s a wholesome experience. Fine gentle mousse but firm enough to keep your palate energised. It smells of salted shortbread, quince and croissant with almond cream. Then nougat and razor-sharp acidity. Crème brûlée and salt flakes. Crunchy almonds and limey acidity. Oyster shell with lemon, the mineral note. Complete balance. And it’s long and delightful. I forgot about sparkling Shiraz for a moment. On that balmy winter day in Sydney.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Ansonica is otherwise known as Inzolia in Sicily. This one is sourced from Merbein Vineyard in Murray Darling. It’s a new addition to the Bio-Logical range at Lowe. I do like the whole organic and biodynamic approach and take on the climate-adaptable varieties that they embrace. However, I put a few question marks on the phrasing in the info that came with the wines. To me, low-intervention wine means a bit more than just sulphur-free, therefore preservative-free is more apt (which they use), as the yeast is cultured and the wines are filtered. I appreciate the winemaking challenges and transparency and while nothing’s wrong with doing so, I feel it sits slightly outside of the concept of low-intervention per se, even though the rules may not be set in stone. Following this, the clear glass (with the highest environmental impact) made me think about the overall bio-approach, while stylistically pleasing. Nevertheless, the organic and preservative-free strategy is worth supporting.

Inzolia is early to mid-ripening and drought-tolerant so perhaps well suited to the Australian climate, it loses acidity quickly, so needs to be picked early. This wine has good acidity. To start it’s not very aromatic, but the aromas it has are nutty and of ripe citrus and nectarines. It’s more about texture here. So there’s a pleasant phenolic grip, that slight bitterness of hazelnuts in skins, brown pear, furry peach skin. Hints of bitter herbs and honeysuckle. Overall it’s a nice white wine of some interest and texture. It’s sealed with Diam10 but I can’t see enough fruit concentration and acidity for it to age that long. Pleasant sipping no less.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Howard Park Wines Past, Present and Future
Review Text:
‘Family business is like extreme sport’, says Natalie Burch with a cheeky smile. She’s the second-generation and general manager at Howard Park. There’s playful humour in her tales. She’s a good storyteller, a raconteur. I’m a good storylistener. And a wine drinker. So I’m doing my task justice. We’re about to try over 20 Howard Park wines across vintages and varieties. Natalie brings us closer to the history of Howard Park, its founder, John Wade and all the successive winemakers up to the current one, Nic Bowen who, in turn, brings us closer to the wines themselves. It’s a delightful evening.

John Wade started Howard Park in 1985 and named it after his father. Back in 1978, John was a winemaker at Wynns Coonawarra and created the praised John Riddoch Cabernet Sauvignon. In 1993, the Burch family, Amy and Jeff, joined Howard Park. John left in 1998 and Michael Kerrigan (owner of Hay Shed Hill) took over the winemaking until 2007 when Tony Davis (co-founder of Snake + Herring) was in charge for four years. In 2011 and for the next 10 years the chief winemaker at Howard Park was award-winning Janice McDonald (now at Flowstone Wines). Since 2021, Nic Bowen who trained overseas, at Hardys and House of Arras, is now at the helm of Howard Park. He comes from a winemaking family and his mother, Denise, designed some of the beautifully painted labels.

Back to the tasting. It’s structured around the eras of the winemakers’ reign which is a chronological affair. I like that angle, however, it slightly disrupts the regular ‘first whites, then reds’ type of approach that allows for immediate tracking of the evolution of each wine. But! Nothing better than a change of routine and a palate challenge.

Note: The featured picture of this article is a painting by Australian artist Alexander Edgar Hills, whose art was sampled at the early labels of Cabernet et al. during the John Wade era. I couldn’t find the exact painting that was used on the label online, so here is an equally beautiful watercolour titled Into The Karris, 1981 (www.mutualart.com/).

John Wade
1992 Great Southern Riesling
The apogee of Riesling’s tertiary development. Golden colour, spiced honey, beeswax, dried lemon. Incredible perfume, honeyed and dried, chamomile extract, the palate is the same with honey lemon tea and gentle grip. I’ll add crushed rocks dust, hints of dried stonefruit and lemon candy, cause it’s there. A beautifully aged, fully mature Riesling. A treat. 93pts

1989 Cabernet Sauvignon
This is the wine with the label design sampled from an original painting by Alexander Hills and I love it. Stewed plums, raspberry jam, all tertiary, sweet tobacco, black tea coolness, pomegranate balsamic, light, dried violets and roses, some cooked spice and herbs, nutmeg, a bit gritty, sandy tannins but fleshed with acidity. Well-matured wine that held itself well. It’s the last moment to enjoy it. 90pts

Michael Kerrigan
2006 Great Southern Riesling
Lemon and lime zest, orange blossom, green pineapple skin, a hint of toast and utter softness of the seamless palate. It has a herbal extraction, a bit of a bay leaf, lime candy and hay. Still drinks so young and fresh. In a great spot encompassing freshness and maturity. 95pts

2004 Scotsdale Shiraz
Meaty with violets and earth, with power, black pepper and other savoury spice, suede type of tannin, sweet mix of dried berries, good intensity but fading into tertiary dusty and dried flavours. 91pts

2001 Abercrombie Cabernet Sauvignon
Mint and earth, sweet spice, some stewed fruit on the palate, fine silty tannin and blood orange tang, dried tobacco leaves, sweet cassis, a fair bit of chew and length. Good going for over 20 years but it’s time. 94pts

Tony Davis
2010 Porongorup Riesling
Eucalyptus lemon candy, plenty of salt and toast, zest but also cream, I love when a wine does it. Grapefruit and hints of orange peel but it’s rather light, savoury, very minerally and soft but with a dart-like acidity, focused, linear. Tingling tonic water, very refreshing and slightly developing but just. So much youthfulness. Let me add a hint of lanolin and cypress tree oil. It does what Riesling does best. 94pts

2008 Abercrombie Cabernet Sauvignon
Smells bright and still young, red plums, pencil shavings, cool and savoury, iron-rich mouthfeel, umami, mineral, this is still so beautifully vibrant and fresh, raspberries and leafy bits, very very soft satin-like tannins. There’s a hint of development of stewed compote fruit, dried earth, and dried raspberries. It’s a complete wine now, drink up. 95pts

Janice McDonald
2017 Grand Jeté
Peach Bellini and pastry with almond glaze, frothy mousse hitting mid-palate with good intensity and with more stone fruit and green apples, wet rocks mineral feel and a limey finish. I enjoy this combination of stonefruit + pastry + mineral acidity a lot. 93pts

2013 Allingham Chardonnay
Buttered popcorn. Dried mushrooms, pomelo type of fleshy chewy citrus, vanilla underneath, grilled lemons, rich exotic spice, curry leaf. Palate is soft, with mushy white peach, a bit broad, mellow and chalky to finish. Feels as if it was losing its tension and nearing the end of its prime. But a delight as is no less. 93pts

2013 Abercrombie Cabernet Sauvignon
Sweet raspberries and sweet cassis and liquorice. That lingering, haunting raspberry note is tantalising. Dried nori on the palate and the softness, it’s very silky, light on its feet. Pure and elegant. A beauty. Drinks well now but could go for another 10 years. 96pts

2014 Museum Release Riesling
Strong perfume, oil essence, pine needles, thick citrus skin. Fresh chamomile, lime zest and leaves. Very youthful in the first sip and impression. There are hints of dried herbs and lavender, slight umami feel to flavours. The palate is soft but with squeaky acidity, satin texture, energetic. This wine is very much full of life still and many years ahead but it’s in the enjoyment zone now. 94pts

2018 Abercrombie Cabernet Sauvignon
Concentrated, spicy, chewy and pleasantly tart. With pure lifted perfume, aromatic dried peppermint, roses and black pepper. All elegant, cedarwood, cloves with plenty of shapely and approachable tannins. It has youthful charm, with a great promise of longevity but it can be fully enjoyed now. 95pts

Nic Bowen
2019 Jeté Rosé
Oyster shell, ruby grapefruit, crystals of acidity, pink peach sorbet, Bellini. Pure and straightforward, flinty finish, pleasing and joyful. 92pts

2021 Jeté En Pointe Meunier
This is Blanc de Noir style. 2021 was a cool year so Grand Jeté wasn’t made. Only Meunier successfully ripened. It’s a one-off, possibly! Fresh button mushrooms and red apple skins, it’s flinty and truffley. Very good, savoury with cherry blossoms. Racy bubbles, ultra mineral, red-berry tinted wine. I wouldn’t mind if they made more of this in the future. 93pts

2022 Arbor Novae Chenin Blanc
Very soft in flavours, slightly diffused, crushed granite and bitter finish. Glazed apple, honey, easy flow, a bit textural, low key. Feels a bit dialled down in intensity but it’s a pleasant wine. 90pts

2022 Allingham Chardonnay
Lots to pull apart here, flint and herbs and nuts and citrus, very silky mouthfeel with fresh dough finish, lemon curd, grapefruit touch, bit of orange citrus, feels tightly packed, understated and a bit subdued, needs decanting if you drink it now, but it’s a sign of great ageing potential, a bit of fennel and anise mix of freshness, creamy yoghurty finish, coolness and white stonefruit with waxy skins. It’s a mouthful and it’s very good. 94+pts

2022 Abercrombie Cabernet Sauvignon
A good mix of red and black fruit, black cherries and raspberries, and a hint of blue fruit too. It’s a blood-rich mouthfeel, electric almost, lightly salty, with plenty of velvety tannins, elegant oak, all well-measured. Powdery finish. It’s a cool, calm, collected wine with purity of fruit, quality tannins and a great potential to age. Very fresh now! 95+pts

Grenache, Malbec and Mourvedre picked together and fermented together, just as a true field blend should be. But it’s not always the case with this wine. Well, in 2018 it is. Lots of freshness, green peppercorns, red fruit, strawberries, red plums, currants, great iodine palate feel, vibrancy and green coffee beans lift. It has almost an oyster shell type of mineral finish, that kind of salty-steely tension and it lingers. Velvety tannins with licks of mint-milk-choc form the palate. Bright fruit and herbs, spice and earth. Intensity, length and bite to finish, all in place. It feels precise and correct, complex and satisfying, all great stuff, but somehow not finding the X factor besides the sole fact that these are very old vines grown on their very old rootstocks. Not taking away from the skilful winemaking either. Might be out of my purchasing power or will, but I had the privilege to try it. Over to you, dear Reader/Buyer.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: The Story of Stonewell – Celebrating 30 Vintages 1987-2017
Review Text:
The Allan Parson’s Project’s fifth studio album (1980) titled The Turn of a Friendly Card has a stained glass window depicting a King of Diamonds on its cover. The King of Diamonds represents material wealth and treasures. The song, of the same name as the album, is a poetic take on the nature of gambling. As weird as it sounds. Now, what does it have to do with the story of Stonewell, you ask? There was a Queen of Clubs on the Stonewell Shiraz label until 2006, which, when I saw it, made me think of the song. I was puzzled. Why is she there? Turns out, and I couldn’t help but think of this analogy, it symbolised taking a huge risk for Peter Lehmann and Andrew Wigan during the late 70s and early 80s. The Queen of Clubs is a card of change representing new beginnings, transitions, and opportunities. No wonder it was chosen. Designed by Rod Schubert, a Barossan artist and placed on labels as a mark of the gamble taken with a new winery set-up during the tough times for red grapes production in the region. Peter left Saltram in 1979 with a promise given earlier to Barossan wine growers to support their work and to buy out their fruit. “My word is my bond”, he said. Masterson Barossa Vignerons (named after the famous gambler, Sky Masterson) was established in the same year and the surplus of fruit was bought from the winegrowers. From 1982 the wines were sold under Peter Lehmann’s name. It took 7-8 years for Peter, Andrew and the team to make a profit. The friendly card turned eventually with the first vintage of Stonewell Shiraz. The Queen of Clubs is no longer relevant with her symbolism (and not on the label anymore) but perhaps it could have been replaced with the Queen of Diamonds, a representation of success, wealth, and power (just as her king on the Parson’s album cover), which Stonewell undoubtedly became. It was called Show Dry Red in 1987 and in 1990, the 1989 vintage of Peter Lehmann Show Reserve Shiraz won Jimmy Watson’s Trophy. Barrel fermentation began in 1989 and until 1996, all Stonewell was fermented entirely in American oak. In 1996, some experimentation with French oak started and now it represents 100%.

That’s the story of Stonewell as I learnt it. Peter Lehmann Wines remains part of Casella Family Brands since 2014. This year, with the release of 2017 Stonewell Shiraz, I tasted not 30 but 17 selected vintages showcased by the Peter Lehmann Wines team, chief winemaker Nigel Westblade, viticulturist Jade Rogge and national business manager, Malcolm Stopp.

“The game never ends when your whole world depends on the turn of a friendly card”.

1987
The first release, only 13% alcohol, sealed with cork, naturally. 1987 was a wet year and the wine spent 2 years in old American oak. This is the quintessence of matured wine charm. Sweet tones of polished leather, chocolate pralines, dusty roses. Dried peppermint, truffles. Flavours immersed in soft acidity and a thick layer of powdery cinnamon and finely ground white pepper, desiccated cherries and dried blood orange slices. Charming but fading.
88pts

1989
This is the Jimmy Watson’s Trophy winner, 5 growers contributed their grapes to this blend. Fermented and aged in new American oak. It was tasted from a magnum. Such a powerful expression at 34 years of age. Chocolate, caramel and dark fruit, spice and mint, leather, so much lively acidity, dried herbs decoction in concentrated pomegranate juice. Perfume is thick but elegant, toasty with sweet liquorice, dusty brick tannins, old dusty bark wood spice. Impressive.
92pts

1990
Slightly subdued compared to ‘87 and ‘89 with cold smoke, violets and mint too, graphite sensation, elegant nose, river stones, chalky mouthfeel, cool to feel, velvety, smooth.
89pts

1991
Sweet tones, milk chocolate, blood orange tang, a mix of dried herbs, juicy black olive and chewy bitey finish with coffee beans and a quite squeaky aftertaste with a bit of beef stock and cooked mushrooms.
89pts

1994
Coffee, dark chocolate, chewy plums with high tannins and bitter skins, reminds me of ‘90 with its elegant velvety flow and savoury expression. Bits of dried flowers, umami, oyster-shell-like minerality.
90pts

1996
This was the first year with new French oak barrels (25%). Considered a superb vintage, with mild days and cool nights, 14% alcohol. Apparently, it was Peters’s favourite. Such power, bite and chew. Creamy but zingy. High-pitched dried raspberries and spice, long finish with a push, iron fist in a velvet glove. Layers of soft powdery tannins still with so much energy. Probably in a great spot to drink just now.
95pts

1998
Vanilla, burnt creme caramel, dried violets, it’s elegant, calm and with a long line of cold brew coffee, steady flow, dark cherries and plums with mocha finish. There’s a bit of game meat, dead flowers, decaying skin type of aroma lingering. Black tea tannin feel, medium weight.
92pts

1999
Black cherries, vanilla, similar to ‘98, black tea with pomegranate squeeze, gently chewy with good intensity, a mix of herbs, bitter herbs on the palate, amaro, fernet kind of mint and bitter herbs concentration with a deeply hidden, understated raspberry sweetness and salty beef stock.
94pts

2002
Cooler year. Aromatic and fresh from the start. Mint and cherries, beef stock, fennel, cumin, fresh coffee beans. Spicy black pepper palate, blood orange, ironstone line, anise and violets, feels cooler and very savoury, almost silky tannins. Special, distinct expression.
96pts, could do with a few more years, but very good now.

2004
Plums, liquorice, big mouthfeel, huge chew of tannins, juicy tart cherries, acidic finish, talcum powder squeaky hit of tannins. Lots happening in the front palate with more minty cherries pushing forward. Still feels youthful and vibrant. Could do with a bit more time in the bottle.
93pts, drink by 2028.

2006
Vanilla and nutmeg, fresh leather, fruit is dense but in the background, zesty orange peel with the spice of cloves comes forth, allspice, coffee and more orange with over-steeped Earl Grey finish.
94pts, drink by 2030

2008
Black fruit, blackberries and black olives, powerful drying tannins, earth and a bit of sous bois, smoke and reductive tones, dead flowers, sweet core. Tannins cover the mouth but flavours sit high, the electric blood-like iron/salty tension runs on the sides of the tongue. Amazing. 10 more years should be fine, but perhaps best by 2030.
95+pts

2010
Deep opaque colour with brick rim. Spice and vanilla bean, stewed fruit, a bit rustic earthy tones, dark and brooding on the nose and palate, big and gritty. Big bold and rugged, chewy and coarse ground coffee beans and black pepper. Feels a bit forward but has a big bold personality not allowing for any shortcomings.
95pts, 2033+

2012
Thinner than 2010, smoother, meaty, earthy, pomegranate, lifted acidity, soft with medium weight. Tart blackberries and currents, savoury and even austere a bit. Cool, quiet expression with some interesting character. Uneasy.
93pts, drink by 2030

2013
2013 was a challenging year with a short and hot season. Elegant cedar wood, plums and black cherries, a suggestion of truffles developing, vivid energetic palate, chewy and purple to feel, a bit of musk, roses and liquorice. Black tea finish with stewed meat and mushrooms.
92pts, drink by 2033

2016
Violets and cherry blossoms, liquorice, velvety blue plums, vanilla bean. Creamy milk coffee palate, tannins still raw, roughly hewn, yet to settle and polish off the edges. Fresh blackberries and mulberries. Dark choc finish, ultra-powerful and with a good acidic fold. Needs time.
94+pts, 2026-2040

2017
Purple ink, so fresh, plenty of freshly squeezed purple fruit, bloody meat, fresh herbs, sage and thyme, mouthwatering and pungent, fresh black pepper tingling in the back palate, a touch smoother than 2016, in my opinion, and cooler, elegant to feel. Thick in the mouth with gooey-chewy tannins. Time, time, time.
93+pts, 2027-2040

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
I’ve been trained by WSET wine evaluation grid and even though it’s not a perfect way to judge a wine, I find it to be a helpful tool to have at my disposal. I immensely enjoy applying a much more relaxed free form to wine, however. So, for fun, I wrote two versions of a tasting note for this Alsatian Riesling, the WSET style and the free style. Here for your judgement.

WSET: Clear, pale lemon colour. Clean, developing aromas of medium plus intensity, displaying citrus, lime, orange blossom, green and red apples, peaches, honey, candle wax, wet-stone/flint. The wine is dry, acidity is high, alcohol is medium, body is medium, the intensity of flavours is medium plus, the finish is long, flavours of citrus, orange, honey, apples, stonefruit, lemon curd, candle wax, wet-stone/flint. The wine is in balance with the complexity of primary freshness and tertiary development. The quality is very good. Drink now with the potential for ageing.

FREE: Paul Fuchs, Jérôme Mader, and Eric Kientzler are the Drei Manner Wie behind this wine. Dubbed ‘rock-breaker’ or ‘rock-splitter’, from the translation of Felsaspranger which in Alsatian means bone-dry Riesling, and it is. Shrill acidity, lemon and white nectarine granita, textural with crushed rocks and crunchy green apples, red apple skin, minty freshness, lots of zesty citrus, some dried, a hint of green melon, candle wax and honeyed blossoms to round off the aromas. Gentle creaminess, powdery finish. High drinkability, very tasty. Super!

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
‘Tasting is the only tool I have to make better and better wines and I use it every day’ says Japo Dalli Cani, the head winemaker at McHenry Hohnen. Japo, a native of Soave, took over as the chief winemaker after Julian Grounds left for Craggy Range in 2019. He was a part of the team since 2017. Transitions are being made, but rest assured, nothing was lost during that time at McHenry Hohnen. Not a drop of flavour was dropped, perhaps even added. I tasted a selection of back vintages and the new release of single vineyard sites, Calgardup Brook Vineyard, Hazel’s Vineyard, and planted in 1981 only to Chardonnay Burnside Vineyard. And a few others, including Rolling Stone, but for me, Chardonnay was the star of the show. Here is.

Calgardup Brook Vineyard Chardonnay
2014
Green zesty grapefruit, green jasmine tea, grilled salted nuts, hazelnuts and lemon balm creaminess. Chewy acidity with interlaced sweetness of orange blossom, chamomile and long mouthwatering chalky finish. Flavours are spread evenly across the palate, with cloves and allspice. Gentle development is happening but there’s a bit more space to push ahead. However, this just might be the apex and the most complete expression of this wine right now.
95, 2023-2029

2017
Such a different animal to 2014. 2017 was a cooler year. Reductive start, grilled lemons, lemony palate, very linear and focused, minerally, with wet stones and white peaches, lemon curd and bitter touch to finish. The theme here is elegance and restrained, understated aromas, with oatmeal, milky top note. It has a Chablis-esque character going on, one might suggest.
94, 2023-2030

2021
Bold and unsettled (yet), vibrating, with high energy. There are almond biscuits, citrus, white pepper pinch and lime zest on the palate. Nougat, brioche, salty tones with textural nuttiness across the flavours. Finishing very much acidic and bitter with a signature yellow grapefruit tang. It has a bright future ahead.
94+, 2024-2034+

Hazel’s Vineyard Chardonnay
2014
Toast with butter, salt and a squeeze of lemon. Can’t help but think of aged Hunter Semillon aromas. Preserved lemons, grilled citrus… lots and lots of citrus essential oils, a trace of eucalyptus, slippery texture like that melted butter on toast. Bitter grapefruit finish, lingering high, refreshingly. Pure in its nature which makes for a very satisfying and moreish wine. Still plenty of that citrusy freshness to keep it alive for a little longer.
95, 2023-2030

2017
Cool, wet stones, flinty character of aromas. Refreshing as tonic water, lightly sparkly-tingling sensation in texture, lime leaves floating in. Fresh almonds and green apples, fennel note. It displays freshness and lightness, linear focus, lean and crisp texture. Just as its Calgardup Brook Vineyard counterpart in 2017. Pine needle type of freshness. Pretty, no doubt but in this sense feels more delicate and ephemeral and would be best to enjoy this beauty soon.
94, 2023-2027

2021
Vanilla, plenty of chewy-pithy-fleshy citrus. Bold on the reduction side, which is flint dialled up. There are crunchy almond biscuits and very-very zesty and bitter pure citrus essence. Fresh cucumber thread of sweetness comes into play too. Milk powder dust on the nose. Powdery chalky mouthfeel. Concentration is through the roof. It needs time to fuse. But it will fuse into one beautiful thing, no doubt.
95+, 2026-2036+

Burnside Vineyard Chardonnay
2014
Cucumber, pink peppercorn, cedarwood, full impact on the palate. Midpalate weight is composed of yellow peaches with a prevalent umami element, struck match too. My oh my, can you have too much umami? Seaweed, salty-umami combination, sweet-sour with aniseed aftertaste. A beautiful expression of full-bodied, aromatic and chewy, almost meaty Chardonnay. Long penetrating back palate finish. Unique and special right now.
96, 2023-2030

2017
As with other 2017s, this one is more focused and thinner in a way. Sweet scents of vanilla custard but with savoury elements of parsley root. Cool, silky cream and salty on the palate. Giving a sensation of lemon tea, spa water and lemon balm. It’s crisp and clean-cut, faceted with a crystal clear feel to it. Gentle and lithe.
94, 2023-2027

2021
This Burnside starts with a jazzy, cheese-rind aroma, and feels shy and tightly packed. Reductive perhaps. Needs air to open up. It unveils with chamomile, flint, white radish and fennel. Plenty of green citrus and nutmeg, the type of spice that’s not too sweet but more on the savoury end. It’s flowing low with a finish that is cool and minty and oak spice that needs to settle.
94+, 2025-2031

2021 Laterite Hills Chardonnay
Gin Gin from four vineyards: Hazel’s, Burnside, Calgardup Brook and Chapman Brook. Balmy perfume, fresh pineapple skin with green bits in it, peaches and a hint of mango. Even though it feels ripe it has a strong zesty note vibrating through the yellow scents. Jasmine and a fancy soap high-pitched perfume, with a touch of parmesan. The palate is relatively light and with fleshy peaches lingering in the back. Lovely. And very satisfying.
93, 2023-2027

Hazel’s Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon
2017
Savoury start with pretty floral accents, straight-away it smells very elegant. Salty, umami texture, beautifully easy flowing with velvety soft tannins of cocoa powder plush feel, topped with orange rind, graphite tension and dried blood orange type of concentrated acidity. All well-balanced, judiciously measured. A bit of mint and moist dark earth and tobacco complexity, and more umami, really strong nori mouthfeel builds with time.
93, 2023-20237

2015
Only 2 years older, but it feels much more forward in colour and aromas. Pomegranate balsamic tang, 5 spice exotic mix, red brick tannin, spiked with bloody citrus, lots of dried herbs and spice, tart currants, some dried. It has lots of tertiary notes of dried earth and cooked wild mushrooms and smoked paprika. All sort of nice and somewhat generous but it feels slightly unfocused and forward for its time. A glass will suffice.
90, 2023-2025

Rolling Stone
2017
The perfume. Cherry blossom, almond blossom, liquorice, lots of cherries, lots of freshness, velvety roses. Then flavour of dark chocolate sprinkled with chunks of burnt caramel and dried concentrated raspberries. Salty edges. Tannins are very powerful but very fine and soft in their nature. Beautiful concentration and length. All just right and in place.
95, 2023-2033+

2012
This looks like a fully matured wine now, and often it’s a bit of a tricky thing with the judgement, because there are plenty of interesting aromas and flavours, intensity and length, but would I drink the whole bottle? Truffles, dried blood, iron-rich, dried cranberries, such power on the palate, great impact with black pepper and high concentration of cocoa. Ripe black cherries and cassis. Dense and thick and with a certain charm of vinous wine, but might be a tad tiring for the palate. Lots of appeals, no less. I’ll drink a glass and a half.
91, 2023-2025

2021 Hazel’s Vineyard BDX
A touch more Malbec than Cabernet Sauvignon and some Petit Verdot in the blend. Bright, light mix of berries, earthy and leafy but not green. Palate has a bit of a grip and chew, tart red and black fruit skins in the mix, earthy feel with bitter finish. It’s uplifting, medium-bodied wine, crunchy with dark cocoa and salty seaweed feel and smooth tannins. Very pleasing.
93, 2023-2030

2021 Hazel’s Vineyard GSM
Sweet edge, strawberry perfume, roses, spicy peppery heat in the throat. A bit of smoke and sous-bois, lots of grippy textural things floating around. There’s milk chocolate grip in the throat, blood orange and pomegrante twist on top. Feels a bit rugged but overall very good.
92, 2023-2028

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
Solo project from Terroir Sense Fronteres and Terroir al Limit head winemaker, Tatjana Peceric. Serbian-born dancer discovered her passion for wine and moved to Spain, met Dominik Huber and here we are now. Her wines come from the cooler, higher vineyards of Cornudella de Montsant, the DO’s northernmost village and are a homage to tradition and place with minimal intervention. Garnacha Negra, Garnacha Peluda (mutation of Negra producing thicker berries with higher acidity) and Cariñena. Previous releases included ‘Pas de Deux’ on the label, this one didn’t and I believe this is because not two but three grapes were blended this time, so something like ‘Pas de Trois’. It’s actually a ballet term too.

Lots of savoury notes to start, umami, dried meat, then come strawberries and cranberries, dried herbs, and all the other perfumed pretty things. There’s an alluring and intriguing detail of decaying flowers or overripe berries, it may sound extreme but it’s not, think of a fresh button mushroom note with a thread of sweetness. Plentiful of shapely tannins form chalky sensation on the palate with infusion of ruby grapefruit juice. It’s very light on its feet and ethereal. Enticing. Very much, indeed.

Mike wrote a few times about the Brutal!!! ideology in detail bringing back the original story, so I’m just going to reiterate that it’s a collective label indicating hands-off approach to wine and zero SO2. Here, Garnacha and Cariñena vinified for 53 days in all stainless steel. Ingredients: just grapes.

What’s going on??? Explosion, my nose buried in thick perfume, red berries, wet leaves, cloves, spice, root vegetables, green peppercorn. All this abundance of aromas is just a zip on the palate, it’s a glide, it’s a pleasure, green elements, yes, decaying flowers, wet forest, berries. It’s brisk and frisky, light, oh so light. Savoury. Characterful with no false notes, just clean vibrations. Surprisingly gentle, this Brutal.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
By popular demand, I present to you, Jack Mann the great Cabernet.

Densley packed perfume. Sweet dark cherries, plums, dark earth. There’s a lot happening, so I need to break it down and go back a few times. And it’s so intense, hard to separate the flavours. Dare I say this, despite the complexity, the finish doesn’t quite live up to the glory of the flavour intensity built upfront and midway. There’s no question it needs more time to evolve. Still, pretty darn good as is.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
A combination of Egyptian and cerulean shades of blue, with gold, illuminated signs of nature, growth, inspiration and love. Alchemical symbols for the four seasons tucked away in the corners of the esoteric label. It was designed by the artist Tim Winters. Sadly, many may not be very familiar with this distinctive label and the label will be no more soon. Jonathon Mattick shows me the new design. It’s pretty! Elegant, minimalistic and it draws on the previous artistic concept. The old one is too polarising, some love it, some hate it, he mentions. I belong to the former group and quietly ask him to keep it, but have a feeling I’ll lose. Jonathon then takes me on a tour of his recently purchased Canobolas winery in Orange. It was planted in 1986 by Murray Smith. It really is a change of an era when a wine gets a new label (and an owner) after 36 years. The vineyard is dry-grown, close-planted, on rich volcanic soils, terra rossa, at 850m altitude. First vintage was 1989 but only for Chardonnay, then 1991 was in full swing for other varieties, like Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc. Murray stepped away and it wasn’t easy to let go, so I’m told. Years of memories; it’s understandable. Now, Jonathon focuses on organic growing with plans for going biodynamic too. We walk into the untouched cellar door and it’s filled with artifacts, old viticultural books, wine trophies and medals, vintage photographs, paintings… Dusty brick walls, a fireplace and windows overlooking hills with vines. A place with a soul. And they have wine too! Jonathon shares with me some of the Murray-era wines, Shine Chardonnay and Alchemy Bordeaux style blend that won many accolades in the 90s and early 2000s. We also decide on his first blend of Chardonnay, amongst reds and a rose. Let me tell you, some very exciting times coming at Canobolas Wines (new winery name). Watch this space.

Mount Canobolas is an extinct volcano and the name comes from the Wiradjuri tribe which translates into “two shoulders”.

2012 Shine Chardonnay
William Rikard-Bell worked during this time with Murray Smith and it’s safe to say, he made this wine. It smells very appealing, undoubtedly a Chardonnay, filled with citrus skins, hazelnuts, baked pear with cloves, almond meal and hints of marzipan. This may seem overly sweet or rich but it’s not, it’s rather elegant and subtle. There’s a hint of creaminess on the palate but it’s mostly tight and fine, crisp and refreshing still. Lemon curd, silky yoghurt texture in mid-palate that reminds me, along with focused, driving acidity, of 1er cru Chablis. 94, 2023-2030, 13%, $70

2014 Shine Chardonnay
I’m told, this one is probably a bit more influenced by oak (approx. 40% new and toasty), more ripeness and therefore more of a Murray-style winemaking. Indeed, it feels riper and richer than the 2012 Shine with rockmelon and some other underripe tropical fruits. It’s full in body, with a creamy round mouthfeel, heavy exotic spice, like nutmeg, cinnamon, star anise. Weighty mid-palate with yellow grapefruit tang but not bitter, more sour and lifted. Long finish. Even though I do appreciate lighter styles, this has a lot of power and intensity that will develop a little more, I believe. 93+, 2023-2033, 14%, $70

2015 Wild Yeast Chardonnay
In 2015 Shine was not produced, so a slightly different Chardonnay was made under a different label and title. It was a warm year and the fruit came from the whole property as opposed to the Shine blend where parcels and barrels would have been selected. It has lifted florals, almond blossom and honeyed yellow flowers to start. Then ripe citrus, stone fruit too, feels rich and in a way fruit forward, not quite butterscotch but brushing on it and a little phenolic grip, adding interest to the spicy-sour texture. Grilled nuts appear here too. It’s definitely a different expression from Shine. Charming in a way. 92, 2023-2028, 13.5%, $55

1991 Cabernet [sic]
This is most likely 50/50 blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc. Most likely as not much data was recorded by Murry in the past. Starts with violets, roses and cherry blossoms. It surprises with lots of freshness still lingering and lifting the wine. Very fragrant. Then comes milk chocolate praline, allspice and a touch of truffle/fresh leather scents of inevitable development after 32 years. It has red currants, cranberries, licks of dusty tannins and acidity that holds it all together. Tight and taut. Heaps of energy and vibrancy in the fruit, remarkably fresh and vivant. So surprising. Dark chocolate finish. I want to say, it will develop more or can be kept, but it’s a risky game and it drinks beautifully now if you’re lucky to have it in your cellar. 95, cork, 13.1%, 2023-2033

2001 Cabernets [sic]
50/50 blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc. This is a different animal from the 10 years older brother. Dark-fruited, meaty, dense and heavier than the ‘91. Dark cherry and dark blood plum, chocolate and slightly salty liquorice, cocoa powder tannin and finish. Rosemary and basil notes, but nothing green, more dried and savoury. Despite richer, denser perfume, it’s medium-bodied with lingering dark fruit, coffee chocolate and a touch of peppery spice. 93+, 13.5%, 2023-2033

2009 Alchemy
Top of the range red blend, composed of 45% Cabernet Sauvignon, 45% Cabernet Franc and 10% Shiraz. It’s meaty, full in aromas, with plush sweet berries, velvety tannins, coffee beans and leather, earthy elements. Shiraz nuance comes through as sweet herbs and barbecue meat, with peppery spice on the palate. More of the sweet cherry oak, liquorice and ground coffee follow. Mid-palate weight shines. It’s a full-bodied, complete, well-balanced red blend in a great spot now. 94, 14%, 2023-2030

The 2010 Cabernets blend was held in tanks for 8 years, bottled in 2018 and started selling in 2021. I believe it’s available for purchase now at $45.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
H is for Hunter and high energy.

Anyone who participated in the 2022 NSW Wine Show (excluding Hunter winemakers) should know by now the importance of Broke Road in the Valley and the vineyards to its north and south. That evening, after the third whole day of judging, it was made very clear to me that Hunter winemakers are deeply passionate and serious about their history and craft (probably no less than others but it’s about Hunter this time). Holding my breath and my glass of Semillon (what else?) halfway from the table to my lips, I wasn’t able to take a sip until I gained full awareness and acknowledgement of the yet-to-be-drunk aged liquid. Even though at that moment I felt like I was back at school, I actually appreciated it. Sharing this crazy passion. As the Polish microbiologist, Ludwik Hirszfeld, once said, to set others on fire you need to burn yourself first. I caught fire that night.

Therefore, this February, I came back to Hunter for the second time in two months to take part in the Backstage Vintage 2023 experience organised by the Hunter Valley Wine and Tourism Association. Mid-way through their vintage, in between Semillon picks and Shiraz baumé checks, you could feel the omnipresent high energy and the same fiery passion of the Hunter winemakers that I felt that night after a tiring judging day. Here’s a snapshot of the memorable drops from this Hunter visit, they were somewhat served in pairs. I also need to note that deciphering what one writes after the 5th pair of wines is challenging. My tasting skills remained unimpaired till the last drop, however.

2006 Brokenwood ILR Semillon aka ‘I Love Riggsy’
Highly perfumed even when chilled. Enticing, seductive ripe rockmelon and lemon bubble gum/curd. Candle wax and pineapple. Strong perfume keeps on giving, wet slate and dried mango with sage. It grows on me quickly, although feels full and ripe at first. Candle wax blows off and moves onto almond blossoms. Lemon balm. Is it peach? Is it pineapple? Is it mango? All of it. -Oh, hi, Stu, just give me a moment, almost done, thanks.- The wine is firm and fine, mellow and on point. Take what you want and be satisfied. 95pts, 2023-2030

GW: 94+pts, tasted: Nov11, 2013-2026+

2006 Thomas Wines Braemore Cellar Reserve Semillon
In comparison, as it was the goal in a way, this one is a bit more savoury and citrus-driven than ILR ‘06. Big-time dried oregano and dusty lavender. Preserved lemons and spa water. It feels very fresh, tingling bright acidity, pushing for more, charging forward. Screaming ‘I’m not done yet!’. So much freshness to uncover, crushed rocks, flint. Unsure why but waterfall breeze freshness comes to mind, pure, clean line, lifted and light. Simply stunning and still so young. 96pts, 2023-2033+

2016 Margan Ceres Hill Albarino
It comes as a surprise to sample an aged Hunter Albarino, but here we are, the day has come. Andrew Margan reminisces about his Camino de Santiago walk and how he thought of growing Albarino in the Hunter. Savagnin was once mistaken to be Albarino but this is it now. Wow, the freshness! Youthful and vibrant from the get go. This one has lots of peaches and cream, underripe pineapple and almonds, running high with citrus aromas and lime leaf. Sea salt sprinkle. Wow again. Is this really 7 years old, I ask myself. I guess, some Albarino can age. Kudos, Andrew. 94pts, 2023-2028

MB: 87pts, tasted: AUG16, 2016-2019

2013 Tyrrell’s Original Plantings SFOV Chardonnay
Fruit of Short Flat Old Vine. First sniff and I know, we’re in for a treat. Interestingly, it doesn’t feel like it’s overly complex at first, but the intensity of the aromas is of top quality. There are plump yellow peaches and vanilla-bean cream. There’s fennel and minty freshness. That’s sort of it but all is of highest quality and comes together in seamless harmony. Fine wine. Yellow grapefruit aftertaste with purity. Very long finish. This is very very good. I want to say elemental, primal but in the greatest expression of the word. 96pts, 2023-2033

GW: 96pts, tasted: Jun17, 2017-2024+

2009 Brokenwood Graveyard Shiraz (magnum)
O9. OK. Oak. It comes forward, no doubt. When is this oak going to fold, I wonder. So there’s chocolate, coffee and caramel, at first. But then, all of it sits on a layer of thick black fruit and perky acidity. They dance and it works out very well. All integrated and smooth. The wine feels rich and dense, yet graceful in style. Velvety tannins cover the tongue and last, and last. 95pts, 2023-2033+

GW: 96pts, tasted: Jul11, 2019-2035

2009 Thomas Wines The Kiss Shiraz
Ripe cherries and crushed granite. Hypertension. Plenty of leafy elements and a bit of rustic feel but vibrant, with sage and game meat. Amaro and bitter herbs. It’s spicy and juicy. Lots of pepper, crushed green peppercorns on the palate and very lively acidity. I like the not-too-sweet character of this wine. 95pts, 2023-20230

GW: 94pts, tasted: Jan11, 2013-2020+

2007 Tyrrell’s Old Patch Shiraz
Cherry oak. Charred meat, spice and a thick cherry glaze but it’s cleansed by aromatic, smoky, bitter orange zest. It has stewed aromas of cooked game meat with rosemary and orange. Crisp and tight but also mellow. Fine. One of those tricks of aged wines, to do the opposite at the same time and quite well too. In a really sweet spot now. And yes, Gary, the Old Patch has delivered after 15+ years. 96pts, 2023-2033

GW: 94+pts, tasted: Jun08, 2016-2027+

2007 Margan Shiraz Mourvedre
Sweet aromatics of red and black berries and chocolaterie. Coffee beans, mocha, dark chocolate, kirsch, compote cherry, dark plum in rum, raspberries and sweet basil. Soft and herbal, mellow and a riper style with truffles and rum bon-bons that feels fully developed and great right now. Indulge yourself. 93pts, 2023-2028

GW: 91pts, tasted: Nov08, 2010-2017

1987 Tyrrell’s Futures Semillon
Now, this is a rarity. Developed golden colour. Aromas are tertiary and oh so delicious. Dried pineapple, dried sage and a baked cheesecake creamy quality. With a hint of vanilla, baked apple pie. Smooth ricotta texture on melting butter toast. Squeeze of lemon. There’s something dusty in it too, tobacco ash perhaps. Drinks well, smooth, acidity is driving it no doubt but it’s all tertiary and ready to go down your throat. 94pts, drink now

1987 Mount Pleasant Rosehill Shiraz
Dig this. Today I met Phil Ryan while visiting MP winery. We shook hands, he asked me about my accent, I asked where he lives… Then I’m drinking his ‘87 Rosehill Shiraz at dinner. Can you feel the energy? Spiritual almost experience. Present meets past and it’s all captured in this 750ml bottle. Got a bit emotional here, forgive me. I’m sure you all have had experiences like the one I had. Onto wine.

Dried cherries, red apple skins and dried meat. Pomegranate reduction. Crisp and crunchy acidity and fine tannin dance. Hazelnuts in skins. Red brick dust texture builds up in the back palate. Vibrant acidity throughout. It drinks more like a Pinot than a Shiraz. 94pts, drink now

1985 Tyrrell’s Vat 6 Pinot Noir
Pinot Noir from the Hunter from the 80s. There are many things that could have gone wrong here. But it’s the opposite. The perfume of this wine is unreal. Potpourri, dried violets, dried cherries and red apple skins. It has the power of Syrah in the intensity of aromas. Polished leather, cooked spices, stewed meat. Vivacious, energetic and so beautifully expressive. Ethereal perfume. Light on its feet. Aged so gracefully and still doesn’t feel tired but definitely the best time to drink it. It’s liquid poetry. 97pts, drink now

1985 Mount Pleasant Philip Shiraz
All tertiary, dusty oak tannins, potpourri. It’s light as Pinot, more than Shiraz, lots of fruit faded but there are still hints of sweet dried cherries and raspberries. It’s probably past its best but you can’t be mad, just vinous, energy slowly leaving and you just get to appreciate it for the snapshot of bottled history that once was. 92pts, drink now

Two bottles of 1998 Brokenwood Graveyard Shiraz were sadly corked.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Wine / Article: Mount Pleasant Museum Release Showcase Dinner
Review Text:
I missed out on the previous Mount Pleasant event, so caught up with the Museum Release at Bentley Restaurant. I have to admit, it’s not an easy task reviewing wines of such gravitas, it’s quite daunting. Let alone realizing they’ve been tasted, commented and studied in-depth by Campbell et al.. Not to mention the importance of the people who created them throughout the years. Well, let’s give it a go.

2017 Lovedale Semillon
There’s something very definitive about this wine, it penetrates your nostrils with confidence. Lemon balm, lavender, candle wax perfume and melting texture. It’s pure-pure, fine and doesn’t need hundreds of descriptors. Self-sufficient type. Teasingly suggesting and promising tertiary development with ultimate youthful, impish charm at the same time. Can be easily enjoyed now but it will keep for about forever and pleasure you along the way whenever you decide to open a bottle.
96+ points, 2022 – 2037+

GW: 92 points, tasted: Aug22, 2022 – 2029+

2014 Lovedale Semillon
Fresh as a daisy. Plenty of fleshy citrus but also whipped butter on toast. Jasmine and lemon blossom too. It hits top and bottom of the palate evenly. Flowery perfume and citrus pulp with almonds. The middle is filled with crushed rocks, slate. In a good spot now, but it will have many more sweet spots to come.
95+ points, 2022 – 2037+

GW: 95+ points, tasted: Jun14, 2024 – 2040

2005 Lovedale Semillon
(it wasn’t a part of this tasting but I wanted to add it here as tasted recently too)
Gold with distinct green reflections. Brine lemons, biting into and chewing on citrus skin, fresh sage leaves. Waxy texture with a generous dose of yellow grapefruit, green mango and parmesan rind. Butter toast crunch flavours, melting with cotton cushiness and tension all at once. Mint-lime and slate finish. Long and firm. Does the magic trick. On me. In a very satisfying spot at 17 years of age, stepping into adulthood.
95 points, 2022 – 2030

GW: 93 points, tasted: Jul11, 2011 – 2014+

1998 Lovedale Semillon
Amber in colour. A wine at 24 years of age hits different spots than a young wine. It strikes different chords. Toffee apples, marzipan and caramel nuts. Ripe quince, lots of dried citrus. It hits the tertiary territory with full potence. That being said, it’s not tired or falling apart, still has a bright spark. Dusty juice, oversteeped green-lemon tea with dried herbs and lavender.
95 points, drink now

CM: 95 points, tasted: Jan05, 2006 – 2013

1984 Elizabeth Semillon
Concentrated nose, nuttiness and umami tones. From under the flor elements, mushrooms, plush acid. It sits in the amontillado zone of aromatics. Yeasty and bruised, burnt orange peel nuance, but flavours still keep the vibrant flintiness going. Cool, fluffy and light like fairy floss. This is a different animal. It won’t go any further but it’s a treat. I think this wine may be very much a personal preference at this age but it’s kindred to some dry sherries and I love that so much.
95 points, drink now

CM: 87 points, tasted: Oct02, drink till – 2004

2014 Rosehill 1965 Vines Shiraz
25% new oak, I’ve been told. Toast and biscuits surface the wine at first sniff. Looking for the fruit et al., and I find concentrated cherries, raspberries, violets and liquorice. It rewards in the mouth with a surprising lightness of being. Layers of ground coffee, cloves and star anise. Palate redeems the nose more, it’s very fine-grained and refreshing in a way. Pumice tannins, all soaked in herb spice stew. Powerful and elegant. It evolves and opens up with time in glass. So much to unveil. Travels into potpourri, wet earth, dried leaves, the list goes on… impressive haunting perfume.
97+ points, 2025 – 2045+

CM: 98 points, tasted: Oct15, 2025 – 2055+
GW: 97+, tasted: Oct15, will go 50 years

2011 Mountain D Dry Red
Spicy oak showing layers of cloves, nutmeg and charred wood. Acidity keeps it vibrant. Game meat as a savoury element, then fresh leather, cherry glaze richness and abundance of oak aromas. The perfume is seductive and sweet. Dusty spice mouthful of tannins with tart savoury cranberries acidity to finish. Will this settle more? Perhaps.
93 points, 2023 – 2033+

CM: 92 points, tasted: Apr15, 2019 – 2034+

1987 Rosehill Hermitage
Dried cherry, cranberry, marzipan, nougat, lots of luscious oak. Palate is still fairly vibrant, with filigree texture, pinot-like tannins, so light. Walnuts and peat, dried leaves and moss. Old polished leather, decomposing wood, truffles. Drinks softly but it’s all tertiary with dried coffee beans, rum and dark chocolate bonbon. It has a charm of a developed wine, no doubt.
94 points, drink now
—

2014 Old Hill 1880 Vines Shiraz
Coffee, milk chocolate pralines. Undeniable concentration and mouthcoating flavours go forever with spicy power. Layers of intense red and black berries. Dark earth, herbs, spice, perfume. Big bursts of flavour. It’s extracted but also graceful. This wine just is. Lots happening but there’s certain calmness in this abundance of aromas and flavours. Harmony. It needs more time to be tamed. A beautiful beast.
96+ points, 2024 – 2040+

CM: 95 points, tasted: Dec15, 2020 – 2040+

2000 Maurice O’Shea Shiraz
This wine defines the ultimate density of colour, fruit and flavour. Cherry, nutmeg, anise mix. Sage, basil, cool citrus peel, dark earth, hazelnuts. The palate feels like a counterbalance, being delicate and lifted, but compliments it too. It’s a relationship, lovers and partners and best friends at once. Push and pull. Fullness. Then comes savoury-sweet soy sauce, cherry reduction. There’s so much future in this wine. Lots of oak, no doubt, but fruit intensity is remarkable and handles it well, plus the long length. It has all it needs to keep on going.
95+ points, 2022 – 2032+

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
I visited Tumbarumba recently, it was a short trip but an intense one and I feel it showcased the region generously along with its still unlocked potential.

Stepping strong into chardonnay territory, below, I comment on a blind lineup tasted to benchmark Tumbarumba wines. Hope the chardonnay master won’t mind. Nudge-nudge, wink-wink. Does she like chardonnay? I bet she does, I bet she does… say no more.

McWilliam’s 842 Chardonnay 2013 Tumbarumba
First wine can be tricky to taste but I already like it. It invites with lemon curd, soft fluffy dairy aromas. Almond blossom. Creamy in the mouth too. I want to say, it feels like a classic chardonnay, with peach ricotta cake and nuts. It’s cool, lots of citrus, clean and crips palate with cucumber water sweetness. Orange zest says hello too. A bit more oak chimes in later, it emerges slowly from under the fruit but all is smooth. Elegantly handled. Knowing (later) this is now almost 10 years old, I’d say it’s in perfect shape but could go for more if you’d like to push some of the fresh citrus into the dried and tertiary territory.
95 points, drink now but by 2030

Courabyra 805 Chardonnay 2016 Tumbarumba
Savoury nose and palate. Stewed mushrooms and sour cream sauce, a bit of reduction, yeasty aromas, butter popcorn. Quite a sour palate with ripe citrus and stonefruit. Tinned pineapple and a salty steely feel in the aftertaste. I sense it’s not the best showing here, unfortunately. Has some umami character that can be liked. Edgy.
87 points, drink now

Collector Tiger Tiger Chardonnay 2018 Tumbarumba
Flint, crunchy nectarines, intense mid-palate core, juicy with orange peel finish. Oatmeal and lavender. Feels very elegant and toned. There’s also vanilla curd but just a touch, not overt, gentle soft palate with a grapefruit pith bite towards the end. Well-measured and composed. Cashew-creamy-salty finish. Feels like true cool climate wine. Right on.
94 points, 2022-2030

Hungerford Hill Chardonnay 2018 Tumbarumba
Jasmine and peach, yellow apples, a bit of lavender and hessian/chamomile grip. Plenty of flavour, citrus zest, it’s aromatic in the mouth. Dried herbs and a long finish with a bit of lemon curd. Nuts in shells. Almond meal, milky finish. Real tasty.
93 points, 2022-2030

Mada Chardonnay 2019 Tumbarumba
Steely at first but then an abundance of cashews, peaches and wet stones. Interesting, it’s minerally and fruity at once. Almond blossom, creamy palate with plenty of grapefruit chew finish. Apples, pears, racy acidity line. Dead on delicious, sucks you right in.
94 points, 2022-2030

Nick O’Leary Chardonnay 2019 Tumbarumba
Toast and struck match come first. Hazelnuts, cream, flinty palate with a generous spread of flavours. Feels like an elegant oak but ample, ripe yellow apples, quince, citrus. Feels ripe and a bit broad with flavour travelling comfortably across the palate. Riper, bolder, richer style. Quite enjoyable, nevertheless.
91 points, 2022-2028

Wondalma Chardonnay 2021 Tumbarumba
Sour lemons, flint, grapefruit. Steely and racy, with jasmine flowers. Lemongrass perfume and watercolour flavours, slightly loose-knit but really pretty and lifted. Delicate with wet stones, minerally. A Chardonnay of lightness and grace.
89 points, 2022-2025

Mount Tumbarumba Vineyards On The Fly Chardonnay 2021 Tumbarumba
Peaches and hazelnuts, mid-palate fruit weight is very decent, brown pears, a mix of orchard fruits. It feels fruity, with a bit of edgy flintiness and good flavour intensity. Finishes slightly honeyed and then salty, which is nice. Not quite flowing smoothly as I wish it would but overall a scrumptious drop.
89 points, 2022-2025

Benjamin Leroux Bourgogne Blanc 2020
Toast, hazelnuts, mushrooms, very minerally palate with a touch of waxy/oily texture. Driving the flavours long with a ripe but solid acid line, crushed rocks and a bitter tang. There’s a noticeable savoury or tertiary element, almond meal and more biscuits. Overall, it has excellent bolder elegance and calmness throughout the wine executed with confidence.
93 points, 2022-2027

Hoddles Creek 1er Yarra Valley Chardonnay 2021
Richly perfumed bouquet, with green mango and zesty lime. Palate punches with flavour, elegant oak, peaches, apples and grapefruit or bitter orange. Distinct oyster shell finish with the intensity of fruit weight at large. Forward, bold but zesty style. Delicious.
95 points, 2023-2033

Kumeu River Mate’s Vineyard Chardonnay 2021 Auckland
Light and floral, flinty, brisk, lemon blossom, lemon balm. Chewy flavours with heaps of grapefruit. There’s a savoury element of cheesecloth here. Appetising. Great texture, that kind of complexity that’s not excessive but elegant and well-measured, rather. Less is more philosophy. All is composed together effortlessly and with excellent flavour and length. Great finesse.
96 points, 2023-2033+

Tolpuddle Chardonnay 2021 Tasmania
Huge reductive nose, preserved lemons, grilled nuts, creme caramel. Lots of fancy oak. Burnt popcorn a bit and lots of sour acidity. But plenty of flavour, no doubt. Limey acid takes over the expression of other flavours. Feels a bit overworked, trying hard, but with ripe and concentrated fruit underneath. Milk powder dust. Power in your face. This may come together better with time.
92+ points, 2024-2034+

Penfolds 311 Chardonnay 2012 (not blind)
Lemon butter toast. Ripe grilled peaches, condensed milk nose and then zesty grapefruit skin. There’s a calm sweetness to it but then a really crisp palate makes a final call. Touch of phenolic grip and salty fold. Fine and really beautiful, pretty. Fennel aniseed freshness throughout. But not shy. I think this may have 10 more years ahead, it will keep well. But drinks beautifully now.
94 points, 2022-2032

Penfolds Yattarna Chardonnay 2019 (not blind)
Very complex nose, hazelnuts, peaches and cream, butter pastry, tightly packed lots of flavours and detail. Layered. Milk powder and a touch of pineapple, flint and sage bitterness and freshness. Palate follows the nose in the same harmonious fashion. Creamy and salty and nutty, with cinnamon spice. All is loud and proud but rightly so. All the flavours are bound together by a chalky-raw phenolic grip. Stunning.
96+ points, 2024-2034

To sum up, in one sentence, Tumbarumba punches above its weight.

Author: Kasia Sobiesiak
Review Text:
From one of amber wine whisperers, Marjan Simčič of Goriška Brda in Slovenia, right at the very border of Friuli-Venezia Giulia in Italy. This is a mid-tier of Marjan’s collection, only the best vintages bear the label Cru Selection, but there is one more, top level. Here, 55-59 year old Rebula vines fruit grapes that ferment on their skins for 8 days in 4,000-litre conical oak barrels with ambient yeast. Softly pressed and patiently matured for 18 months on lees. Finally, the wine spends at least 4 months in bottle before release.

This orange-style wine is slowly getting into golden colour with the haunting citrus rind and beeswax perfume. Followed by ripe yellow apples, Beurre Bosc pears, quince and Mirabelle plums with mouthwatering chalky tannins. Nuances of blossoms, dry hay and toast can be found too. It’s all about texture and layers of flavours, from mineral base through fleshy crunchy middle and aromatic skinsy scents on top. Molto delizioso. Or should I say: zelo okusno vino.

Review Text:
This was a mini vertical tasting of St Henri at the WLOTY 2022 presented by Penfolds winemaker, Shavaughn Wells. There were 20 people in the room and only two women, Shavaughn and myself. And it felt empowering amongst big flavours and high tannins. Even the wine is a he—St Henri! Or is it…?

From Penfolds website:
The first vintage of St Henri – then Auldana Cellars St Henri Claret – was produced in 1888, beginning one of the most famous and enduring names in Australian wine. It was likely named after Auldana’s winemaker Léon Edmond Mazure’s son Henri or his wife, Philomine Henriette.

What a beautiful piece of history and a beautiful wine.

1991
A stellar vintage in South Australia, here with 10% of cabernet sauvignon
Colour is still pretty vivid, translucent with orange rim. Dense perfume of highly polished leather interlaced with dark concentrated cherry juice. Velvety flavours are thick with cooked spice and stewed meat, cracked black pepper, vanilla bean and liquorice mixed and merged well, dried rose petals. Beautiful. Stepping strong into tertiary territory but with vigour and great energy. Delicious. 96, drink now
